instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.
OPEN THREADS: eleven exemptions (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a weekly habit, then a pattern in a report; brother's score (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a threshold, a warning letter, a deadline; evasion group (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a meeting, then a distributed method; update history (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): nightly shifts, then a readable archive.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rosa grants a first unwarranted exemption, discovers how easy it is, and starts a weekly pattern she tells herself is mercy | The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail | Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other
ENDING: She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the score actually measures; Rosa's pattern will be discovered; the exemption budget will run out.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.
You want your novel's scenes to carry more than one kind of weight, and the method of fusing duties is undecided.
Establish the method for designing multi-duty scenes: how plot, character, world, and information work are fused into single events.
You are planning a novel.
Work the problem at the level of architecture, so drafting stands on decisions rather than habits.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime. Rosa grants a first unwarranted exemption, discovers how easy it is, and starts a weekly pattern she tells herself is mercy. The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail. Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other. She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Plan each scene's duties before its events, then invert: search for the single event that would produce all the assigned effects as consequences of one another. The search usually fails twice before it succeeds, and the failures, a scene doing plot and character side by side, are where the extra work gets spent. Hold out for the intersection.

Rank the duties by what happens if each is dropped. The duty whose loss damages the book's spine is primary; the rest are payload, and payload duties must attach to the primary's event so tightly that cutting them would damage the primary's staging. This ranking is what keeps multi-duty scenes coherent under the pressure of drafting.

Use the conflict between duties as the scene's engine. When the plot duty and the relationship duty demand different outcomes from the same event, the scene generates its own drama: the character cannot serve both, and the choice between them is the scene's turn. Design duty conflicts into at least the major scenes, and the loading will never feel mechanical.

Verify the fusion at the sentence level while drafting. Multi-duty scenes fail when the duties take turns: a paragraph of plot, a paragraph of character. The test is whether the scene's key beats carry two registers simultaneously, the line that is both a threat and a confession, the object that is both a clue and a wound. Revise any beat that serves only one master.

Scene density is the ratio of consequence to page count. The dense scene fuses duties into single events; the thin scene performs one obligation and leaves the rest of its length unspent.

Keep the character's interpretation of events consistent with their personality, their history, and their mood, not with the author's understanding of what is happening. The same event seen by two people should arrive differently structured: different order of attention, different assumptions, different thing at the center of the frame.

When intensity rises, physical grounding should rise with it. The character should still be in contact with the room, still feel the chair, the strap, the cold, the weight in a pocket. Grounding is not decoration; it is what makes extreme situations legible and keeps the scene from floating into abstraction.

Commit to fused construction: no duty delivered in isolation, no beat serving one register. Plan the coming scenes as intersections, and let the book's density be structural rather than accreted.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.
THREE-ACT ARC: Sessions establish terms; Jun alters one position to prevent a stalemate; the visitors confirm it back exactly, which tells the delegation nothing | The alteration costs the delegation its mining leverage; Sabel's recordings surface; Ollun demonstrates knowledge of the delegation's private arguments | The window closes with an unsigned treaty; Jun must either admit the manipulation publicly or deliver an exchange built on it
ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.
You are planning a novel at the level of its scenes, and the definition of what a scene is for is still open.
Establish the scene as your story's unit of change: what each scene must alter, and how the alterations chain into the book's motion.
You are planning a novel.
Think it through as planning: what must be true, in what order, and why.
response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Sessions establish terms; Jun alters one position to prevent a stalemate; the visitors confirm it back exactly, which tells the delegation nothing. The alteration costs the delegation its mining leverage; Sabel's recordings surface; Ollun demonstrates knowledge of the delegation's private arguments. The window closes with an unsigned treaty; Jun must either admit the manipulation publicly or deliver an exchange built on it. She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Plan the book as a chain of irreversible deltas. Each scene delivers one or two changes to the story's state, and the next scene inherits the changed state as its ground. Before drafting, decide the size of the unit's delta: a scene that changes everything is a climax, a scene that changes nothing is a pause, and the book's pace is the distribution between them.

Define the change types your scenes will draw on, and keep the list short: knowledge, position, relationship, intention, capability. Every scene shifts at least one, and the type should vary across consecutive scenes, because three knowledge scenes in a row thin the story even when each is individually strong. Plan the type sequence for each stretch as deliberately as the events.

Make the changes legible at their scene's end without narration summarizing them. The reader should feel the delta in the situation's altered pressure: the door that closed, the name that can no longer be spoken, the plan that now requires a different skill. If a scene's change needs a sentence of explanation to register, the change was staged too abstractly.

Connect the deltas causally, not just sequentially. The change one scene delivers should be the ground the next scene stands on: the knowledge gained is used, the position lost is mourned and compensated, the decision made is implemented. A chain of unrelated deltas is a string of incidents; a causal chain is a plot.

Enter late, leave early, and let the margins go. The scene's power concentrates at its point of attack and its turn, and everything else is either instrument or overhead.

Internal thought should be short, partial, and interruptible, working the way thought works when a person is also doing something. Long passages of abstract reflection belong to the planning stage, not to the page; on the page, decision pressure and physical circumstance should keep breaking the reflection into fragments that carry information.

Prefer the incidental specific to the atmosphere word. Generic atmosphere is interchangeable between scenes and therefore carries no information, while an incidental particular, chosen well, implies place, class, history, and mood at once. Let the details that exist for their own sake do the atmospheric work.

Adopt the unit standard: every scene alters at least one of the five state types, irreversibly where it matters, and inherits the altered state from its predecessor. Draft from the standard, and the book will move by construction.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.
OPEN THREADS: moved stones (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): survey discrepancy, then proof, then a deliberate trap; Sera's raider dealings (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): supply ledgers, a survivor's testimony; brother's death (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): rumor, then the ward-fire's old scar; the offer behind the ward (opens chapter 6, pays off chapter 10): voices at the turning, then terms.
THREE-ACT ARC: Maren and Torell meet at the stones, each prepared to withdraw, and both are prevented by a third event: the ward fails early and something gets through | Forced to work together to reseat the stones, each betrays the arrangement in ways the other detects and misreads; the border settlements become the currency | The thing behind the ward offers each heir exactly what they want in exchange for the covenant broken; both nearly accept, and the resolution is a choice neither wanted
ENDING: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning the novel described above, and the question below concerns the book's architecture rather than one scene.
You are deciding how much change each unit of your narrative must carry and how the units connect.
Establish the scene as your story's unit of change: what each scene must alter, and how the alterations chain into the book's motion.
You are architecting a novel before drafting begins.
Reason through the interactions at stake and end with the rules you will follow.
response:
The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power. The movements the book has to pay for: Maren and Torell meet at the stones, each prepared to withdraw, and both are prevented by a third event: the ward fails early and something gets through. Forced to work together to reseat the stones, each betrays the arrangement in ways the other detects and misreads; the border settlements become the currency. The thing behind the ward offers each heir exactly what they want in exchange for the covenant broken; both nearly accept, and the resolution is a choice neither wanted. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

A scene is a machine for changing one thing that cannot be unchanged: a fact learned, a position lost, a decision made, a bond broken. Hold your scenes to that standard from the start, and the book's motion is guaranteed by its construction; release the standard, and no amount of eventful incident will make the story move.

Make the changes legible at their scene's end without narration summarizing them. The reader should feel the delta in the situation's altered pressure: the door that closed, the name that can no longer be spoken, the plan that now requires a different skill. If a scene's change needs a sentence of explanation to register, the change was staged too abstractly.

Connect the deltas causally, not just sequentially. The change one scene delivers should be the ground the next scene stands on: the knowledge gained is used, the position lost is mourned and compensated, the decision made is implemented. A chain of unrelated deltas is a string of incidents; a causal chain is a plot.

Budget the irreversible against the reversible. Most scene-level changes can theoretically be undone, and a story that undoes them freely teaches the reader that nothing is at stake. Decide which changes across the book are permanent, mark them as the story's real spine, and treat every other change as negotiation around those fixed points.

The reader experiences structure as rhythm: real-time against summary, beat against break, density against breath. Make the rhythm deliberate at every scale, and the book will feel designed without ever seeming managed.

When intensity rises, physical grounding should rise with it. The character should still be in contact with the room, still feel the chair, the strap, the cold, the weight in a pocket. Grounding is not decoration; it is what makes extreme situations legible and keeps the scene from floating into abstraction.

Even at the story's largest moments, keep smaller and irrelevant concerns alive in the character's mind. Petty resentment, a physical discomfort, a task left unfinished: these coexist with catastrophe and are a primary source of the sense that a person, not a narrative function, is present.

Fix the delta budget: which changes are permanent, how the types rotate, and how each delta seeds the next. Write the scenes as links in that chain, and the story's motion will be structural rather than habitual.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's sea wall work is funded by a levy charged to properties above the high-water line; The couple's house is below the line and cannot be repaired after a flood without a licensed surveyor; The harbour's fishing fleet is co-owned in shares that must be sold to existing holders.
CAST IN PLAY: Aidan, harbour master, the husband: wants the house repaired and the marriage continued without discussion; flaw, he maintains things instead of understanding them; secret, he has been quietly selling his fleet shares to cover the flood damage; knows, the sea wall's true schedule | Bryn, surveyor, the wife: wants the marriage assessed honestly before the season ends; flaw, she mistakes accuracy for kindness; secret, she has accepted a post in another county and not told him; knows, the house cannot be sold or insured in its current state | Ondine, Bryn's colleague and client: wants the sea wall built before spring; flaw, she values the town's survival over its people's arrangements; secret, her survey supports using the couple's property line as the wall's footing; knows, the levy's distribution.
OPEN THREADS: flood damage (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): water in the floor, then a condemned structure; share sales (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a ledger of shares, then an empty holding; job offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a letter, a date, a county; wall footing (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a survey line through the back garden.
THREE-ACT ARC: A flood damages the house; the two spouses disagree about repair, sale, and what the damage means | The wall survey, the share sales, and the job offer surface in the wrong order, and each spouse reads the other's decision as betrayal | The final storm decides the house, and the choice is between a marriage held together by property and two separate lives that are both viable
ENDING: The house is condemned and demolished for the wall footing, the fleet shares are gone, and the two of them separate with the paperwork clean and no reconciliation scene.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the sea wall will be built or abandoned; the house will be decided by the season; one of them will say the decisive thing out loud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year | The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route | Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day
ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately; the bond will be resolved, bought or broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.
CAST IN PLAY: Mistress Ode, master printer: wants the house and its apprentices through the crisis; flaw, she takes on obligations to avoid choosing; secret, she has accepted all three commissions; knows, the paper allocation's real controller | Hal, senior pressman: wants the sheets set in the order that keeps people alive; flaw, he believes he can judge consequences from the shop floor; secret, he has been passing proofs to the organizers; knows, which document is a forgery | Young Cass, apprentice: wants to be trusted with a real task; flaw, she reads everything she sets; secret, she has told a friend what one commission says; knows, all three commissions exist.
OPEN THREADS: three commissions (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a levy notice, a denunciation, a committee's address; forgery (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a signature on a document nobody in the shop wrote; leaked proofs (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a friend, a copied page; warrant timetable (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): three days, one magistrate.
THREE-ACT ARC: Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority | One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock | The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first
ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.
PROMISES TO THE READER: all three documents will be printed or refused; the house's mark will be used against it; the apprentice's leak will reach the street.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority. One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock. The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first. instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.

The multi-duty scene is not a scene doing several things in sequence but one event whose consequences radiate through several registers at once: the confrontation that advances the plot, exposes the character, and plants the information in the same motion. The design method is to find the event where the duties naturally intersect, rather than bolting duties onto an occasion.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A ward holds only while its maker is alive and named in its grain; Thornwood cannot be cut by anyone who has not been formally released from apprenticeship; A failed ward does not fall; it turns, and it takes its maker's mark with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Tess, apprentice, the narrator: wants to be released and named; flaw, she revises the past as she tells it; secret, she has been making wards that turn; knows, the master's hands no longer work | Master Orr, wardwright, last of the guild: wants the workshop left to someone; flaw, he teaches by withholding and calls it testing; secret, he has been using Tess's hands for a year while signing the work himself; knows, the turning wards will come home | Pell, forest warden, outside the guild: wants the wards maintained by any means; flaw, he trusts systems more than people; secret, he has been reporting the turning wards to the forest villages; knows, which wards failed first.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see a ward turn; Tess will either be named or not be named; the workshop will close or continue, not both.

Before drafting, decide the size of the unit's delta: a scene that changes everything is a climax, a scene that changes nothing is a pause, and the book's pace is the distribution between them.

The reader should feel the delta in the situation's altered pressure: the door that closed, the name that can no longer be spoken, the plan that now requires a different skill. If a scene's change needs a sentence of explanation to register, the change was staged too abstractly.

The change one scene delivers should be the ground the next scene stands on: the knowledge gained is used, the position lost is mourned and compensated, the decision made is implemented. A chain of unrelated deltas is a string of incidents; a causal chain is a plot.

Budget the irreversible against the reversible. Most scene-level changes can theoretically be undone, and a story that undoes them freely teaches the reader that nothing is at stake. Decide which changes across the book are permanent, mark them as the story's real spine, and treat every other change as negotiation around those fixed points.

A scene exists to change something that cannot be unchanged. Every other virtue, atmosphere, wit, beauty, is welcome, but the change is the reason the scene occupies the reader's time.

Choose the entry and exit points by dramatic usefulness rather than chronology. Entering after the introductions and leaving before the tidying keep the scene's work at the center; the material on either side can be implied by how the characters behave once the scene has begun.

Only include what the viewpoint can actually perceive or infer from what they have perceived. TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.

response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next. Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year. The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route. Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day. She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

A scene is a machine for changing one thing that cannot be unchanged: a fact learned, a position lost, a decision made, a bond broken. Hold your scenes to that standard from the start, and the book's motion is guaranteed by its construction; release the standard, and no amount of eventful incident will make the story move.

Define the change types your scenes will draw on, and keep the list short: knowledge, position, relationship, intention, capability. Every scene shifts at least one, and the type should vary across consecutive scenes, because three knowledge scenes in a row thin the story even when each is individually strong. Plan the type sequence for each stretch as deliberately as the events.

Connect the deltas causally, not just sequentially. The change one scene delivers should be the ground the next scene stands on: the knowledge gained is used, the position lost is mourned and compensated, the decision made is implemented. A chain of unrelated deltas is a string of incidents; a causal chain is a plot.

Budget the irreversible against the reversible. Most scene-level changes can theoretically be undone, and a story that undoes them freely teaches the reader that nothing is at stake. Decide which changes across the book are permanent, mark them as the story's real spine, and treat every other change as negotiation around those fixed points.

A scene exists to change something that cannot be unchanged. Every other virtue, atmosphere, wit, beauty, is welcome, but the change is the reason the scene occupies the reader's time.

Choose the entry and exit points by dramatic usefulness rather than chronology. Entering after the introductions and leaving before the tidying keep the scene's work at the center; the material on either side can be implied by how the characters behave once the scene has begun.

Prefer the incidental specific to the atmosphere word. Generic atmosphere is interchangeable between scenes and therefore carries no information, while an incidental particular, chosen well, implies place, class, history, and mood at once. Let the details that exist for their own sake do the atmospheric work.

Fix the delta budget: which changes are permanent, how the types rotate, and how each delta seeds the next. Write the scenes as links in that chain, and the story's motion will be structural rather than habitual.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.
You are planning a dense book, and the design of multi-purpose scenes is the central craft question.
Establish the method for designing multi-duty scenes: how plot, character, world, and information work are fused into single events.
You are mapping out a novel you are about to write.
Set the load-bearing decisions down in full, so the draft has something solid to stand on.
response:
The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying. The movements the book has to pay for: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient. The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating. The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Plan each scene's duties before its events, then invert: search for the single event that would produce all the assigned effects as consequences of one another. The search usually fails twice before it succeeds, and the failures, a scene doing plot and character side by side, are where the extra work gets spent. Hold out for the intersection.

Rank the duties by what happens if each is dropped. The duty whose loss damages the book's spine is primary; the rest are payload, and payload duties must attach to the primary's event so tightly that cutting them would damage the primary's staging. This ranking is what keeps multi-duty scenes coherent under the pressure of drafting.

Use the conflict between duties as the scene's engine. When the plot duty and the relationship duty demand different outcomes from the same event, the scene generates its own drama: the character cannot serve both, and the choice between them is the scene's turn. Design duty conflicts into at least the major scenes, and the loading will never feel mechanical.

Distribute the load across the cast. A scene carries more duties legitimately when its several participants bring their own agendas into the event: the visitor who needs a favor advances the plot by asking, exposes character by how they ask, and plants the information by what they noticed on the way. Orchestrate the participants as carriers, and the scene's density will be social rather than authorial.

Scene density is the ratio of consequence to page count. The dense scene fuses duties into single events; the thin scene performs one obligation and leaves the rest of its length unspent.

Prefer the incidental specific to the atmosphere word. Generic atmosphere is interchangeable between scenes and therefore carries no information, while an incidental particular, chosen well, implies place, class, history, and mood at once. Let the details that exist for their own sake do the atmospheric work.

Even at the story's largest moments, keep smaller and irrelevant concerns alive in the character's mind. Petty resentment, a physical discomfort, a task left unfinished: these coexist with catastrophe and are a primary source of the sense that a person, not a narrative function, is present.

Adopt the method: duties ranked, event searched for at the intersection, conflict between duties as engine, load distributed through the cast. Design the next scene by this method from the duties backward, and expect the search to be the real work.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Slow Light -- standalone, science fiction, generation ship.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Eleven generations into a voyage whose destination no longer exists, a ship's council must decide whether to turn the vessel around, and the only functioning navigation officer is nineteen.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Ship law permits a course change only with the concurrence of three departments; Life support is rationed by population segment, and the segments vote; Navigation data cannot be transmitted between decks without passing the council.
CAST IN PLAY: Tavi Osen, navigation officer, nineteen: wants the ship pointed somewhere real; flaw, she trusts the instruments more than the people; secret, she has been decelerating without authorization; knows, the destination star has been gone for decades | Councillor Bess, chair of the livestock segment: wants her population fed and her seat kept; flaw, she trades in order rather than in outcomes; secret, she has known about the missing star for six years; knows, the ration math behind the concealment | Engineer Ho, drive-room chief: wants the drive run within tolerances; flaw, he identifies with the machinery; secret, he has been falsifying the drive's wear reports; knows, the ship can decelerate once and never accelerate again.
OPEN THREADS: the missing star (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a dark frame, then a verifiable absence; unauthorized deceleration (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): fuel figures trending wrong; drive wear reports (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): tolerances, then a forging pen; birth deck organizing (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): ration complaints, then a vote bloc.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tavi discovers the star's absence, tries to report it through channels, and is folded into the concealment she wanted to break | The three departments trade the truth for ration shares; the drive-room wear reports become the leverage; the birth decks organize | Turning the ship requires one burn and one irreversible vote, and the only person who can pilot it is the person with the least authority
ENDING: The ship decelerates toward an empty system with a usable belt, the voyage ends without arrival, and the population becomes a settlement rather than a crew.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what is at the destination; the course will change or the concealment will hold; the ship's population will vote on something that cannot be undone.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Establish the method for designing multi-duty scenes: how plot, character, world, and information work are fused into single events.

response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Tavi discovers the star's absence, tries to report it through channels, and is folded into the concealment she wanted to break. The three departments trade the truth for ration shares; the drive-room wear reports become the leverage; the birth decks organize. Turning the ship requires one burn and one irreversible vote, and the only person who can pilot it is the person with the least authority. The ship decelerates toward an empty system with a usable belt, the voyage ends without arrival, and the population becomes a settlement rather than a crew. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

The multi-duty scene is not a scene doing several things in sequence but one event whose consequences radiate through several registers at once: the confrontation that advances the plot, exposes the character, and plants the information in the same motion. The design method is to find the event where the duties naturally intersect, rather than bolting duties onto an occasion.

Rank the duties by what happens if each is dropped. The duty whose loss damages the book's spine is primary; the rest are payload, and payload duties must attach to the primary's event so tightly that cutting them would damage the primary's staging. This ranking is what keeps multi-duty scenes coherent under the pressure of drafting.

Distribute the load across the cast. A scene carries more duties legitimately when its several participants bring their own agendas into the event: the visitor who needs a favor advances the plot by asking, exposes character by how they ask, and plants the information by what they noticed on the way. Orchestrate the participants as carriers, and the scene's density will be social rather than authorial.

Verify the fusion at the sentence level while drafting. Multi-duty scenes fail when the duties take turns: a paragraph of plot, a paragraph of character. The test is whether the scene's key beats carry two registers simultaneously, the line that is both a threat and a confession, the object that is both a clue and a wound. Revise any beat that serves only one master.

Scene density is the ratio of consequence to page count. The dense scene fuses duties into single events; the thin scene performs one obligation and leaves the rest of its length unspent.

Keep the character's interpretation of events consistent with their personality, their history, and their mood, not with the author's understanding of what is happening. The same event seen by two people should arrive differently structured: different order of attention, different assumptions, different thing at the center of the frame.

Character before description: choose whose attention the scene runs through and what they want from the room before deciding what the room contains. Description that exists to establish a setting will sit inert; description that exists because a person is looking for something inside the setting becomes part of the action.

Adopt the method: duties ranked, event searched for at the intersection, conflict between duties as engine, load distributed through the cast. Design the next scene by this method from the duties backward, and expect the search to be the real work.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Ilsa Verrane, junior archivist: wants to keep her post and her mother's medical debt off the block; flaw, she edits what she cannot face; secret, she has been copying sealed pages for two years; knows, the seal sequence changed after the flood | Registrar Otte, keeper of the seals: wants to hold the city together through one more winter; flaw, he treats people as accounts; secret, he ordered the re-sequencing himself to pay for grain; knows, the grain ships never arrived | Cassian Rhee, debt collector for the merchant floor: wants his brother's seal released; flaw, violence is his first fluent language; secret, he owes the register more than his brother does; knows, Ilsa copies pages.
OPEN THREADS: the altered sequence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): anomaly noticed, then dismissed, then provable; mother's medical debt (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): refinanced twice, then transferred; carter fire plot (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): accelerant cached, dates moved twice; Otte's grain payments (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): receipts referenced, never shown.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ilsa finds the anomaly in the sequence, tests it, and is caught copying by Cassian, who uses her instead of reporting her | The two of them trace the re-sequencing to Otte while the carters plan a fire; Ilsa's mother's seal comes up for transfer and the market price of mercy collapses | Ilsa must choose between publishing the true ledger, which would free the poor but strip the city's grain credit, and burning the register, which would kill thousands of sealed debtors including her mother
ENDING: She publishes the ledger, transfers her mother's seal to her own name, and stays in the archive she has just ruined, which is the only place the rebuilding can happen.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the ledger will be exposed or destroyed by the end; Ilsa's copying habit will cost her something specific; the poor's seals will be settled one way or the other.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.
CAST IN PLAY: Marguerite, shift supervisor, eighteen years: wants the shift closed clean and the report signed; flaw, she protects the shift from management and from itself; secret, she has been signing reports with an outdated injury count; knows, the conveyor's failure pattern | Nate, forklift operator: wants the promotion that requires a clean record; flaw, he trades truth for advancement; secret, he reported a colleague's near-miss as his own error to look diligent; knows, the loading bay's blind corner | Sofia, agency worker, six weeks: wants to be kept on after the season; flaw, she will not report anything that creates a form; secret, she has been working with a wrist injury for nine days; knows, the exact rate the line is set to.
OPEN THREADS: the report (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): four signatures required by dawn; Sofia's wrist (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a hidden injury, nine days old; photographs (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): three failed repairs, timestamped; the blind corner (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a near-miss Nate reattributed.
THREE-ACT ARC: The shift begins, the report is announced as due at dawn, and the conveyor's first fault is patched instead of fixed | Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree | Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision
ENDING: They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the report will be signed or not before dawn; the line will fail in a way that involves a person; one of the four will change position on the report.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree. Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

A scene is a machine for changing one thing that cannot be unchanged: a fact learned, a position lost, a decision made, a bond broken. Hold your scenes to that standard from the start, and the book's motion is guaranteed by its construction; release the standard, and no amount of eventful incident will make the story move.

Define the change types your scenes will draw on, and keep the list short: knowledge, position, relationship, intention, capability. Every scene shifts at least one, and the type should vary across consecutive scenes, because three knowledge scenes in a row thin the story even when each is individually strong. Plan the type sequence for each stretch as deliberately as the events.

Make the changes legible at their scene's end without narration summarizing them. The reader should feel the delta in the situation's altered pressure: the door that closed, the name that can no longer be spoken, the plan that now requires a different skill. If a scene's change needs a sentence of explanation to register, the change was staged too abstractly.

Budget the irreversible against the reversible. Most scene-level changes can theoretically be undone, and a story that undoes them freely teaches the reader that nothing is at stake. Novel outline:
TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Fell, cataloguer, the narrator: wants the commission finished and paid so she can settle a debt; flaw, she trusts documents over people; secret, she has already indexed one owner out of existence; knows, the rooms move when she is not looking | Mrs. Ivey, housekeeper, second of her name: wants the house inhabited the way it was; flaw, she serves the arrangement instead of questioning it; secret, she has been in the house since before the current owners and remembers two more; knows, which owners the previous cataloguer removed | Mr. Lamb, owner who hired her: wants his family's library kept intact and his house entered from outside; flaw, he bargains without understanding the terms; secret, he has not been outside in eleven years; knows, the previous cataloguer's fate.
OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ada arrives, is given rules she does not believe, and finds the previous index with entries in three hands | As she indexes, the house's occupancy thins; the owners become attentive to her work in ways that are not merely proprietary | She must decide whether to finish the index, which will fix the house's population to what she chooses, or to leave the index open and remain inside
ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Design duty conflicts into at least the major scenes, and the loading will never feel mechanical.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists | The service's original instructions prove obsolete and contradictory; the second generation becomes the deciding bloc; the missing previous crew surfaces | The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes
ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning a novel at the level of its scenes, and the definition of what a scene is for is still open.
Establish the scene as your story's unit of change: what each scene must alter, and how the alterations chain into the book's motion.
You are architecting a novel before drafting begins.
Build the framework now, before any drafting begins.
response:
The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved. The movements the book has to pay for: The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists. The service's original instructions prove obsolete and contradictory; the second generation becomes the deciding bloc; the missing previous crew surfaces. The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

A scene is a machine for changing one thing that cannot be unchanged: a fact learned, a position lost, a decision made, a bond broken. Hold your scenes to that standard from the start, and the book's motion is guaranteed by its construction; release the standard, and no amount of eventful incident will make the story move.

Define the change types your scenes will draw on, and keep the list short: knowledge, position, relationship, intention, capability. Every scene shifts at least one, and the type should vary across consecutive scenes, because three knowledge scenes in a row thin the story even when each is individually strong. Plan the type sequence for each stretch as deliberately as the events.

Connect the deltas causally, not just sequentially. The change one scene delivers should be the ground the next scene stands on: the knowledge gained is used, the position lost is mourned and compensated, the decision made is implemented. A chain of unrelated deltas is a string of incidents; a causal chain is a plot.

Budget the irreversible against the reversible. Most scene-level changes can theoretically be undone, and a story that undoes them freely teaches the reader that nothing is at stake. Decide which changes across the book are permanent, mark them as the story's real spine, and treat every other change as negotiation around those fixed points.

The reader experiences structure as rhythm: real-time against summary, beat against break, density against breath. Make the rhythm deliberate at every scale, and the book will feel designed without ever seeming managed.

Prefer the incidental specific to the atmosphere word. Generic atmosphere is interchangeable between scenes and therefore carries no information, while an incidental particular, chosen well, implies place, class, history, and mood at once. Let the details that exist for their own sake do the atmospheric work.

Let the character misread the scene and do not correct them. A misunderstanding that survives several scenes accumulates pressure, and its eventual correction lands as a turn rather than a clarification. While planning, note what this character will get wrong here so later scenes can inherit the error rather than the fact.

Adopt the unit standard: every scene alters at least one of the five state types, irreversibly where it matters, and inherits the altered state from its predecessor. Draft from the standard, and the book will move by construction.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.
OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.
THREE-ACT ARC: Corin reads the harvest rite, omits the sentence that no one likes hearing, and the first field fails | As the blight spreads, Mette's outside seed divides the valley, Sorrel's authorship surfaces, and Hale's purchases reveal what the lowlands intend | Corin must either restore the omitted sentence, which the valley will refuse, or finish the bargain the saint left unfinished, which requires the valley to pay a new price
ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.
CAST IN PLAY: Priya, bakery owner, three generations: wants the family shop kept open through the season; flaw, she hears every suggestion as a takeover; secret, she has already taken a loan against the building she does not own; knows, the landlord's redevelopment plans | Dan, cafe owner, second year: wants a business that lasts past the following spring; flaw, he solves problems by spending; secret, his cafe is funded by severance from the company he left; knows, the association's voting arithmetic | Mr. Hallow, landlord: wants one tenant paying a single higher rent; flaw, he uses courteous language as leverage; secret, he has a development partner waiting on the outcome; knows, the lease's co-signature clause and its limits.
OPEN THREADS: co-lease (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a shared signature, then a joint renewal notice; loan against the building (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a bank letter, a repayment schedule; buyout clause (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): an assessor's appointment; development offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price, a deadline.
THREE-ACT ARC: The co-lease is presented as fait accompli, the two businesses share a wall and a delivery yard, and each tries to outlast the other | Shared hours, a stolen delivery, and a broken oven force real collaboration, and the buyout clause becomes a weapon both consider | The redevelopment offer arrives with a deadline, and the choice is between a joint purchase neither can afford alone and one of them taking the buyout money
ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.
OPEN THREADS: the removed page (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report with a gap, then the missing sheet; the burned coat (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): ash in the stove, then a button; the girl's plan (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a bus timetable, a packed bag; Ruth's brother (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): an alibi, a dispute, a confession.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.
CAST IN PLAY: Rennick, planner, retired: wants one final job that pays his debts; flaw, he plans for machinery and not for people; secret, he has already been paid by the bank's owner to test the building; knows, the owner's security revisions | Sabine, locksmith: wants her brother's release from a debt prison; flaw, she trusts nobody's plan but her own; secret, she has copied the vault key pattern; knows, the second door's true difficulty | Ode, inside man, night clerk: wants out of the city with his daughter; flaw, he cannot lie under pressure; secret, he has already told the owner that a crew is coming; knows, the guard rotation posted tonight.
OPEN THREADS: identity registrations (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): ninety-second windows, then a record of a previous test; copied key (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a wax impression, then a duplicate; clerk's disclosure (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a phone call logged; guard's documentation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): photographs of the ledgers.
THREE-ACT ARC: The plan is assembled and rehearsed against the layout, and the first door is easier than the plan predicted | The ease of the first door is the trap: the owner is watching the test. Identity registrations, a copied key, and the clerk's nerve converge | The ledgers are only useful if they reach the front door and daylight, and the crew has to choose between the plan and the captives' safety
ENDING: Rennick breaks his own plan to move the ledgers out through the front with the staff, the door system records all five of them, and the crew walks into arrest with the ledgers in the hands of the guard captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: five doors will be opened in order; the crew's own rule about staff will be tested; one member has already betrayed the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.
