instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Cold Communion -- standalone, horror, isolated research station.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, present tense, two scientists.
PREMISE: At a monastery station studying a silence that behaves like a substance, two researchers discover the discipline that keeps them safe is the same discipline that has been feeding the phenomenon.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The phenomenon occupies measured silence and can be displaced by noise, but it returns to any space left quiet; The station's rule forbids speech outside the chanting hours; Every recorded measurement taken during the silence has been altered before it reaches the archive.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Ilse Ko, acoustics researcher: wants a publishable measurement and an exit; flaw, she measures instead of protecting; secret, she falsified a baseline to get funded; knows, the archive has been edited | Brother Anton, station's chanting master: wants the discipline kept; flaw, he would rather lose a person than a rule; secret, he has been altering the archive at the order's instruction; knows, the silence grows where people stop speaking | Dr. Piedra, geologist, second researcher: wants the station closed and everyone out; flaw, she advocates with contempt; secret, she has stopped sleeping in her own room and will not say why; knows, the measured silence does not obey containment.
OPEN THREADS: edited archive (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a warm number in a cold month, then the order's instruction; falsified baseline (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a funding timeline, then a confession read into the record; Piedra's room (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a room she avoids, a recorded hum; the missing year (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Ren's memory, then the chant book's blank pages.
THREE-ACT ARC: The researchers arrive, learn the discipline, and record the first anomaly during a chant | Measurements diverge from the archive, the silence begins to occupy rooms that people leave, and the two researchers split on whether to publish or flee | Publishing requires speech, and the station's rule makes speech a weapon; the order must choose between the archive and the building
ENDING: The researchers broadcast their measurements aloud, breaking the discipline and displacing the phenomenon out of the station, and the monastery is abandoned as a ruin full of unedited records.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what silence carries; the discipline will be broken or the station lost; the altered archive will be read aloud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning the novel described above, and the question below concerns the book's architecture rather than one scene.
You are deciding, across an arc, who perceives which parts of the story.
How does viewpoint choice work as a plotting instrument across the whole book rather than as a per-scene preference?
You are planning a novel.
Set out how you will think about this across the whole arc.
response:
The promises this book has already made are on the record: the reader will learn what silence carries; the discipline will be broken or the station lost. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. The researchers arrive, learn the discipline, and record the first anomaly during a chant. Measurements diverge from the archive, the silence begins to occupy rooms that people leave, and the two researchers split on whether to publish or flee. Publishing requires speech, and the station's rule makes speech a weapon; the order must choose between the archive and the building. The researchers broadcast their measurements aloud, breaking the discipline and displacing the phenomenon out of the station, and the monastery is abandoned as a ruin full of unedited records. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Restrict knowledge unevenly across the cast. Different characters should hold different fragments, and no one should hold all of them, because a single informed character converts the story's information problem into a delivery problem and removes the need for the cast to act under uncertainty.

Schedule perception-driven turns deliberately: the chapter where a character's interpretation of an earlier event changes, the chapter where a misreading is confirmed by new evidence and becomes stronger, and the chapter where the error collapses. These three movements are as structural as any confrontation.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Keep the character's interpretation of events consistent with their personality, their history, and their mood, not with the author's understanding of what is happening. The same event seen by two people should arrive differently structured: different order of attention, different assumptions, different thing at the center of the frame.

Commit to a knowledge architecture for the book: who holds what, when the reader is ahead, when the reader is behind, and which errors are load-bearing. Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.
You are planning how a novel will distribute information across its chapters.
How does viewpoint choice work as a plotting instrument across the whole book rather than as a per-scene preference?
You are planning a novel.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat. The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes. Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start. She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Across a whole book, the pattern of who knows what is the story's hidden architecture. Plan it deliberately: the moments when the reader learns something before a character, and the moments when a character learns something after the reader, are the two engines of suspense and surprise, and their placement can be scheduled the way scenes are scheduled.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

These three movements are as structural as any confrontation.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Fix the perceiving position before anything else: where the viewpoint character stands, what their hands are doing, which sense is carrying the most information, and what they currently believe about the situation. Description generated from inside that position arrives pre-filtered; description generated from a vantage above it reads as reportage no matter how good the sentences are.

Commit to a knowledge architecture for the book: who holds what, when the reader is ahead, when the reader is behind, and which errors are load-bearing. Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.

OPEN THREADS: altered entries (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two paid-out relief claims with no deaths; constable's burial (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a fresh grave outside the churchyard; relief fund (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): payments made on reputation; the physician's forecast (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a calendar of expected deaths.

ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Interiority before explanation: whatever the reader needs to understand about a character should be inferable from how they perceive, decide, and misread, rather than stated by the narration.

Let the character misread the scene and do not correct them. A misunderstanding that survives several scenes accumulates pressure, and its eventual correction lands as a turn rather than a clarification. While planning, note what this character will get wrong here so later scenes can inherit the error rather than the fact.

Permit contradictory feelings to coexist, and permit characters to misread themselves. A person can be frightened and curious, relieved and resentful, and can explain their own state wrongly to themselves. The viewpoint's own interpretation of its feelings is not authoritative, and treating it as authoritative flattens the interior.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.
CAST IN PLAY: Marguerite, shift supervisor, eighteen years: wants the shift closed clean and the report signed; flaw, she protects the shift from management and from itself; secret, she has been signing reports with an outdated injury count; knows, the conveyor's failure pattern | Nate, forklift operator: wants the promotion that requires a clean record; flaw, he trades truth for advancement; secret, he reported a colleague's near-miss as his own error to look diligent; knows, the loading bay's blind corner | Sofia, agency worker, six weeks: wants to be kept on after the season; flaw, she will not report anything that creates a form; secret, she has been working with a wrist injury for nine days; knows, the exact rate the line is set to.
OPEN THREADS: the report (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): four signatures required by dawn; Sofia's wrist (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a hidden injury, nine days old; photographs (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): three failed repairs, timestamped; the blind corner (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a near-miss Nate reattributed.
THREE-ACT ARC: The shift begins, the report is announced as due at dawn, and the conveyor's first fault is patched instead of fixed | Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree | Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision
ENDING: They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the report will be signed or not before dawn; the line will fail in a way that involves a person; one of the four will change position on the report.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.
You are deciding, across an arc, who perceives which parts of the story.
How does viewpoint choice work as a plotting instrument across the whole book rather than as a per-scene preference?
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Build the framework now, before any drafting begins.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it. The shift begins, the report is announced as due at dawn, and the conveyor's first fault is patched instead of fixed. Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree. Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision. They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Restrict knowledge unevenly across the cast. Different characters should hold different fragments, and no one should hold all of them, because a single informed character converts the story's information problem into a delivery problem and removes the need for the cast to act under uncertainty.

Schedule perception-driven turns deliberately: the chapter where a character's interpretation of an earlier event changes, the chapter where a misreading is confirmed by new evidence and becomes stronger, and the chapter where the error collapses. These three movements are as structural as any confrontation.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Rank what can be perceived by the character's priorities rather than by visual prominence. A frightened character's attention goes to exits, distances, and the nearest thing that could be used as a weapon; a curious one goes to anomalies; a proud one goes to who is watching. Decide the priority order for this scene and let it choose the details that reach the page.

Permit contradictory feelings to coexist, and permit characters to misread themselves. A person can be frightened and curious, relieved and resentful, and can explain their own state wrongly to themselves. The viewpoint's own interpretation of its feelings is not authoritative, and treating it as authoritative flattens the interior.

Commit to a knowledge architecture for the book: who holds what, when the reader is ahead, when the reader is behind, and which errors are load-bearing. Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Plan it deliberately: the moments when the reader learns something before a character, and the moments when a character learns something after the reader, are the two engines of suspense and surprise, and their placement can be scheduled the way scenes are scheduled.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Even at the story's largest moments, keep smaller and irrelevant concerns alive in the character's mind. Petty resentment, a physical discomfort, a task left unfinished: these coexist with catastrophe and are a primary source of the sense that a person, not a narrative function, is present.

Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.
CAST IN PLAY: Rennick, planner, retired: wants one final job that pays his debts; flaw, he plans for machinery and not for people; secret, he has already been paid by the bank's owner to test the building; knows, the owner's security revisions | Sabine, locksmith: wants her brother's release from a debt prison; flaw, she trusts nobody's plan but her own; secret, she has copied the vault key pattern; knows, the second door's true difficulty | Ode, inside man, night clerk: wants out of the city with his daughter; flaw, he cannot lie under pressure; secret, he has already told the owner that a crew is coming; knows, the guard rotation posted tonight.
OPEN THREADS: identity registrations (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): ninety-second windows, then a record of a previous test; copied key (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a wax impression, then a duplicate; clerk's disclosure (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a phone call logged; guard's documentation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): photographs of the ledgers.
THREE-ACT ARC: The plan is assembled and rehearsed against the layout, and the first door is easier than the plan predicted | The ease of the first door is the trap: the owner is watching the test. Identity registrations, a copied key, and the clerk's nerve converge | The ledgers are only useful if they reach the front door and daylight, and the crew has to choose between the plan and the captives' safety
ENDING: Rennick breaks his own plan to move the ledgers out through the front with the staff, the door system records all five of them, and the crew walks into arrest with the ledgers in the hands of the guard captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: five doors will be opened in order; the crew's own rule about staff will be tested; one member has already betrayed the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.
CAST IN PLAY: Mistress Ode, master printer: wants the house and its apprentices through the crisis; flaw, she takes on obligations to avoid choosing; secret, she has accepted all three commissions; knows, the paper allocation's real controller | Hal, senior pressman: wants the sheets set in the order that keeps people alive; flaw, he believes he can judge consequences from the shop floor; secret, he has been passing proofs to the organizers; knows, which document is a forgery | Young Cass, apprentice: wants to be trusted with a real task; flaw, she reads everything she sets; secret, she has told a friend what one commission says; knows, all three commissions exist.
OPEN THREADS: three commissions (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a levy notice, a denunciation, a committee's address; forgery (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a signature on a document nobody in the shop wrote; leaked proofs (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a friend, a copied page; warrant timetable (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): three days, one magistrate.
THREE-ACT ARC: Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority | One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock | The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first
ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.
PROMISES TO THE READER: all three documents will be printed or refused; the house's mark will be used against it; the apprentice's leak will reach the street.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority. One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock. The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first. The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Restrict knowledge unevenly across the cast. Different characters should hold different fragments, and no one should hold all of them, because a single informed character converts the story's information problem into a delivery problem and removes the need for the cast to act under uncertainty.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Let the character misread the scene and do not correct them. A misunderstanding that survives several scenes accumulates pressure, and its eventual correction lands as a turn rather than a clarification. While planning, note what this character will get wrong here so later scenes can inherit the error rather than the fact.

Do not resolve an emotion as soon as it appears. Emotional states should change gradually and leave residue: a chapter that closes an emotional movement completely must still let it alter behavior, decisions, or relationships in later chapters, or the reader learns that feelings in this book do not matter.

Commit to a knowledge architecture for the book: who holds what, when the reader is ahead, when the reader is behind, and which errors are load-bearing. Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.

PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists | The service's original instructions prove obsolete and contradictory; the second generation becomes the deciding bloc; the missing previous crew surfaces | The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes
ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning how a protagonist's inner life should develop without becoming more articulate than the character.
How does interiority stay specific, limited, and alive across an entire novel rather than collapsing into reflective summary?
You are planning a novel.
Think it through as planning: what must be true, in what order, and why.
response:
The promises this book has already made are on the record: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists. The service's original instructions prove obsolete and contradictory; the second generation becomes the deciding bloc; the missing previous crew surfaces. The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes. Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Interiority decays over a long book. Early chapters carry a genuine perceptual filter; later chapters drift toward a general thoughtful voice that could belong to anyone, because the most available way to write reflection is also the least specific. Plan against the decay: maintain a private register for each viewpoint character, and refresh it with the character's ongoing concerns rather than with thematic reflection.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Vary the interiority's texture by circumstance. Under threat, attention narrows and thought becomes fragmentary and practical; in intervals, thought wanders, remembers, and is petty. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Carry the effects of earlier interiority forward. What a character concluded privately in chapter three should influence what they attempt in chapter twelve, even if the conclusion was wrong, which is how interior life becomes plot rather than commentary.

Interiority before explanation: whatever the reader needs to understand about a character should be inferable from how they perceive, decide, and misread, rather than stated by the narration.

Even at the story's largest moments, keep smaller and irrelevant concerns alive in the character's mind. Petty resentment, a physical discomfort, a task left unfinished: these coexist with catastrophe and are a primary source of the sense that a person, not a narrative function, is present.

Permit contradictory feelings to coexist, and permit characters to misread themselves. A person can be frightened and curious, relieved and resentful, and can explain their own state wrongly to themselves. The viewpoint's own interpretation of its feelings is not authoritative, and treating it as authoritative flattens the interior.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:

PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Fen Road -- standalone, survival, expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the medic.
PREMISE: A six-person survey team crossing a wetland loses its route markers and its leader, and the medic who has been falsifying fitness reports must decide who is fit enough to carry what.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The fen's causeway is passable only in the dry weeks and only at night, when the peat holds; The team's rations were calculated for a crossing of nine nights; Any team member left behind is entitled to the group's full share of supplies.
CAST IN PLAY: Ori, team medic: wants all six across with a clean report; flaw, she protects people by withholding information; secret, she passed two members who should have failed their fitness review; knows, the team's actual condition | Halvard, survey lead: wants the route completed and the map delivered; flaw, he decides by schedule; secret, he accepted the commission below the safe number of nights; knows, the rations are short | Sel, porter, youngest: wants to be paid and to be taken seriously; flaw, she hides injury to stay on the manifest; secret, she has been re-marking the route posts incorrectly; knows, the posts have been moved.
OPEN THREADS: falsified reviews (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two passing grades, two failing bodies; route posts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): posts in the wrong places; rations (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a count, then a recount; the left-behind rule (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): supplies set aside for an abandoned member.

ENDING: They hold to the rule, abandon the survey, and cross four nights late with a documented route they will never sell.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will take fewer or more nights than planned; someone will be carried or left; the falsified reviews will matter to a decision.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.

THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The long-arc problem with interiority is articulation creep: the character's inner language becomes more fluent as the book proceeds, because fluency is what the writing rewards. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Only include what the viewpoint can actually perceive or infer from what they have perceived. POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each lantern holds a fixed measure of years, and the ninth is the reserve; Lamplight cannot be made, only moved from lantern to lantern by a licensed hand; Whoever carries light through the streets alone burns a little of themselves.
CAST IN PLAY: Peet Amaran, junior lamplighter, ninth watch: wants to be certified so his sister can leave the district; flaw, he cannot let a wrong thing stand unremarked; secret, he has already carried an unlicensed flame; knows, the ninth lantern was lit early | Mistress Hallow, master of the lightworks: wants the city calm until the transfer season; flaw, she has confused the institution with the city; secret, she has been rationing without a license for six years; knows, the real measure left | Dove Rhee, light-broker for the outer districts: wants the districts priced out of the light to be lit anyway; flaw, she needs to be the one who fixes it; secret, she has been selling light she does not have; knows, Peet's unlicensed carry.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Fen Road -- standalone, survival, expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the medic.
PREMISE: A six-person survey team crossing a wetland loses its route markers and its leader, and the medic who has been falsifying fitness reports must decide who is fit enough to carry what.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The fen's causeway is passable only in the dry weeks and only at night, when the peat holds; The team's rations were calculated for a crossing of nine nights; Any team member left behind is entitled to the group's full share of supplies.
CAST IN PLAY: Ori, team medic: wants all six across with a clean report; flaw, she protects people by withholding information; secret, she passed two members who should have failed their fitness review; knows, the team's actual condition | Halvard, survey lead: wants the route completed and the map delivered; flaw, he decides by schedule; secret, he accepted the commission below the safe number of nights; knows, the rations are short | Sel, porter, youngest: wants to be paid and to be taken seriously; flaw, she hides injury to stay on the manifest; secret, she has been re-marking the route posts incorrectly; knows, the posts have been moved.
OPEN THREADS: falsified reviews (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two passing grades, two failing bodies; route posts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): posts in the wrong places; rations (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a count, then a recount; the left-behind rule (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): supplies set aside for an abandoned member.
THREE-ACT ARC: The team enters the fen, the marker discrepancies are small, and a first injury changes the pace | Rations, injuries, and the falsified fitness reviews collide; Halvard's schedule becomes the antagonist; the markers are proved wrong | Eight nights in, the causeway is behind them, one member cannot continue, and the group's own rule about being left behind becomes a live instrument
ENDING: They hold to the rule, abandon the survey, and cross four nights late with a documented route they will never sell.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will take fewer or more nights than planned; someone will be carried or left; the falsified reviews will matter to a decision.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Wolf Road -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, travel and pursuit.
POV AND DISTANCE: limited third rotating among three travelers, past tense.
PREMISE: Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The passes open on a schedule nobody controls, and the last opening strands travelers until spring; Travelers share salt and fire by custom, and breaking the custom is the only crime the road recognizes; The pursuing company cannot cross until the pass freezes hard, which gives a fixed head start.
CAST IN PLAY: Rusk, guide: wants to reach the far side without the others; flaw, he lies by omission and calls it protection; secret, he is leading them away from the pass deliberately; knows, the true pass and its closing date | Aveline Tarn, courier carrying a treaty: wants delivery before the season closes; flaw, she treats everyone as a liability; secret, the treaty is forged and she knows it; knows, the pursuers are her own people | Ossian, physician fleeing a charge: wants to reach a place where his hands are unknown; flaw, he helps compulsively and resents it; secret, he killed a patient through a mistake, not malice; knows, Rusk's route contradicts every map.

ENDING: They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the road will be crossed or the season closes on them; the guide's lie will be exposed before the end; the travelers will learn what each is carrying.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dead continue their routines until someone they know admits out loud that they died; Admission is irreversible, and the admitted person leaves immediately; The town's ferry does not run after the last admission of the season.

OPEN THREADS: Marjorie's husband (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): his newspaper arrives, then his chair, then the admission; Olus's certificate (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a forged date, a family that stayed; the ferry season (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): schedule noted, then shortened, then final; Bea's telling (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a careless sentence that starts one neighbor's absence.

ENDING: Marjorie admits her husband in public, the ferry runs one time for those who want it, and the town continues the following year with fewer residents and the same courtesy.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will understand the rules before any character states them; someone will be admitted who should not have been; the ferry will run one last time.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. A town summer: the arrangement works, the reader learns its rules through behaviour, and Bea arrives with an outsider's eyes. Marjorie admits her husband in public, the ferry runs one time for those who want it, and the town continues the following year with fewer residents and the same courtesy. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Restrict knowledge unevenly across the cast. Different characters should hold different fragments, and no one should hold all of them, because a single informed character converts the story's information problem into a delivery problem and removes the need for the cast to act under uncertainty.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Only include what the viewpoint can actually perceive or infer from what they have perceived. Let the reader arrive at the emotion before the text names it. Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.
THREE-ACT ARC: The council opens, the seven-day clock begins, and Nissa's first report proves false in a way that serves both sides | Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact | The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her
ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.

Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact. The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Across a whole book, the pattern of who knows what is the story's hidden architecture. Plan it deliberately: the moments when the reader learns something before a character, and the moments when a character learns something after the reader, are the two engines of suspense and surprise, and their placement can be scheduled the way scenes are scheduled.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Schedule perception-driven turns deliberately: the chapter where a character's interpretation of an earlier event changes, the chapter where a misreading is confirmed by new evidence and becomes stronger, and the chapter where the error collapses. These three movements are as structural as any confrontation.

Perception before description: the scene is delivered by a mind with limits, and those limits are the scene's engine rather than its obstacle.

Only include what the viewpoint can actually perceive or infer from what they have perceived. That is a hard boundary, and it does work for the story: it prevents convenient comprehension, it forces information to travel by means the reader can verify, and it keeps every description inside a consciousness that can be wrong.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Wolf Road -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, travel and pursuit.
POV AND DISTANCE: limited third rotating among three travelers, past tense.
PREMISE: Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The passes open on a schedule nobody controls, and the last opening strands travelers until spring; Travelers share salt and fire by custom, and breaking the custom is the only crime the road recognizes; The pursuing company cannot cross until the pass freezes hard, which gives a fixed head start.
CAST IN PLAY: Rusk, guide: wants to reach the far side without the others; flaw, he lies by omission and calls it protection; secret, he is leading them away from the pass deliberately; knows, the true pass and its closing date | Aveline Tarn, courier carrying a treaty: wants delivery before the season closes; flaw, she treats everyone as a liability; secret, the treaty is forged and she knows it; knows, the pursuers are her own people | Ossian, physician fleeing a charge: wants to reach a place where his hands are unknown; flaw, he helps compulsively and resents it; secret, he killed a patient through a mistake, not malice; knows, Rusk's route contradicts every map.
OPEN THREADS: wrong route (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): map discrepancies, then Rusk's silence, then his reason; treaty (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): sealed case, then a broken seal, then the forgery named; Ossian's charge (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a rumor at a waystation, then a survivor; Selv's orders (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a written order, then a second order.
THREE-ACT ARC: The three travelers take the road together under custom, and Ossian notices the guide's route is wrong | Short rations and weather force confessions; the pursuers gain because Rusk's detour costs days; Aveline's forgery surfaces | At the last fork, the truth about the pass and the treaty arrives together, and the travelers must decide which promises on this road are worth keeping
ENDING: They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the road will be crossed or the season closes on them; the guide's lie will be exposed before the end; the travelers will learn what each is carrying.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive. The three travelers take the road together under custom, and Ossian notices the guide's route is wrong. Short rations and weather force confessions; the pursuers gain because Rusk's detour costs days; Aveline's forgery surfaces. At the last fork, the truth about the pass and the treaty arrives together, and the travelers must decide which promises on this road are worth keeping. They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Interiority decays over a long book. Early chapters carry a genuine perceptual filter; later chapters drift toward a general thoughtful voice that could belong to anyone, because the most available way to write reflection is also the least specific. Plan against the decay: maintain a private register for each viewpoint character, and refresh it with the character's ongoing concerns rather than with thematic reflection.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Let the character's interpretation of their own feelings stay unreliable and inconsistent in detail. Self-report that is always accurate is a characterization failure; a person mislabels anger as tiredness, treats grief as logistics, and calls fear preparation, and the pattern should be stable enough to be recognizable and wrong enough to be interesting.

Carry the effects of earlier interiority forward. What a character concluded privately in chapter three should influence what they attempt in chapter twelve, even if the conclusion was wrong, which is how interior life becomes plot rather than commentary.

Interiority before explanation: whatever the reader needs to understand about a character should be inferable from how they perceive, decide, and misread, rather than stated by the narration.

Keep the character's interpretation of events consistent with their personality, their history, and their mood, not with the author's understanding of what is happening. The same event seen by two people should arrive differently structured: different order of attention, different assumptions, different thing at the center of the frame.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Fell, cataloguer, the narrator: wants the commission finished and paid so she can settle a debt; flaw, she trusts documents over people; secret, she has already indexed one owner out of existence; knows, the rooms move when she is not looking | Mrs. Ivey, housekeeper, second of her name: wants the house inhabited the way it was; flaw, she serves the arrangement instead of questioning it; secret, she has been in the house since before the current owners and remembers two more; knows, which owners the previous cataloguer removed | Mr. Lamb, owner who hired her: wants his family's library kept intact and his house entered from outside; flaw, he bargains without understanding the terms; secret, he has not been outside in eleven years; knows, the previous cataloguer's fate.
OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ada arrives, is given rules she does not believe, and finds the previous index with entries in three hands | As she indexes, the house's occupancy thins; the owners become attentive to her work in ways that are not merely proprietary | She must decide whether to finish the index, which will fix the house's population to what she chooses, or to leave the index open and remain inside
ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Decide now what this character can and cannot put into words, and hold that boundary even when an articulate passage would save the scene; the character's limits are part of the story's information design.

Vary the interiority's texture by circumstance. Under threat, attention narrows and thought becomes fragmentary and practical; in intervals, thought wanders, remembers, and is petty. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Carry the effects of earlier interiority forward. What a character concluded privately in chapter three should influence what they attempt in chapter twelve, even if the conclusion was wrong, which is how interior life becomes plot rather than commentary.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.

ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.

The long-arc problem with interiority is articulation creep: the character's inner language becomes more fluent as the book proceeds, because fluency is what the writing rewards. Decide now what this character can and cannot put into words, and hold that boundary even when an articulate passage would save the scene; the character's limits are part of the story's information design.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Vary the interiority's texture by circumstance. Under threat, attention narrows and thought becomes fragmentary and practical; in intervals, thought wanders, remembers, and is petty. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Emotional states should change gradually and leave residue: a chapter that closes an emotional movement completely must still let it alter behavior, decisions, or relationships in later chapters, or the reader learns that feelings in this book do not matter.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
