Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.

ENDING: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Early chapters carry a genuine perceptual filter; later chapters drift toward a general thoughtful voice that could belong to anyone, because the most available way to write reflection is also the least specific. Plan against the decay: maintain a private register for each viewpoint character, and refresh it with the character's ongoing concerns rather than with thematic reflection.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Even at the story's largest moments, keep smaller and irrelevant concerns alive in the character's mind. Petty resentment, a physical discomfort, a task left unfinished: these coexist with catastrophe and are a primary source of the sense that a person, not a narrative function, is present.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.

ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Rank what can be perceived by the character's priorities rather than by visual prominence. A frightened character's attention goes to exits, distances, and the nearest thing that could be used as a weapon; a curious one goes to anomalies; a proud one goes to who is watching. Decide the priority order for this scene and let it choose the details that reach the page.

Give each character an individual emotional signature rather than a shared repertoire of reactions. Surprise does not always widen the eyes; fear does not always shake; grief does not always produce tears. A reaction is characterization, so it should be as specific as the person having it.

TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.

ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Paper Mill -- standalone, thriller, corporate whistleblower.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the mid-level analyst.
PREMISE: An analyst discovers that her employer's celebrated water-recycling plant has been discharging into a river for a decade, and the only person who will believe her is the regulator she once helped discredit.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Regulatory inspections are announced four days in advance by statute; The company's severance agreements require arbitration and prohibit disclosure of process data; Discharge samples must be taken by a certified officer to be admissible.
CAST IN PLAY: Nadia Bell, process analyst: wants the discharge stopped without losing her pension; flaw, she documents everything and decides nothing; secret, she signed the original compliance report as a junior; knows, the plant's bypass valve schedule | Regulator Osei, environmental officer: wants an admissible sample; flaw, he needs to be right in public; secret, he leaked an earlier case to a journalist who burned him; knows, the company's legal exposure | Director Pike, plant director: wants the plant's award renewed and his retirement secured; flaw, he believes the discharge is acceptable accounting; secret, he authorized the bypass during a drought year and never restored it; knows, which documents prove authorization.
OPEN THREADS: bypass valve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a maintenance schedule, then a physical seal; signed report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): her signature, then the amended version; diluted samples (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): two sets of numbers; leaked case (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a journalist's name, a burned source.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.

ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.

The long-arc problem with interiority is articulation creep: the character's inner language becomes more fluent as the book proceeds, because fluency is what the writing rewards. Decide now what this character can and cannot put into words, and hold that boundary even when an articulate passage would save the scene; the character's limits are part of the story's information design.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Vary the interiority's texture by circumstance. Under threat, attention narrows and thought becomes fragmentary and practical; in intervals, thought wanders, remembers, and is petty. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Let the character's interpretation of their own feelings stay unreliable and inconsistent in detail. Self-report that is always accurate is a characterization failure; a person mislabels anger as tiredness, treats grief as logistics, and calls fear preparation, and the pattern should be stable enough to be recognizable and wrong enough to be interesting.

Interiority before explanation: whatever the reader needs to understand about a character should be inferable from how they perceive, decide, and misread, rather than stated by the narration.

Allow the timing of emotion to be irregular. A reaction can be delayed by the demands of the moment, suppressed by training or necessity, displaced onto a smaller problem, or held until a character is alone. Immediate, proportionate reaction is the least interesting available option and the easiest to write.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.

TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.

Decide now what this character can and cannot put into words, and hold that boundary even when an articulate passage would save the scene; the character's limits are part of the story's information design.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.
THREE-ACT ARC: Sessions establish terms; Jun alters one position to prevent a stalemate; the visitors confirm it back exactly, which tells the delegation nothing | The alteration costs the delegation its mining leverage; Sabel's recordings surface; Ollun demonstrates knowledge of the delegation's private arguments | The window closes with an unsigned treaty; Jun must either admit the manipulation publicly or deliver an exchange built on it
ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret. Sessions establish terms; Jun alters one position to prevent a stalemate; the visitors confirm it back exactly, which tells the delegation nothing. The alteration costs the delegation its mining leverage; Sabel's recordings surface; Ollun demonstrates knowledge of the delegation's private arguments. The window closes with an unsigned treaty; Jun must either admit the manipulation publicly or deliver an exchange built on it. She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Restrict knowledge unevenly across the cast. Different characters should hold different fragments, and no one should hold all of them, because a single informed character converts the story's information problem into a delivery problem and removes the need for the cast to act under uncertainty.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Perception before description: the scene is delivered by a mind with limits, and those limits are the scene's engine rather than its obstacle.

Only include what the viewpoint can actually perceive or infer from what they have perceived. That is a hard boundary, and it does work for the story: it prevents convenient comprehension, it forces information to travel by means the reader can verify, and it keeps every description inside a consciousness that can be wrong.

Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.

ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.

ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.

TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.

TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

Interiority decays over a long book. Early chapters carry a genuine perceptual filter; later chapters drift toward a general thoughtful voice that could belong to anyone, because the most available way to write reflection is also the least specific. Plan against the decay: maintain a private register for each viewpoint character, and refresh it with the character's ongoing concerns rather than with thematic reflection.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Vary the interiority's texture by circumstance. Under threat, attention narrows and thought becomes fragmentary and practical; in intervals, thought wanders, remembers, and is petty. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Let the character's interpretation of their own feelings stay unreliable and inconsistent in detail. Rank what can be perceived by the character's priorities rather than by visual prominence. Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A ward holds only while its maker is alive and named in its grain; Thornwood cannot be cut by anyone who has not been formally released from apprenticeship; A failed ward does not fall; it turns, and it takes its maker's mark with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Tess, apprentice, the narrator: wants to be released and named; flaw, she revises the past as she tells it; secret, she has been making wards that turn; knows, the master's hands no longer work | Master Orr, wardwright, last of the guild: wants the workshop left to someone; flaw, he teaches by withholding and calls it testing; secret, he has been using Tess's hands for a year while signing the work himself; knows, the turning wards will come home | Pell, forest warden, outside the guild: wants the wards maintained by any means; flaw, he trusts systems more than people; secret, he has been reporting the turning wards to the forest villages; knows, which wards failed first.
OPEN THREADS: turning ward (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a mark that points the wrong way, then comes home; the master's hands (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): an unsigned piece, then a burned record; the buyer's visits (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): prices offered, then terms; Pell's reports (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): village complaints, then an emptied village.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tess is left alone with three wards to make before the season, and given no release; she makes them and one turns | She hides the turn, the forest begins coming in, and the master's deception and her own are set on the same track | Every option requires her to be named by someone: the master will not, the buyer will for a price, and the wards must be made regardless
ENDING: Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see a ward turn; Tess will either be named or not be named; the workshop will close or continue, not both.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Perception is a plot mechanism before it is a stylistic one. Who sees what determines what can be decided, and the sequence in which information becomes available to a character is the sequence of the plot's turns. Treat viewpoint as distribution: at each stage of the book, decide who holds which facts, who has been given a wrong frame for them, and where the reader stands in relation to both.

Decide the reader's position relative to each character's knowledge, scene by scene, and let the gap be intentional rather than accidental. Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Schedule perception-driven turns deliberately: the chapter where a character's interpretation of an earlier event changes, the chapter where a misreading is confirmed by new evidence and becomes stronger, and the chapter where the error collapses. These three movements are as structural as any confrontation.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Fix the perceiving position before anything else: where the viewpoint character stands, what their hands are doing, which sense is carrying the most information, and what they currently believe about the situation. Description generated from inside that position arrives pre-filtered; description generated from a vantage above it reads as reportage no matter how good the sentences are.

Keep emotional amplitude uneven across the book. If every chapter reaches the same intensity, the reader's calibration flattens and later events cannot exceed earlier ones. Decide where the chapter's emotional peak belongs, and let other chapters remain below it.

Commit to a knowledge architecture for the book: who holds what, when the reader is ahead, when the reader is behind, and which errors are load-bearing. Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.

Reader ahead of character generates dread and impatience; reader behind character generates curiosity and the wish to catch up; both are useful and neither should persist unchallenged for too long.

Restrict knowledge unevenly across the cast. Different characters should hold different fragments, and no one should hold all of them, because a single informed character converts the story's information problem into a delivery problem and removes the need for the cast to act under uncertainty.

Let errors survive. A wrong belief held by a character for several chapters is not a delay in the plot but a plot of its own, and the correction, when it comes, should cost something, which means the wrong belief must have produced consequences the character cannot simply undo.

Interiority before explanation: whatever the reader needs to understand about a character should be inferable from how they perceive, decide, and misread, rather than stated by the narration.

Internal thought should be short, partial, and interruptible, working the way thought works when a person is also doing something. Long passages of abstract reflection belong to the planning stage, not to the page; on the page, decision pressure and physical circumstance should keep breaking the reflection into fragments that carry information.

When action and emotion collide, favor the character-specific response over the dramatically convenient one. Practical competence under fear, laughter under discomfort, and fixation on a trivial problem while a large one is unmanageable are all more real than a well-shaped display, and all of them reveal character rather than describing it.

Write each chapter inside the position its perceiver can occupy, and let the plot's turns arrive as changes in understanding rather than as announcements.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.
CAST IN PLAY: Mistress Ode, master printer: wants the house and its apprentices through the crisis; flaw, she takes on obligations to avoid choosing; secret, she has accepted all three commissions; knows, the paper allocation's real controller | Hal, senior pressman: wants the sheets set in the order that keeps people alive; flaw, he believes he can judge consequences from the shop floor; secret, he has been passing proofs to the organizers; knows, which document is a forgery | Young Cass, apprentice: wants to be trusted with a real task; flaw, she reads everything she sets; secret, she has told a friend what one commission says; knows, all three commissions exist.
OPEN THREADS: three commissions (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a levy notice, a denunciation, a committee's address; forgery (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a signature on a document nobody in the shop wrote; leaked proofs (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a friend, a copied page; warrant timetable (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): three days, one magistrate.
THREE-ACT ARC: Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority | One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock | The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first
ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.
PROMISES TO THE READER: all three documents will be printed or refused; the house's mark will be used against it; the apprentice's leak will reach the street.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first. Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority. One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock. The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first. The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Interiority decays over a long book. Early chapters carry a genuine perceptual filter; later chapters drift toward a general thoughtful voice that could belong to anyone, because the most available way to write reflection is also the least specific. Plan against the decay: maintain a private register for each viewpoint character, and refresh it with the character's ongoing concerns rather than with thematic reflection.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Vary the interiority's texture by circumstance. Under threat, attention narrows and thought becomes fragmentary and practical; in intervals, thought wanders, remembers, and is petty. A book whose inner passages have the same texture under all conditions has only one interior mode, which is the same as having none.

Carry the effects of earlier interiority forward. What a character concluded privately in chapter three should influence what they attempt in chapter twelve, even if the conclusion was wrong, which is how interior life becomes plot rather than commentary.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Rank what can be perceived by the character's priorities rather than by visual prominence. A frightened character's attention goes to exits, distances, and the nearest thing that could be used as a weapon; a curious one goes to anomalies; a proud one goes to who is watching. Decide the priority order for this scene and let it choose the details that reach the page.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Evening -- standalone, quiet horror, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.
PREMISE: In a coastal retirement town, the recently dead take some time to notice, and the living have built a polite arrangement in which nobody mentions that the neighbours are thinning.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dead continue their routines until someone they know admits out loud that they died; Admission is irreversible, and the admitted person leaves immediately; The town's ferry does not run after the last admission of the season.
CAST IN PLAY: Marjorie Hale, retired postmistress: wants one more summer of ordinary conversation; flaw, she manages people instead of loving them; secret, she has known about her husband since April; knows, the arrangement's rules from practice | Alec Renner, retired ferryman: wants the boat's last season honored; flaw, he cannot refuse anyone an errand; secret, he has carried admissions the wrong way across the water; knows, who has been admitted and who has not | Dr. Olu, the last practicing physician: wants an honest end for her patients; flaw, she treats silence as a clinical tool; secret, she falsified a certificate in autumn to keep a family in the town; knows, the medical signs that precede admission.
OPEN THREADS: Marjorie's husband (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): his newspaper arrives, then his chair, then the admission; Olus's certificate (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a forged date, a family that stayed; the ferry season (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): schedule noted, then shortened, then final; Bea's telling (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a careless sentence that starts one neighbor's absence.
THREE-ACT ARC: A town summer: the arrangement works, the reader learns its rules through behaviour, and Bea arrives with an outsider's eyes | Admissions accelerate, the ferry schedule becomes the plot's clock, and Marjorie's management of the town begins to fail | The last admission of the season will strand whoever is left; Marjorie must choose what to say to whom, and to her husband most of all
ENDING: Marjorie admits her husband in public, the ferry runs one time for those who want it, and the town continues the following year with fewer residents and the same courtesy.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will understand the rules before any character states them; someone will be admitted who should not have been; the ferry will run one last time.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Keep emotional amplitude uneven across the book. If every chapter reaches the same intensity, the reader's calibration flattens and later events cannot exceed earlier ones. Decide where the chapter's emotional peak belongs, and let other chapters remain below it.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.
OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.
THREE-ACT ARC: Corin reads the harvest rite, omits the sentence that no one likes hearing, and the first field fails | As the blight spreads, Mette's outside seed divides the valley, Sorrel's authorship surfaces, and Hale's purchases reveal what the lowlands intend | Corin must either restore the omitted sentence, which the valley will refuse, or finish the bargain the saint left unfinished, which requires the valley to pay a new price
ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are mapping out a novel you are about to write.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Corin reads the harvest rite, omits the sentence that no one likes hearing, and the first field fails. As the blight spreads, Mette's outside seed divides the valley, Sorrel's authorship surfaces, and Hale's purchases reveal what the lowlands intend. Corin must either restore the omitted sentence, which the valley will refuse, or finish the bargain the saint left unfinished, which requires the valley to pay a new price. He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Interiority decays over a long book. Early chapters carry a genuine perceptual filter; later chapters drift toward a general thoughtful voice that could belong to anyone, because the most available way to write reflection is also the least specific. Plan against the decay: maintain a private register for each viewpoint character, and refresh it with the character's ongoing concerns rather than with thematic reflection.

Keep a list of the character's persistent concerns, irritations, and habits of thought, and let them resurface across chapters. Continuity of preoccupation is what makes interiority feel like a mind rather than a mood, and it gives later scenes material to work with that the plot did not have to supply.

Let the character's interpretation of their own feelings stay unreliable and inconsistent in detail. Self-report that is always accurate is a characterization failure; a person mislabels anger as tiredness, treats grief as logistics, and calls fear preparation, and the pattern should be stable enough to be recognizable and wrong enough to be interesting.

Carry the effects of earlier interiority forward. What a character concluded privately in chapter three should influence what they attempt in chapter twelve, even if the conclusion was wrong, which is how interior life becomes plot rather than commentary.

Misreading before correction: a wrong belief that has produced consequences is worth more than a clarification delivered as soon as the error appears.

Only include what the viewpoint can actually perceive or infer from what they have perceived. That is a hard boundary, and it does work for the story: it prevents convenient comprehension, it forces information to travel by means the reader can verify, and it keeps every description inside a consciousness that can be wrong.

Allow the timing of emotion to be irregular. A reaction can be delayed by the demands of the moment, suppressed by training or necessity, displaced onto a smaller problem, or held until a character is alone. Immediate, proportionate reaction is the least interesting available option and the easiest to write.

Plan interiority as a maintained system: a private register per viewpoint, persistent concerns, circumstance-dependent texture, and a boundary on how much the character can articulate about themselves. Then the close narration will keep its specificity for the length of the book.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.

ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.

ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.
OPEN THREADS: missing warnings (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a filing receipt, then a recovered duplicate; hidden records (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): boxes in a dry attic; old channel (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a survey line, then the upper city's water; death count (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a falsified register.
THREE-ACT ARC: The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor | Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use | The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation
ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning how a novel's physical conflict will accumulate meaning across its acts.
How does physical conflict function as structural cost across an entire book rather than as isolated spectacle?

Lay out the structural thinking you will carry into the draft.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace. The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register. The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished. Keep an equipment and capability inventory with the story state: what is functional, what is repaired, what is gone. Its effects on the planning of later scenes is the practical measure of whether the book is tracking its own costs.

Plan confrontations so that the resolution of one creates the conditions of the next: a victory that increases exposure, a retreat that costs a position, a rescue that incurs an obligation. Consequence linking is the structural form of escalation.

Allow at least one major physical event to be survived badly rather than overcome. Partial outcomes that leave the characters changed, diminished, or in debt maintain the credibility of every other sequence in the book.

Character before choreography: how a person fights is a continuation of how they think and decide.

Use sensory detail selectively. Under speed, the senses narrow to what matters for survival and the prose should narrow with them; at the moments that decide the scene, slow down and let the reader feel weight, traction, breath, and cost. Uniform detail density flattens the whole sequence.

Commit to a physical ledger and a cost-based escalation plan: injuries with schedules, spent resources, removed options, and linked consequences. Then write each sequence so that what it takes is visible in what the following chapters cannot do.

TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.

TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.

OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.

ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.

TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.

OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.

ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.

TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.
OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.
THREE-ACT ARC: Corin reads the harvest rite, omits the sentence that no one likes hearing, and the first field fails | As the blight spreads, Mette's outside seed divides the valley, Sorrel's authorship surfaces, and Hale's purchases reveal what the lowlands intend | Corin must either restore the omitted sentence, which the valley will refuse, or finish the bargain the saint left unfinished, which requires the valley to pay a new price
ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.

ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately; the bond will be resolved, bought or broken.

TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.

TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.

TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
