Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.

TITLE: The Long Evening -- standalone, quiet horror, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.
PREMISE: In a coastal retirement town, the recently dead take some time to notice, and the living have built a polite arrangement in which nobody mentions that the neighbours are thinning.

OPEN THREADS: Marjorie's husband (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): his newspaper arrives, then his chair, then the admission; Olus's certificate (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a forged date, a family that stayed; the ferry season (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): schedule noted, then shortened, then final; Bea's telling (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a careless sentence that starts one neighbor's absence.

TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.
OPEN THREADS: the cellar (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a search grid gap, then an excavation request; the object (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): carried then, kept now; sealed statement (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a transcript with an omission; second exit (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a plan, then a door under plaster.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.
CAST IN PLAY: Surveyor Alder, the narrator: wants an accurate map and a promotion; flaw, he believes accuracy is neutral; secret, he has left two settlements off the preliminary sheet; knows, the map will displace whoever it records | Lieutenant Cray, escort commander: wants the valley pacified without casualties; flaw, he needs the expedition to justify itself; secret, he has authorization to remove settlements that resist; knows, the compensation schedule's inadequacy | Mira, valley guide: wants her village registered under its own name; flaw, she trusted the party's ledger; secret, she has been guiding the survey to the settlements least able to leave; knows, the valley's flood seasons.
OPEN THREADS: preliminary sheet (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a filed map, then a removal order; compensation schedule (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): payment per acre, assessed from the map; removal authorization (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a written power the surveyor must sign; flood season (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a road that closes for five months.
THREE-ACT ARC: The party enters the valley, the survey begins, and Alder's preliminary sheet is sent to the capital without his approval | Mira's guidance, Cray's authorization, and the compensation schedule intersect; the filed sheet's consequences reach the valley | The flood season closes the only road, the escort demands its authorization, and Alder must choose what the final map will say
ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.
THREE-ACT ARC: Sessions establish terms; Jun alters one position to prevent a stalemate; the visitors confirm it back exactly, which tells the delegation nothing | The alteration costs the delegation its mining leverage; Sabel's recordings surface; Ollun demonstrates knowledge of the delegation's private arguments | The window closes with an unsigned treaty; Jun must either admit the manipulation publicly or deliver an exchange built on it
ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Ilsa Verrane, junior archivist: wants to keep her post and her mother's medical debt off the block; flaw, she edits what she cannot face; secret, she has been copying sealed pages for two years; knows, the seal sequence changed after the flood | Registrar Otte, keeper of the seals: wants to hold the city together through one more winter; flaw, he treats people as accounts; secret, he ordered the re-sequencing himself to pay for grain; knows, the grain ships never arrived | Cassian Rhee, debt collector for the merchant floor: wants his brother's seal released; flaw, violence is his first fluent language; secret, he owes the register more than his brother does; knows, Ilsa copies pages.

TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.

OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.

PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Slow Light -- standalone, science fiction, generation ship.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Eleven generations into a voyage whose destination no longer exists, a ship's council must decide whether to turn the vessel around, and the only functioning navigation officer is nineteen.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Ship law permits a course change only with the concurrence of three departments; Life support is rationed by population segment, and the segments vote; Navigation data cannot be transmitted between decks without passing the council.

OPEN THREADS: the missing star (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a dark frame, then a verifiable absence; unauthorized deceleration (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): fuel figures trending wrong; drive wear reports (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): tolerances, then a forging pen; birth deck organizing (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): ration complaints, then a vote bloc.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tavi discovers the star's absence, tries to report it through channels, and is folded into the concealment she wanted to break | The three departments trade the truth for ration shares; the drive-room wear reports become the leverage; the birth decks organize | Turning the ship requires one burn and one irreversible vote, and the only person who can pilot it is the person with the least authority
ENDING: The ship decelerates toward an empty system with a usable belt, the voyage ends without arrival, and the population becomes a settlement rather than a crew.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what is at the destination; the course will change or the concealment will hold; the ship's population will vote on something that cannot be undone.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's sea wall work is funded by a levy charged to properties above the high-water line; The couple's house is below the line and cannot be repaired after a flood without a licensed surveyor; The harbour's fishing fleet is co-owned in shares that must be sold to existing holders.
CAST IN PLAY: Aidan, harbour master, the husband: wants the house repaired and the marriage continued without discussion; flaw, he maintains things instead of understanding them; secret, he has been quietly selling his fleet shares to cover the flood damage; knows, the sea wall's true schedule | Bryn, surveyor, the wife: wants the marriage assessed honestly before the season ends; flaw, she mistakes accuracy for kindness; secret, she has accepted a post in another county and not told him; knows, the house cannot be sold or insured in its current state | Ondine, Bryn's colleague and client: wants the sea wall built before spring; flaw, she values the town's survival over its people's arrangements; secret, her survey supports using the couple's property line as the wall's footing; knows, the levy's distribution.

THREE-ACT ARC: A flood damages the house; the two spouses disagree about repair, sale, and what the damage means | The wall survey, the share sales, and the job offer surface in the wrong order, and each spouse reads the other's decision as betrayal | The final storm decides the house, and the choice is between a marriage held together by property and two separate lives that are both viable
ENDING: The house is condemned and demolished for the wall footing, the fleet shares are gone, and the two of them separate with the paperwork clean and no reconciliation scene.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the sea wall will be built or abandoned; the house will be decided by the season; one of them will say the decisive thing out loud.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.
PREMISE: A records officer in a ministry that assigns citizens to work discovers that her own file has been edited to make her suitable for a job she has been doing for six years.

ENDING: She submits nothing, her brother is reassigned out of the city, and she stays in the section with her file still wrong and her corrections stopped.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.

ENDING: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.

TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.

Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.

OPEN THREADS: flood damage (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): water in the floor, then a condemned structure; share sales (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a ledger of shares, then an empty holding; job offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a letter, a date, a county; wall footing (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a survey line through the back garden.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.

OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.

instruction:

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.

TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.

TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Fell, cataloguer, the narrator: wants the commission finished and paid so she can settle a debt; flaw, she trusts documents over people; secret, she has already indexed one owner out of existence; knows, the rooms move when she is not looking | Mrs. Ivey, housekeeper, second of her name: wants the house inhabited the way it was; flaw, she serves the arrangement instead of questioning it; secret, she has been in the house since before the current owners and remembers two more; knows, which owners the previous cataloguer removed | Mr. Lamb, owner who hired her: wants his family's library kept intact and his house entered from outside; flaw, he bargains without understanding the terms; secret, he has not been outside in eleven years; knows, the previous cataloguer's fate.
OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ada arrives, is given rules she does not believe, and finds the previous index with entries in three hands | As she indexes, the house's occupancy thins; the owners become attentive to her work in ways that are not merely proprietary | She must decide whether to finish the index, which will fix the house's population to what she chooses, or to leave the index open and remain inside
ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.

TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.
OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.

ENDING: The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.

Give each speaker an identifiable verbal world derived from personality, background, confidence, age, relationship, and current circumstance. Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.

Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Wolf Road -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, travel and pursuit.
POV AND DISTANCE: limited third rotating among three travelers, past tense.
PREMISE: Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The passes open on a schedule nobody controls, and the last opening strands travelers until spring; Travelers share salt and fire by custom, and breaking the custom is the only crime the road recognizes; The pursuing company cannot cross until the pass freezes hard, which gives a fixed head start.
CAST IN PLAY: Rusk, guide: wants to reach the far side without the others; flaw, he lies by omission and calls it protection; secret, he is leading them away from the pass deliberately; knows, the true pass and its closing date | Aveline Tarn, courier carrying a treaty: wants delivery before the season closes; flaw, she treats everyone as a liability; secret, the treaty is forged and she knows it; knows, the pursuers are her own people | Ossian, physician fleeing a charge: wants to reach a place where his hands are unknown; flaw, he helps compulsively and resents it; secret, he killed a patient through a mistake, not malice; knows, Rusk's route contradicts every map.
OPEN THREADS: wrong route (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): map discrepancies, then Rusk's silence, then his reason; treaty (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): sealed case, then a broken seal, then the forgery named; Ossian's charge (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a rumor at a waystation, then a survivor; Selv's orders (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a written order, then a second order.

ENDING: They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the road will be crossed or the season closes on them; the guide's lie will be exposed before the end; the travelers will learn what each is carrying.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Plan the book's knowledge from the end state backward. At the final page, who must know what, and what must the reader have understood. Then design the sequence of movements by which the three positions, reader, protagonist, and world, arrive at that state, and place the story's reversals at the moments of largest relative motion.

Chart the reader's knowledge as a curve with deliberate plateaus and climbs. Long flats, where nothing significant is learned, starve curiosity; constant climbing exhausts it. Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

Plan the knowledge gaps between characters as sources of conflict independent of their goals. Two people wanting the same thing but knowing different amounts will collide differently than their aligned aims suggest: the better-informed one's patience, the worse-informed one's confidence. Let the information differences, not just the desire differences, drive the cast's collisions.

Track character knowledge separately from what the book has established for the reader. A character may only act on information they possess, and any scene that requires a character to know something they were never told is a structural error, not a detail to fix later.

Set the knowledge arc in place: the reader's curve, the convergence points, the narrative-held facts with their fair trails, and the character-to-character gaps. Draft from the map, and every scene's information decisions will have a reason the structure can name.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Plan the knowledge arc of the whole book: how the reader's and the characters' knowledge grow, gap, and converge from first page to last.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Set the load-bearing decisions down in full, so the draft has something solid to stand on.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying. The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient. The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating. The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her. Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Plan the book's knowledge from the end state backward. At the final page, who must know what, and what must the reader have understood. Then design the sequence of movements by which the three positions, reader, protagonist, and world, arrive at that state, and place the story's reversals at the moments of largest relative motion.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

Decide which knowledge is withheld from everyone, held only by the narrative itself. This is the most powerful and most dangerous position: it generates the fairest surprises and the worst cheats. For each narrative-held fact, require a fair trail, perceivable in hindsight, that a rereading reader can follow from the first page.

Plan the knowledge gaps between characters as sources of conflict independent of their goals. Two people wanting the same thing but knowing different amounts will collide differently than their aligned aims suggest: the better-informed one's patience, the worse-informed one's confidence. Let the information differences, not just the desire differences, drive the cast's collisions.

The reader's curiosity is a budget you spend: every withheld fact must be worth its carrying cost, every answered question must purchase more attention than it closes. Manage the ledger ruthlessly.

Carry consequences forward across chapters rather than resetting to a neutral baseline. Fatigue, resentment, trust, debt, and reputation should all reflect what has happened, and the gradual accumulation of that reflection is what makes a long book feel cumulative rather than episodic.

Keep characters from explaining what they already know for the reader's benefit. Information in dialogue should be information someone has a reason to say aloud: a challenge, a correction, a lie, a question that conceals a different question. Where the reader needs a fact and no speaker would state it, move the fact out of the conversation entirely.

Set the knowledge arc in place: the reader's curve, the convergence points, the narrative-held facts with their fair trails, and the character-to-character gaps. Draft from the map, and every scene's information decisions will have a reason the structure can name.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Ilsa Verrane, junior archivist: wants to keep her post and her mother's medical debt off the block; flaw, she edits what she cannot face; secret, she has been copying sealed pages for two years; knows, the seal sequence changed after the flood | Registrar Otte, keeper of the seals: wants to hold the city together through one more winter; flaw, he treats people as accounts; secret, he ordered the re-sequencing himself to pay for grain; knows, the grain ships never arrived | Cassian Rhee, debt collector for the merchant floor: wants his brother's seal released; flaw, violence is his first fluent language; secret, he owes the register more than his brother does; knows, Ilsa copies pages.
OPEN THREADS: the altered sequence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): anomaly noticed, then dismissed, then provable; mother's medical debt (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): refinanced twice, then transferred; carter fire plot (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): accelerant cached, dates moved twice; Otte's grain payments (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): receipts referenced, never shown.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ilsa finds the anomaly in the sequence, tests it, and is caught copying by Cassian, who uses her instead of reporting her | The two of them trace the re-sequencing to Otte while the carters plan a fire; Ilsa's mother's seal comes up for transfer and the market price of mercy collapses | Ilsa must choose between publishing the true ledger, which would free the poor but strip the city's grain credit, and burning the register, which would kill thousands of sealed debtors including her mother
ENDING: She publishes the ledger, transfers her mother's seal to her own name, and stays in the archive she has just ruined, which is the only place the rebuilding can happen.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the ledger will be exposed or destroyed by the end; Ilsa's copying habit will cost her something specific; the poor's seals will be settled one way or the other.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Decide the allocation between surprise and suspense across the book: which questions are withheld from the reader, and which are granted early to burn.

Lay out the structural thinking you will carry into the draft.
response:
The promises this book has already made are on the record: the ledger will be exposed or destroyed by the end; Ilsa's copying habit will cost her something specific. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. Ilsa finds the anomaly in the sequence, tests it, and is caught copying by Cassian, who uses her instead of reporting her. The two of them trace the re-sequencing to Otte while the carters plan a fire; Ilsa's mother's seal comes up for transfer and the market price of mercy collapses. Ilsa must choose between publishing the true ledger, which would free the poor but strip the city's grain credit, and burning the register, which would kill thousands of sealed debtors including her mother. She publishes the ledger, transfers her mother's seal to her own name, and stays in the archive she has just ruined, which is the only place the rebuilding can happen. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Plan the tension modes as a portfolio. A book of pure surprise resets to zero with each reveal; a book of pure suspense spends its dread in one long note. Decide the mix for each movement: where the reader should hold knowledge the characters lack, and where they should be one step behind, and where the two positions trade.

Grant suspense its fuel early and completely. The scenario that will burn for two hundred pages must be delivered to the reader in full: what is coming, roughly when, and what it will mean. Withheld suspense is not suspense but confusion, and the dread you want is only available to a reader who knows exactly enough to fear precisely.

Interleave the modes at the sequence level. After a surprise, the reader must rebuild their model, which is a moment of heightened attention; a stretch of suspense immediately after, with the new knowledge granted, converts that attention into dread. Plan the alternation deliberately: shock, then the long burn the shock enables.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

The strongest disclosure changes the past rather than adding to it. Rank revelations by how much prior material they recolor, and stage them where the recoloring can still alter a decision.

Dialogue is speech shaped by situation, relationship, and purpose, not prose wearing quotation marks. Fix what each speaker wants out of the exchange and what each is unwilling to say before writing the exchange, because those two facts generate the shape of the conversation more reliably than any line-by-line plan.

Treat the story state as a live ledger carried into the chapter: injuries and their recovery stage, possessions and who holds them, promises made and to whom, secrets and exactly who knows them, unresolved threads, and the last significant conversation each pair of characters had. Assemble the ledger before drafting and update it after.

Fix the portfolio: which questions are granted early to burn, which are held to detonate, and how the modes alternate across the book's movements. Draft with the allocation in hand, and the tension will have architecture rather than weather.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.
OPEN THREADS: eleven exemptions (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a weekly habit, then a pattern in a report; brother's score (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a threshold, a warning letter, a deadline; evasion group (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a meeting, then a distributed method; update history (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): nightly shifts, then a readable archive.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rosa grants a first unwarranted exemption, discovers how easy it is, and starts a weekly pattern she tells herself is mercy | The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail | Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other
ENDING: She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the score actually measures; Rosa's pattern will be discovered; the exemption budget will run out.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail. Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Surprise and suspense draw on the same resource, the reader's knowledge, in opposite ways: surprise withholds, suspense grants. Before drafting, allocate: which of the story's major questions will be answered early and allowed to generate dread, and which will be held to detonate. The allocation is the book's tension architecture.

Grant suspense its fuel early and completely. The scenario that will burn for two hundred pages must be delivered to the reader in full: what is coming, roughly when, and what it will mean. Withheld suspense is not suspense but confusion, and the dread you want is only available to a reader who knows exactly enough to fear precisely.

Spend surprise on recontextualization rather than on novelty. The withheld revelation should change the meaning of what the reader already holds, not simply add a new fact, because recontextualizing surprise compounds backward through the book, making the reader's memory itself a scene of the story.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

The reader's curiosity is a budget you spend: every withheld fact must be worth its carrying cost, every answered question must purchase more attention than it closes. Manage the ledger ruthlessly.

Let subtext and evasion do the work. Characters can lie, refuse, stall, deflect, answer a different question, or defend themselves against an attack that never came. The gap between what is said and what is happening is where dialogue becomes drama instead of transcription.

Re-read the relevant earlier material before writing a chapter that depends on it, especially when the dependence is on a conversation, a physical description, or a decision from many chapters back. Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.

Fix the portfolio: which questions are granted early to burn, which are held to detonate, and how the modes alternate across the book's movements. Draft with the allocation in hand, and the tension will have architecture rather than weather.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.

ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the roll will be read aloud with something wrong in it; the sealing rule will be applied to someone the reader knows; the year will end with a count that matters.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before drafting, map the second as deliberately as the first: what each major character knows at each stage, what the reader knows, and where the gaps sit. Every scene's tension can then be read off the map, and every reveal can be scheduled where the map says the pressure peaks.

Chart the reader's knowledge as a curve with deliberate plateaus and climbs. Long flats, where nothing significant is learned, starve curiosity; constant climbing exhausts it. Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

Commit to the schedule: which knowledge moves when, where reader and character meet, and what the final state of knowing must be. Write forward with the map in hand, and let each scene move exactly one position, on purpose.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.
CAST IN PLAY: Marguerite, shift supervisor, eighteen years: wants the shift closed clean and the report signed; flaw, she protects the shift from management and from itself; secret, she has been signing reports with an outdated injury count; knows, the conveyor's failure pattern | Nate, forklift operator: wants the promotion that requires a clean record; flaw, he trades truth for advancement; secret, he reported a colleague's near-miss as his own error to look diligent; knows, the loading bay's blind corner | Sofia, agency worker, six weeks: wants to be kept on after the season; flaw, she will not report anything that creates a form; secret, she has been working with a wrist injury for nine days; knows, the exact rate the line is set to.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.
THREE-ACT ARC: The council opens, the seven-day clock begins, and Nissa's first report proves false in a way that serves both sides | Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact | The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her
ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.

ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.

Plan the tension modes as a portfolio. A book of pure surprise resets to zero with each reveal; a book of pure suspense spends its dread in one long note. Decide the mix for each movement: where the reader should hold knowledge the characters lack, and where they should be one step behind, and where the two positions trade.

Grant suspense its fuel early and completely. The scenario that will burn for two hundred pages must be delivered to the reader in full: what is coming, roughly when, and what it will mean. Withheld suspense is not suspense but confusion, and the dread you want is only available to a reader who knows exactly enough to fear precisely.

Plan the alternation deliberately: shock, then the long burn the shock enables.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

Information is the substance of story: events are only the occasions on which knowledge changes hands. Plan who knows what at every stage, and the drama can be read directly off the map.

Keep the wit budget low and distributed. Not every exchange can be sharp, not every character can deliver the perfect comeback, and the perfect response that arrives five minutes later is more useful characterization than the one that arrives on time. Humor should come from personality, circumstance, timing, or contrast rather than from an obligation to be funny.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years. The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes. A novel has two plots: the plot of events and the plot of knowledge. Before drafting, map the second as deliberately as the first: what each major character knows at each stage, what the reader knows, and where the gaps sit. Every scene's tension can then be read off the map, and every reveal can be scheduled where the map says the pressure peaks.

Chart the reader's knowledge as a curve with deliberate plateaus and climbs. Long flats, where nothing significant is learned, starve curiosity; constant climbing exhausts it. Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Decide which knowledge is withheld from everyone, held only by the narrative itself. This is the most powerful and most dangerous position: it generates the fairest surprises and the worst cheats. For each narrative-held fact, require a fair trail, perceivable in hindsight, that a rereading reader can follow from the first page.

Plan the knowledge gaps between characters as sources of conflict independent of their goals. Two people wanting the same thing but knowing different amounts will collide differently than their aligned aims suggest: the better-informed one's patience, the worse-informed one's confidence. Let the information differences, not just the desire differences, drive the cast's collisions.

The strongest disclosure changes the past rather than adding to it. Rank revelations by how much prior material they recolor, and stage them where the recoloring can still alter a decision.

Allow conversation to be inefficient. Interruptions, hesitations, subject changes, irrelevant remarks, corrections, unfinished thoughts, laughter at the wrong moment, and answers to questions nobody asked all belong, because efficiency is a property of written information transfer rather than of speech.

Re-read the relevant earlier material before writing a chapter that depends on it, especially when the dependence is on a conversation, a physical description, or a decision from many chapters back. Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.

Commit to the schedule: which knowledge moves when, where reader and character meet, and what the final state of knowing must be. Write forward with the map in hand, and let each scene move exactly one position, on purpose.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.

ENDING: She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the score actually measures; Rosa's pattern will be discovered; the exemption budget will run out.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.
