instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.
THREE-ACT ARC: Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates | Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate | Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth
ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Fen Road -- standalone, survival, expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the medic.
PREMISE: A six-person survey team crossing a wetland loses its route markers and its leader, and the medic who has been falsifying fitness reports must decide who is fit enough to carry what.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The fen's causeway is passable only in the dry weeks and only at night, when the peat holds; The team's rations were calculated for a crossing of nine nights; Any team member left behind is entitled to the group's full share of supplies.
CAST IN PLAY: Ori, team medic: wants all six across with a clean report; flaw, she protects people by withholding information; secret, she passed two members who should have failed their fitness review; knows, the team's actual condition | Halvard, survey lead: wants the route completed and the map delivered; flaw, he decides by schedule; secret, he accepted the commission below the safe number of nights; knows, the rations are short | Sel, porter, youngest: wants to be paid and to be taken seriously; flaw, she hides injury to stay on the manifest; secret, she has been re-marking the route posts incorrectly; knows, the posts have been moved.
OPEN THREADS: falsified reviews (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two passing grades, two failing bodies; route posts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): posts in the wrong places; rations (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a count, then a recount; the left-behind rule (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): supplies set aside for an abandoned member.
THREE-ACT ARC: The team enters the fen, the marker discrepancies are small, and a first injury changes the pace | Rations, injuries, and the falsified fitness reviews collide; Halvard's schedule becomes the antagonist; the markers are proved wrong | Eight nights in, the causeway is behind them, one member cannot continue, and the group's own rule about being left behind becomes a live instrument
ENDING: They hold to the rule, abandon the survey, and cross four nights late with a documented route they will never sell.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will take fewer or more nights than planned; someone will be carried or left; the falsified reviews will matter to a decision.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before drafting, map the second as deliberately as the first: what each major character knows at each stage, what the reader knows, and where the gaps sit. Every scene's tension can then be read off the map, and every reveal can be scheduled where the map says the pressure peaks.

Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

The strongest disclosure changes the past rather than adding to it. Rank revelations by how much prior material they recolor, and stage them where the recoloring can still alter a decision.

Track character knowledge separately from what the book has established for the reader. A character may only act on information they possess, and any scene that requires a character to know something they were never told is a structural error, not a detail to fix later.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.
THREE-ACT ARC: The council opens, the seven-day clock begins, and Nissa's first report proves false in a way that serves both sides | Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact | The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her
ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Grant suspense its fuel early and completely. The scenario that will burn for two hundred pages must be delivered to the reader in full: what is coming, roughly when, and what it will mean. Interleave the modes at the sequence level. After a surprise, the reader must rebuild their model, which is a moment of heightened attention; a stretch of suspense immediately after, with the new knowledge granted, converts that attention into dread. Plan the alternation deliberately: shock, then the long burn the shock enables.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

The reader's curiosity is a budget you spend: every withheld fact must be worth its carrying cost, every answered question must purchase more attention than it closes. Manage the ledger ruthlessly.

Keep characters from explaining what they already know for the reader's benefit. Information in dialogue should be information someone has a reason to say aloud: a challenge, a correction, a lie, a question that conceals a different question. Where the reader needs a fact and no speaker would state it, move the fact out of the conversation entirely.

Whatever state the chapter inherits must be reflected in behavior, not merely noted. An injured arm, a broken trust, a debt owed: these are conditions that constrain the scene's options, and any chapter that logs a condition without being changed by it has not really carried it forward.

Commit to the allocation and both terminal conditions: suspense resolved through agency, surprise reconstructable in memory. Write toward the first long burn now, with its fuel scheduled for early and complete delivery.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Slow Light -- standalone, science fiction, generation ship.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Eleven generations into a voyage whose destination no longer exists, a ship's council must decide whether to turn the vessel around, and the only functioning navigation officer is nineteen.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Ship law permits a course change only with the concurrence of three departments; Life support is rationed by population segment, and the segments vote; Navigation data cannot be transmitted between decks without passing the council.
CAST IN PLAY: Tavi Osen, navigation officer, nineteen: wants the ship pointed somewhere real; flaw, she trusts the instruments more than the people; secret, she has been decelerating without authorization; knows, the destination star has been gone for decades | Councillor Bess, chair of the livestock segment: wants her population fed and her seat kept; flaw, she trades in order rather than in outcomes; secret, she has known about the missing star for six years; knows, the ration math behind the concealment | Engineer Ho, drive-room chief: wants the drive run within tolerances; flaw, he identifies with the machinery; secret, he has been falsifying the drive's wear reports; knows, the ship can decelerate once and never accelerate again.
OPEN THREADS: the missing star (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a dark frame, then a verifiable absence; unauthorized deceleration (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): fuel figures trending wrong; drive wear reports (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): tolerances, then a forging pen; birth deck organizing (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): ration complaints, then a vote bloc.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tavi discovers the star's absence, tries to report it through channels, and is folded into the concealment she wanted to break | The three departments trade the truth for ration shares; the drive-room wear reports become the leverage; the birth decks organize | Turning the ship requires one burn and one irreversible vote, and the only person who can pilot it is the person with the least authority
ENDING: The ship decelerates toward an empty system with a usable belt, the voyage ends without arrival, and the population becomes a settlement rather than a crew.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what is at the destination; the course will change or the concealment will hold; the ship's population will vote on something that cannot be undone.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. The three departments trade the truth for ration shares; the drive-room wear reports become the leverage; the birth decks organize. Turning the ship requires one burn and one irreversible vote, and the only person who can pilot it is the person with the least authority. The ship decelerates toward an empty system with a usable belt, the voyage ends without arrival, and the population becomes a settlement rather than a crew. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Plan the book's knowledge from the end state backward. At the final page, who must know what, and what must the reader have understood. Then design the sequence of movements by which the three positions, reader, protagonist, and world, arrive at that state, and place the story's reversals at the moments of largest relative motion.

Chart the reader's knowledge as a curve with deliberate plateaus and climbs. Long flats, where nothing significant is learned, starve curiosity; constant climbing exhausts it. Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

Decide which knowledge is withheld from everyone, held only by the narrative itself. This is the most powerful and most dangerous position: it generates the fairest surprises and the worst cheats. For each narrative-held fact, require a fair trail, perceivable in hindsight, that a rereading reader can follow from the first page.

Information is the substance of story: events are only the occasions on which knowledge changes hands. Plan who knows what at every stage, and the drama can be read directly off the map.

Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.

Commit to the schedule: which knowledge moves when, where reader and character meet, and what the final state of knowing must be. Write forward with the map in hand, and let each scene move exactly one position, on purpose.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.
OPEN THREADS: moved stones (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): survey discrepancy, then proof, then a deliberate trap; Sera's raider dealings (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): supply ledgers, a survivor's testimony; brother's death (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): rumor, then the ward-fire's old scar; the offer behind the ward (opens chapter 6, pays off chapter 10): voices at the turning, then terms.
THREE-ACT ARC: Maren and Torell meet at the stones, each prepared to withdraw, and both are prevented by a third event: the ward fails early and something gets through | Forced to work together to reseat the stones, each betrays the arrangement in ways the other detects and misreads; the border settlements become the currency | The thing behind the ward offers each heir exactly what they want in exchange for the covenant broken; both nearly accept, and the resolution is a choice neither wanted
ENDING: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power. Maren and Torell meet at the stones, each prepared to withdraw, and both are prevented by a third event: the ward fails early and something gets through. Forced to work together to reseat the stones, each betrays the arrangement in ways the other detects and misreads; the border settlements become the currency. They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border. A novel has two plots: the plot of events and the plot of knowledge. Before drafting, map the second as deliberately as the first: what each major character knows at each stage, what the reader knows, and where the gaps sit. Every scene's tension can then be read off the map, and every reveal can be scheduled where the map says the pressure peaks.

Chart the reader's knowledge as a curve with deliberate plateaus and climbs. Long flats, where nothing significant is learned, starve curiosity; constant climbing exhausts it. Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

Plan the knowledge gaps between characters as sources of conflict independent of their goals. Two people wanting the same thing but knowing different amounts will collide differently than their aligned aims suggest: the better-informed one's patience, the worse-informed one's confidence. Let the information differences, not just the desire differences, drive the cast's collisions.

Withholding is a promise: the reader accepts darkness on the guarantee that the darkness is structured, motivated, and payable. Every unmotivated silence spends the guarantee, and the guarantee is not renewable.

Carry consequences forward across chapters rather than resetting to a neutral baseline. Fatigue, resentment, trust, debt, and reputation should all reflect what has happened, and the gradual accumulation of that reflection is what makes a long book feel cumulative rather than episodic.

Let subtext and evasion do the work. Characters can lie, refuse, stall, deflect, answer a different question, or defend themselves against an attack that never came. The gap between what is said and what is happening is where dialogue becomes drama instead of transcription.

Set the knowledge arc in place: the reader's curve, the convergence points, the narrative-held facts with their fair trails, and the character-to-character gaps. Draft from the map, and every scene's information decisions will have a reason the structure can name.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.
OPEN THREADS: the removed page (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report with a gap, then the missing sheet; the burned coat (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): ash in the stove, then a button; the girl's plan (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a bus timetable, a packed bag; Ruth's brother (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): an alibi, a dispute, a confession.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty. Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for. Surprise and suspense draw on the same resource, the reader's knowledge, in opposite ways: surprise withholds, suspense grants. Before drafting, allocate: which of the story's major questions will be answered early and allowed to generate dread, and which will be held to detonate. The allocation is the book's tension architecture.

Grant suspense its fuel early and completely. The scenario that will burn for two hundred pages must be delivered to the reader in full: what is coming, roughly when, and what it will mean. Withheld suspense is not suspense but confusion, and the dread you want is only available to a reader who knows exactly enough to fear precisely.

Interleave the modes at the sequence level. After a surprise, the reader must rebuild their model, which is a moment of heightened attention; a stretch of suspense immediately after, with the new knowledge granted, converts that attention into dread. Plan the alternation deliberately: shock, then the long burn the shock enables.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

The strongest disclosure changes the past rather than adding to it. Rank revelations by how much prior material they recolor, and stage them where the recoloring can still alter a decision.

Dialogue is speech shaped by situation, relationship, and purpose, not prose wearing quotation marks. Fix what each speaker wants out of the exchange and what each is unwilling to say before writing the exchange, because those two facts generate the shape of the conversation more reliably than any line-by-line plan.

Whatever state the chapter inherits must be reflected in behavior, not merely noted. An injured arm, a broken trust, a debt owed: these are conditions that constrain the scene's options, and any chapter that logs a condition without being changed by it has not really carried it forward.

Fix the portfolio: which questions are granted early to burn, which are held to detonate, and how the modes alternate across the book's movements. Draft with the allocation in hand, and the tension will have architecture rather than weather.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.
CAST IN PLAY: Priya, bakery owner, three generations: wants the family shop kept open through the season; flaw, she hears every suggestion as a takeover; secret, she has already taken a loan against the building she does not own; knows, the landlord's redevelopment plans | Dan, cafe owner, second year: wants a business that lasts past the following spring; flaw, he solves problems by spending; secret, his cafe is funded by severance from the company he left; knows, the association's voting arithmetic | Mr. Hallow, landlord: wants one tenant paying a single higher rent; flaw, he uses courteous language as leverage; secret, he has a development partner waiting on the outcome; knows, the lease's co-signature clause and its limits.
OPEN THREADS: co-lease (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a shared signature, then a joint renewal notice; loan against the building (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a bank letter, a repayment schedule; buyout clause (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): an assessor's appointment; development offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price, a deadline.

ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.

CAST IN PLAY: Nia, stage manager, sixteen: wants the production to open; flaw, she manages other people's feelings instead of stating her own; secret, she gave the supervisor's notes to the principal; knows, the supervisor's medical leave | Mr. Okafor, drama teacher and supervisor: wants the cast protected from the reason he is being investigated; flaw, he handles accusation by going quiet; secret, a complaint has been filed against him and he has not told the students; knows, the cancellation's real cause | Devi, lead actor, Nia's best friend: wants the play and the audition tape that will get her out of this town; flaw, she reads every delay as a personal insult; secret, she recorded a rehearsal to use as an audition tape; knows, the recording exists.

TITLE: Paper Mill -- standalone, thriller, corporate whistleblower.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Cold Communion -- standalone, horror, isolated research station.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, present tense, two scientists.
PREMISE: At a monastery station studying a silence that behaves like a substance, two researchers discover the discipline that keeps them safe is the same discipline that has been feeding the phenomenon.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The phenomenon occupies measured silence and can be displaced by noise, but it returns to any space left quiet; The station's rule forbids speech outside the chanting hours; Every recorded measurement taken during the silence has been altered before it reaches the archive.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Ilse Ko, acoustics researcher: wants a publishable measurement and an exit; flaw, she measures instead of protecting; secret, she falsified a baseline to get funded; knows, the archive has been edited | Brother Anton, station's chanting master: wants the discipline kept; flaw, he would rather lose a person than a rule; secret, he has been altering the archive at the order's instruction; knows, the silence grows where people stop speaking | Dr. Piedra, geologist, second researcher: wants the station closed and everyone out; flaw, she advocates with contempt; secret, she has stopped sleeping in her own room and will not say why; knows, the measured silence does not obey containment.
OPEN THREADS: edited archive (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a warm number in a cold month, then the order's instruction; falsified baseline (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a funding timeline, then a confession read into the record; Piedra's room (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a room she avoids, a recorded hum; the missing year (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Ren's memory, then the chant book's blank pages.
THREE-ACT ARC: The researchers arrive, learn the discipline, and record the first anomaly during a chant | Measurements diverge from the archive, the silence begins to occupy rooms that people leave, and the two researchers split on whether to publish or flee | Publishing requires speech, and the station's rule makes speech a weapon; the order must choose between the archive and the building
ENDING: The researchers broadcast their measurements aloud, breaking the discipline and displacing the phenomenon out of the station, and the monastery is abandoned as a ruin full of unedited records.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what silence carries; the discipline will be broken or the station lost; the altered archive will be read aloud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.

TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.

instruction:

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.
OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.
THREE-ACT ARC: Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged | Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds | Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public
ENDING: The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The promises this book has already made are on the record: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged. Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds. Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public. The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Surprise and suspense draw on the same resource, the reader's knowledge, in opposite ways: surprise withholds, suspense grants. Before drafting, allocate: which of the story's major questions will be answered early and allowed to generate dread, and which will be held to detonate. The allocation is the book's tension architecture.

Spend surprise on recontextualization rather than on novelty. The withheld revelation should change the meaning of what the reader already holds, not simply add a new fact, because recontextualizing surprise compounds backward through the book, making the reader's memory itself a scene of the story.

Interleave the modes at the sequence level. After a surprise, the reader must rebuild their model, which is a moment of heightened attention; a stretch of suspense immediately after, with the new knowledge granted, converts that attention into dread. Plan the alternation deliberately: shock, then the long burn the shock enables.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

Withholding is a promise: the reader accepts darkness on the guarantee that the darkness is structured, motivated, and payable. Every unmotivated silence spends the guarantee, and the guarantee is not renewable.

Give each speaker an identifiable verbal world derived from personality, background, confidence, age, relationship, and current circumstance. Vocabulary, sentence length, willingness to interrupt, tolerance for silence, and preferred evasion should differ measurably between characters and stay stable across the book.

Keep unresolved threads and their intended resolutions visible in the working notes. A thread tracked only in memory is likely to be dropped, and a thread that disappears without recognition teaches the reader that the book's promises are unreliable.

Commit to the allocation and both terminal conditions: suspense resolved through agency, surprise reconstructable in memory. Write toward the first long burn now, with its fuel scheduled for early and complete delivery.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.
OPEN THREADS: missing warnings (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a filing receipt, then a recovered duplicate; hidden records (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): boxes in a dry attic; old channel (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a survey line, then the upper city's water; death count (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a falsified register.
THREE-ACT ARC: The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor | Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use | The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation
ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

response:
The promises this book has already made are on the record: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor. Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use. The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation. The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Plan the book's knowledge from the end state backward. At the final page, who must know what, and what must the reader have understood. Then design the sequence of movements by which the three positions, reader, protagonist, and world, arrive at that state, and place the story's reversals at the moments of largest relative motion.

Chart the reader's knowledge as a curve with deliberate plateaus and climbs. Long flats, where nothing significant is learned, starve curiosity; constant climbing exhausts it. Choose three or four major climbs, spaced across the book, each one a reorganization of what the reader understands, and let the flats between them be spent on deepening the value of what is already known.

Design the convergence points: the moments where reader knowledge and character knowledge meet. A convergence is always an event, the character learns what the reader has known, or the reader finally learns what the character has been hiding, and each convergence resets the story's tension formula. Schedule them where the story can absorb a change of formula.

Decide which knowledge is withheld from everyone, held only by the narrative itself. This is the most powerful and most dangerous position: it generates the fairest surprises and the worst cheats. For each narrative-held fact, require a fair trail, perceivable in hindsight, that a rereading reader can follow from the first page.

The strongest disclosure changes the past rather than adding to it. Rank revelations by how much prior material they recolor, and stage them where the recoloring can still alter a decision.

Track character knowledge separately from what the book has established for the reader. A character may only act on information they possess, and any scene that requires a character to know something they were never told is a structural error, not a detail to fix later.

Commit to the schedule: which knowledge moves when, where reader and character meet, and what the final state of knowing must be. Write forward with the map in hand, and let each scene move exactly one position, on purpose.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.
OPEN THREADS: the removed page (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report with a gap, then the missing sheet; the burned coat (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): ash in the stove, then a button; the girl's plan (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a bus timetable, a packed bag; Ruth's brother (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): an alibi, a dispute, a confession.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Plan the tension modes as a portfolio. A book of pure surprise resets to zero with each reveal; a book of pure suspense spends its dread in one long note. Decide the mix for each movement: where the reader should hold knowledge the characters lack, and where they should be one step behind, and where the two positions trade.

Grant suspense its fuel early and completely. The scenario that will burn for two hundred pages must be delivered to the reader in full: what is coming, roughly when, and what it will mean. Withheld suspense is not suspense but confusion, and the dread you want is only available to a reader who knows exactly enough to fear precisely.

Interleave the modes at the sequence level. After a surprise, the reader must rebuild their model, which is a moment of heightened attention; a stretch of suspense immediately after, with the new knowledge granted, converts that attention into dread. Plan the alternation deliberately: shock, then the long burn the shock enables.

Protect the endings of both modes. Suspense must resolve through the character's agency in some form, a choice, a stand, a refusal, or the dread was idle; surprise must be reconstructable, the trail visible in memory, or the shock was noise. Decide each mode's terminal conditions now, and hold both to them.

The strongest disclosure changes the past rather than adding to it. Rank revelations by how much prior material they recolor, and stage them where the recoloring can still alter a decision.

Do not underline significance. If an object, gesture, or remark matters, the craft is to let its placement and consequence do the underlining; announcing importance draws attention to the author's hand and, worse, tells the reader what to conclude before their own conclusion has formed.

Carry consequences forward across chapters rather than resetting to a neutral baseline. Fatigue, resentment, trust, debt, and reputation should all reflect what has happened, and the gradual accumulation of that reflection is what makes a long book feel cumulative rather than episodic.

Fix the portfolio: which questions are granted early to burn, which are held to detonate, and how the modes alternate across the book's movements. Draft with the allocation in hand, and the tension will have architecture rather than weather.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.

ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.
OPEN THREADS: altered entries (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two paid-out relief claims with no deaths; constable's burial (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a fresh grave outside the churchyard; relief fund (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): payments made on reputation; the physician's forecast (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a calendar of expected deaths.
THREE-ACT ARC: The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing | The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows | The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history
ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the roll will be read aloud with something wrong in it; the sealing rule will be applied to someone the reader knows; the year will end with a count that matters.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are in planning, with the outline above as the working material, settling the book's structural approach.
Your novel will carry two or three secondary storylines alongside a demanding central plot.
Decide how the secondary threads relate to the main line across the whole book: their loads, their rhythms, and their convergence.

Work the problem at the level of architecture, so drafting stands on decisions rather than habits.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared. The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing. The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows. The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history. He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Subplots are structural instruments, not decorations or rest stops. Before drafting, assign each thread its load, its rhythm against the main line, and its point of convergence, so the book's architecture holds the threads in deliberate relation instead of letting them drift parallel.

Assign each thread a distinct function the main line cannot perform: testing the theme under conditions the main conflict cannot produce, developing a relationship the goal does not touch, or carrying information the main antagonist has no channel to deliver. Functions that overlap split the same work twice and halve the book's apparent depth.

Use the threads to manage the main line's pressure. Cutting away at peak tension trades present intensity for forward pull; cutting away at low tension trades attention for nothing. Decide, for each planned cut, what the departure leaves unresolved and what the return will have altered, and cut accordingly.

Budget the endings of threads against the main line's ending. Each thread must resolve before, during, or after the climax, and each position says something: early resolution frees attention for the peak, simultaneous resolution binds the thread's meaning to the central choice, late resolution extends the story's claim into the aftermath. Choose positions on purpose.

A plot is a chain of forced moves: each situation makes some responses impossible, some costly, and one inevitable for this particular person. The quality of a plot is the quality of its forcing, not the quantity of its events.

Keep unresolved threads and their intended resolutions visible in the working notes. A thread tracked only in memory is likely to be dropped, and a thread that disappears without recognition teaches the reader that the book's promises are unreliable.

Set the convergence plan down as commitment: what each thread carries, when it returns, and where it meets the main line. From here, every subplot scene is written as a pressure on the spine, and the book's threads move as one structure.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Evening -- standalone, quiet horror, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.
PREMISE: In a coastal retirement town, the recently dead take some time to notice, and the living have built a polite arrangement in which nobody mentions that the neighbours are thinning.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dead continue their routines until someone they know admits out loud that they died; Admission is irreversible, and the admitted person leaves immediately; The town's ferry does not run after the last admission of the season.
CAST IN PLAY: Marjorie Hale, retired postmistress: wants one more summer of ordinary conversation; flaw, she manages people instead of loving them; secret, she has known about her husband since April; knows, the arrangement's rules from practice | Alec Renner, retired ferryman: wants the boat's last season honored; flaw, he cannot refuse anyone an errand; secret, he has carried admissions the wrong way across the water; knows, who has been admitted and who has not | Dr. Olu, the last practicing physician: wants an honest end for her patients; flaw, she treats silence as a clinical tool; secret, she falsified a certificate in autumn to keep a family in the town; knows, the medical signs that precede admission.
OPEN THREADS: Marjorie's husband (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): his newspaper arrives, then his chair, then the admission; Olus's certificate (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a forged date, a family that stayed; the ferry season (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): schedule noted, then shortened, then final; Bea's telling (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a careless sentence that starts one neighbor's absence.
THREE-ACT ARC: A town summer: the arrangement works, the reader learns its rules through behaviour, and Bea arrives with an outsider's eyes | Admissions accelerate, the ferry schedule becomes the plot's clock, and Marjorie's management of the town begins to fail | The last admission of the season will strand whoever is left; Marjorie must choose what to say to whom, and to her husband most of all
ENDING: Marjorie admits her husband in public, the ferry runs one time for those who want it, and the town continues the following year with fewer residents and the same courtesy.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will understand the rules before any character states them; someone will be admitted who should not have been; the ferry will run one last time.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning the novel described above, and the question below concerns the book's architecture rather than one scene.
Your novel exists as a premise, a protagonist, and an ending you are confident about, with the overall shape still undecided.
Before drafting, decide the overall shape of the arc: how the story's direction, pressure, and meaning are distributed across its whole length.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Lay out the structural thinking you will carry into the draft.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. In a coastal retirement town, the recently dead take some time to notice, and the living have built a polite arrangement in which nobody mentions that the neighbours are thinning. A town summer: the arrangement works, the reader learns its rules through behaviour, and Bea arrives with an outsider's eyes. Admissions accelerate, the ferry schedule becomes the plot's clock, and Marjorie's management of the town begins to fail. The last admission of the season will strand whoever is left; Marjorie must choose what to say to whom, and to her husband most of all. Marjorie admits her husband in public, the ferry runs one time for those who want it, and the town continues the following year with fewer residents and the same courtesy. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Before drafting, commit to the story's gross shape: the number of major reorganizations, their approximate positions, and the direction of travel between them. Scenes are cheap to change; the shape is not, and every structural indecision left open now will be paid for in the middle.

Think of the arc as three different stories told at different rates: the external situation changes on one schedule, the protagonist's understanding changes on another, and the reader's question changes on a third. Plot the three schedules against each other, and place the major turns where two or more of them move at once, because those coincidences are what a turning point actually is.

Fix the positions of the irreversible moments: the first crossing where the protagonist cannot return to their starting position, the middle reorganization that reframes the pursuit, and the terminal choice that settles the argument. Everything else in the book can bend; those three points carry the shape, and their spacing determines the experience of pace across the whole.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.

OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.

TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.

OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.
CAST IN PLAY: Isaac Rell, tracker, the narrator: wants the debt cleared without killing anyone; flaw, he believes restraint is a form of payment; secret, he took the wrong man and knows it; knows, the warrant was bought by a rancher | Widow Sarn, boarding house keeper, creditor: wants the town to survive the winter; flaw, she has learned to spend other people's losses; secret, she paid the tracker's debt to hold the water claim; knows, the ditch head's owner | Rancher Coel, ditch head owner: wants the valley's water consolidated; flaw, he purchases with patience instead of force; secret, he filed the original warrant to remove a claimant; knows, the truth about the wrong man.

ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the debt will be settled or refused; the truth about the wrong man will be entered somewhere; the council will meet and decide something.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.
OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.
THREE-ACT ARC: Corin reads the harvest rite, omits the sentence that no one likes hearing, and the first field fails | As the blight spreads, Mette's outside seed divides the valley, Sorrel's authorship surfaces, and Hale's purchases reveal what the lowlands intend | Corin must either restore the omitted sentence, which the valley will refuse, or finish the bargain the saint left unfinished, which requires the valley to pay a new price
ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
