instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.
CAST IN PLAY: Rennick, planner, retired: wants one final job that pays his debts; flaw, he plans for machinery and not for people; secret, he has already been paid by the bank's owner to test the building; knows, the owner's security revisions | Sabine, locksmith: wants her brother's release from a debt prison; flaw, she trusts nobody's plan but her own; secret, she has copied the vault key pattern; knows, the second door's true difficulty | Ode, inside man, night clerk: wants out of the city with his daughter; flaw, he cannot lie under pressure; secret, he has already told the owner that a crew is coming; knows, the guard rotation posted tonight.
OPEN THREADS: identity registrations (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): ninety-second windows, then a record of a previous test; copied key (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a wax impression, then a duplicate; clerk's disclosure (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a phone call logged; guard's documentation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): photographs of the ledgers.
THREE-ACT ARC: The plan is assembled and rehearsed against the layout, and the first door is easier than the plan predicted | The ease of the first door is the trap: the owner is watching the test. Identity registrations, a copied key, and the clerk's nerve converge | The ledgers are only useful if they reach the front door and daylight, and the crew has to choose between the plan and the captives' safety
ENDING: Rennick breaks his own plan to move the ledgers out through the front with the staff, the door system records all five of them, and the crew walks into arrest with the ledgers in the hands of the guard captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: five doors will be opened in order; the crew's own rule about staff will be tested; one member has already betrayed the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Assign each thread a distinct function the main line cannot perform: testing the theme under conditions the main conflict cannot produce, developing a relationship the goal does not touch, or carrying information the main antagonist has no channel to deliver. instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.

TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.

OPEN THREADS: moved stones (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): survey discrepancy, then proof, then a deliberate trap; Sera's raider dealings (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): supply ledgers, a survivor's testimony; brother's death (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): rumor, then the ward-fire's old scar; the offer behind the ward (opens chapter 6, pays off chapter 10): voices at the turning, then terms.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each lantern holds a fixed measure of years, and the ninth is the reserve; Lamplight cannot be made, only moved from lantern to lantern by a licensed hand; Whoever carries light through the streets alone burns a little of themselves.
CAST IN PLAY: Peet Amaran, junior lamplighter, ninth watch: wants to be certified so his sister can leave the district; flaw, he cannot let a wrong thing stand unremarked; secret, he has already carried an unlicensed flame; knows, the ninth lantern was lit early | Mistress Hallow, master of the lightworks: wants the city calm until the transfer season; flaw, she has confused the institution with the city; secret, she has been rationing without a license for six years; knows, the real measure left | Dove Rhee, light-broker for the outer districts: wants the districts priced out of the light to be lit anyway; flaw, she needs to be the one who fixes it; secret, she has been selling light she does not have; knows, Peet's unlicensed carry.
OPEN THREADS: the empty reserve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): measure books, then the physical gauge; unlicensed carry (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): a burned palm, a witness, a price; Sister's transfer (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): permit papers that require certification; Tull's old falsification (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): an old sheet in Hallow's hand.
THREE-ACT ARC: Peet lights the ninth lantern, learns the reserve is empty, and is offered promotion to keep the fact quiet | He carries light to the dark districts with Dove's network while Hallow audits the works, and the audit closes on the person who taught him | The works must either admit the deficit or steal the light back from the districts, and Peet is the only licensed hand able to move it either way
ENDING: He redistributes the remaining light across the whole city, ending the districts' distinction, and loses his certification in a city that is dimmer but even.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see what the ninth lantern actually contains; the dark districts will get light or the reason they do not; Peet's certification will be tested against the truth.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Assign each thread a distinct function the main line cannot perform: testing the theme under conditions the main conflict cannot produce, developing a relationship the goal does not touch, or carrying information the main antagonist has no channel to deliver. Functions that overlap split the same work twice and halve the book's apparent depth.

Rhythm the threads deliberately. A thread re-entered too often becomes the main line; a thread abandoned too long loses the reader's grip on its state. Decide the maximum distance between appearances for each thread, and treat re-entry as an event: each return should bring changed state, so the thread advances rather than resumes.

Use the threads to manage the main line's pressure. Cutting away at peak tension trades present intensity for forward pull; cutting away at low tension trades attention for nothing. Decide, for each planned cut, what the departure leaves unresolved and what the return will have altered, and cut accordingly.

Change is the only cumulative resource a story has. Incidents repeat, settings tire, but a character or situation that is genuinely different at page two hundred from page one has paid the reader's fare. Spend scenes on what changes, and summarize what merely continues.

When introducing something that will matter later, establish now how it can matter: by its capabilities, its cost, its ownership, or the interest it attracts. A detail introduced without consequence available to it is either decoration or a promise the ending will have to improvise.

Re-read the relevant earlier material before writing a chapter that depends on it, especially when the dependence is on a conversation, a physical description, or a decision from many chapters back. Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.

Set the convergence plan down as commitment: what each thread carries, when it returns, and where it meets the main line. From here, every subplot scene is written as a pressure on the spine, and the book's threads move as one structure.

TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.

Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit

PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.

instruction:

TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.

OPEN THREADS: the altered sequence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): anomaly noticed, then dismissed, then provable; mother's medical debt (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): refinanced twice, then transferred; carter fire plot (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): accelerant cached, dates moved twice; Otte's grain payments (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): receipts referenced, never shown.

instruction:

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Wolf Road -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, travel and pursuit.
POV AND DISTANCE: limited third rotating among three travelers, past tense.
PREMISE: Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The passes open on a schedule nobody controls, and the last opening strands travelers until spring; Travelers share salt and fire by custom, and breaking the custom is the only crime the road recognizes; The pursuing company cannot cross until the pass freezes hard, which gives a fixed head start.

ENDING: They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the road will be crossed or the season closes on them; the guide's lie will be exposed before the end; the travelers will learn what each is carrying.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Fell, cataloguer, the narrator: wants the commission finished and paid so she can settle a debt; flaw, she trusts documents over people; secret, she has already indexed one owner out of existence; knows, the rooms move when she is not looking | Mrs. Ivey, housekeeper, second of her name: wants the house inhabited the way it was; flaw, she serves the arrangement instead of questioning it; secret, she has been in the house since before the current owners and remembers two more; knows, which owners the previous cataloguer removed | Mr. Lamb, owner who hired her: wants his family's library kept intact and his house entered from outside; flaw, he bargains without understanding the terms; secret, he has not been outside in eleven years; knows, the previous cataloguer's fate.

ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.

TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.

ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the roll will be read aloud with something wrong in it; the sealing rule will be applied to someone the reader knows; the year will end with a count that matters.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

A novel's shape is decided before its scenes: where the pressure enters, where it reorganizes, and where it resolves are structural commitments that every scene will either serve or fight. Decide the contour now, at the level of the whole, and let individual scenes be chosen by it rather than invented against it.

Decide the story's baseline of pressure and its variations. A book held at maximum pitch for its full length numbs the reader; a book that never rises above its baseline never earns attention. Choose where the pressure deliberately falls, and make those falls serve comprehension or attachment, so the rises land on a reader who is ready rather than exhausted.

Fix the positions of the irreversible moments: the first crossing where the protagonist cannot return to their starting position, the middle reorganization that reframes the pursuit, and the terminal choice that settles the argument. Decide what the arc's direction is as a claim. By the end, the book will have demonstrated something: a value tested, a cost paid, a belief revised. Structure is a promise about consequence: the reader's willingness to continue is purchased with the guarantee that what happens will matter downstream. Every planning decision should be tested against whether it strengthens or spends that guarantee.

When resolving something the outline has promised, make the resolution follow from information already established. Settle the contour as a working commitment: where pressure enters, where it reorganizes, where the point of no return falls, and what the ending must demonstrate. Every scene from here forward is selected by that contour, not improvised against it.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat. The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes. Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start. Subplots are structural instruments, not decorations or rest stops. Before drafting, assign each thread its load, its rhythm against the main line, and its point of convergence, so the book's architecture holds the threads in deliberate relation instead of letting them drift parallel.

Assign each thread a distinct function the main line cannot perform: testing the theme under conditions the main conflict cannot produce, developing a relationship the goal does not touch, or carrying information the main antagonist has no channel to deliver. Functions that overlap split the same work twice and halve the book's apparent depth.

Rhythm the threads deliberately. A thread re-entered too often becomes the main line; a thread abandoned too long loses the reader's grip on its state. Decide the maximum distance between appearances for each thread, and treat re-entry as an event: each return should bring changed state, so the thread advances rather than resumes.

Use the threads to manage the main line's pressure. Cutting away at peak tension trades present intensity for forward pull; cutting away at low tension trades attention for nothing. Decide, for each planned cut, what the departure leaves unresolved and what the return will have altered, and cut accordingly.

Structure is a promise about consequence: the reader's willingness to continue is purchased with the guarantee that what happens will matter downstream. Every planning decision should be tested against whether it strengthens or spends that guarantee.

The outline is a constraint, not a suggestion. Every planned beat in this chapter must survive into the draft in a recognizable form; where a beat resists dramatization, the correct response is to find the staging that makes it work rather than to substitute a different event that happens to write more easily.

Re-read the relevant earlier material before writing a chapter that depends on it, especially when the dependence is on a conversation, a physical description, or a decision from many chapters back. Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.

Set the convergence plan down as commitment: what each thread carries, when it returns, and where it meets the main line. From here, every subplot scene is written as a pressure on the spine, and the book's threads move as one structure.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.

ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.
THREE-ACT ARC: The council opens, the seven-day clock begins, and Nissa's first report proves false in a way that serves both sides | Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact | The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her
ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.

TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.

TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.

instruction:

TITLE: Wolf Road -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, travel and pursuit.
POV AND DISTANCE: limited third rotating among three travelers, past tense.
PREMISE: Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The passes open on a schedule nobody controls, and the last opening strands travelers until spring; Travelers share salt and fire by custom, and breaking the custom is the only crime the road recognizes; The pursuing company cannot cross until the pass freezes hard, which gives a fixed head start.

ENDING: They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the road will be crossed or the season closes on them; the guide's lie will be exposed before the end; the travelers will learn what each is carrying.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.

ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.
CAST IN PLAY: Surveyor Alder, the narrator: wants an accurate map and a promotion; flaw, he believes accuracy is neutral; secret, he has left two settlements off the preliminary sheet; knows, the map will displace whoever it records | Lieutenant Cray, escort commander: wants the valley pacified without casualties; flaw, he needs the expedition to justify itself; secret, he has authorization to remove settlements that resist; knows, the compensation schedule's inadequacy | Mira, valley guide: wants her village registered under its own name; flaw, she trusted the party's ledger; secret, she has been guiding the survey to the settlements least able to leave; knows, the valley's flood seasons.
OPEN THREADS: preliminary sheet (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a filed map, then a removal order; compensation schedule (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): payment per acre, assessed from the map; removal authorization (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a written power the surveyor must sign; flood season (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a road that closes for five months.
THREE-ACT ARC: The party enters the valley, the survey begins, and Alder's preliminary sheet is sent to the capital without his approval | Mira's guidance, Cray's authorization, and the compensation schedule intersect; the filed sheet's consequences reach the valley | The flood season closes the only road, the escort demands its authorization, and Alder must choose what the final map will say
ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: The Afternoon Hours -- standalone, young adult, school and theatre.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: School productions require a staff supervisor present at every rehearsal; The auditorium is booked by the district for examinations in the final week; Cast changes after the programme is printed require the principal's approval.

OPEN THREADS: the notes (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): copied pages, then a principal's drawer; the recording (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a phone, a rehearsal, a file; the complaint (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a filed document with no evidence; auditorium booking (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a calendar, an exam week.
THREE-ACT ARC: The production is running; the cancellation arrives; the cast is told it is a scheduling problem | The real cause leaks through Nia, Devi's recording circulates, and the rehearsals continue off-site in defiance of the rules | The auditorium is lost to examinations, the cast must choose between a public performance that risks the teacher and silence that saves him
ENDING: They perform a stripped version in the car park, the complaint is dismissed and the teacher does not return, and Nia tells Devi the truth about the notes.

TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.

TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.

POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.

TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.

ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.

Give the rules priority in specific terms: where two stylistic options conflict, the explicit rule wins, and where the rules are silent, consistency with the surrounding book wins over local improvement. Ambiguity about precedence is what allows drift.

Build in a periodic check that compares the current chapter against the early chapters on the measurable features: sentence length distribution, ratio of description to action, density of figurative language, and frequency of the named tells. Measured drift is correctable; felt drift is usually invisible until the end.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.
OPEN THREADS: the cellar (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a search grid gap, then an excavation request; the object (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): carried then, kept now; sealed statement (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a transcript with an omission; second exit (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a plan, then a door under plaster.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.
OPEN THREADS: eleven exemptions (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a weekly habit, then a pattern in a report; brother's score (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a threshold, a warning letter, a deadline; evasion group (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a meeting, then a distributed method; update history (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): nightly shifts, then a readable archive.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rosa grants a first unwarranted exemption, discovers how easy it is, and starts a weekly pattern she tells herself is mercy | The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail | Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other
ENDING: She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the score actually measures; Rosa's pattern will be discovered; the exemption budget will run out.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Rosa grants a first unwarranted exemption, discovers how easy it is, and starts a weekly pattern she tells herself is mercy. The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail. Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other. She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Plan knowledge as a map rather than a list. For each secret in the book, decide who knows it, when each of them learned it, what they believe about who else knows, and what each would do if they found out more. The map produces scenes, while a secret tracked as a single fact only produces a reveal.

Keep commitments from characters to each other in the same ledger as plot facts. Promises, agreements, and debts are the most reliable source of later scene pressure, and they are the easiest obligations to lose.

Maintain a recovery schedule for physical and emotional damage. What the characters cannot do is as structural as what they can, and the schedule keeps the book's costs visible across acts.

Review the ledgers at act boundaries and use the review to plan the next act: what must be paid, what must be renewed, and what the accumulated state now makes possible.

Outline before improvisation: the plan's obligations are structural, and any genuine change to them belongs in planning rather than in a scene.

Keep a written style guide as an artifact and keep it current, including terminology, register, and the specific tells the book must avoid. Rules held only in context drift as the context grows.

Track character knowledge separately from what the book has established for the reader. A character may only act on information they possess, and any scene that requires a character to know something they were never told is a structural error, not a detail to fix later.

Commit to the tracking systems as working documents and treat the book's accumulated state as the material of every later chapter. Continuity maintained this way stops being a correction and becomes an engine.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.

TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are deciding what tracking systems the book needs before drafting begins.
How should state, knowledge, and obligation tracking be designed as part of the book's architecture rather than managed as a maintenance burden?
You are mapping out a novel you are about to write.
Reason through the whole problem at the planning level and stop when the structure is decided.
response:
The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died. The movements the book has to pay for: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat. The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes. Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Plan knowledge as a map rather than a list. For each secret in the book, decide who knows it, when each of them learned it, what they believe about who else knows, and what each would do if they found out more. The map produces scenes, while a secret tracked as a single fact only produces a reveal.

Keep commitments from characters to each other in the same ledger as plot facts. Promises, agreements, and debts are the most reliable source of later scene pressure, and they are the easiest obligations to lose.

Maintain a recovery schedule for physical and emotional damage. What the characters cannot do is as structural as what they can, and the schedule keeps the book's costs visible across acts.

Review the ledgers at act boundaries and use the review to plan the next act: what must be paid, what must be renewed, and what the accumulated state now makes possible.

State before scene: what the story has already spent and established constrains what the chapter can do, and the constraint is a source of pressure.

Hold the style steady across the whole book rather than establishing it in the opening chapters. Drift is cumulative and quiet, and by the middle of a long book a voice that has relaxed toward the model's statistical default is unrecoverable without a full pass.

Re-read the relevant earlier material before writing a chapter that depends on it, especially when the dependence is on a conversation, a physical description, or a decision from many chapters back. Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.

Commit to the tracking systems as working documents and treat the book's accumulated state as the material of every later chapter. Continuity maintained this way stops being a correction and becomes an engine.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.
THREE-ACT ARC: Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates | Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate | Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth
ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate. Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth. Design the tracking before drafting: character sheets with current condition and knowledge, a thread ledger with setup and payoff positions, an object and possession inventory, a chronology, and a rules sheet for the world's mechanics. Each becomes a pressure source, since a constraint the book respects generates plot.

Keep commitments from characters to each other in the same ledger as plot facts. Promises, agreements, and debts are the most reliable source of later scene pressure, and they are the easiest obligations to lose.

Maintain a recovery schedule for physical and emotional damage. What the characters cannot do is as structural as what they can, and the schedule keeps the book's costs visible across acts.

Review the ledgers at act boundaries and use the review to plan the next act: what must be paid, what must be renewed, and what the accumulated state now makes possible.

Outline before improvisation: the plan's obligations are structural, and any genuine change to them belongs in planning rather than in a scene.

Treat the voice as a property of the entire book, which means a passage is only good if it does not cost the surrounding pages. A brilliant paragraph that breaks the register is a net loss, and the same material delivered inside the register will usually carry further.

Carry consequences forward across chapters rather than resetting to a neutral baseline. Fatigue, resentment, trust, debt, and reputation should all reflect what has happened, and the gradual accumulation of that reflection is what makes a long book feel cumulative rather than episodic.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.
CAST IN PLAY: Isaac Rell, tracker, the narrator: wants the debt cleared without killing anyone; flaw, he believes restraint is a form of payment; secret, he took the wrong man and knows it; knows, the warrant was bought by a rancher | Widow Sarn, boarding house keeper, creditor: wants the town to survive the winter; flaw, she has learned to spend other people's losses; secret, she paid the tracker's debt to hold the water claim; knows, the ditch head's owner | Rancher Coel, ditch head owner: wants the valley's water consolidated; flaw, he purchases with patience instead of force; secret, he filed the original warrant to remove a claimant; knows, the truth about the wrong man.
OPEN THREADS: the wrong man (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a face he cannot forget; the warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a filed claim, a rancher's signature; the ditch head (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a filing that transfers water rights; tracker's own warrant (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a poster with his name on it.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper | The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears | The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly
ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the debt will be settled or refused; the truth about the wrong man will be entered somewhere; the council will meet and decide something.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Paper Mill -- standalone, thriller, corporate whistleblower.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the mid-level analyst.
PREMISE: An analyst discovers that her employer's celebrated water-recycling plant has been discharging into a river for a decade, and the only person who will believe her is the regulator she once helped discredit.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Regulatory inspections are announced four days in advance by statute; The company's severance agreements require arbitration and prohibit disclosure of process data; Discharge samples must be taken by a certified officer to be admissible.
CAST IN PLAY: Nadia Bell, process analyst: wants the discharge stopped without losing her pension; flaw, she documents everything and decides nothing; secret, she signed the original compliance report as a junior; knows, the plant's bypass valve schedule | Regulator Osei, environmental officer: wants an admissible sample; flaw, he needs to be right in public; secret, he leaked an earlier case to a journalist who burned him; knows, the company's legal exposure | Director Pike, plant director: wants the plant's award renewed and his retirement secured; flaw, he believes the discharge is acceptable accounting; secret, he authorized the bypass during a drought year and never restored it; knows, which documents prove authorization.
OPEN THREADS: bypass valve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a maintenance schedule, then a physical seal; signed report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): her signature, then the amended version; diluted samples (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): two sets of numbers; leaked case (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a journalist's name, a burned source.
THREE-ACT ARC: Nadia finds the valve schedule, takes a sample improperly, and is offered a promotion for her diligence | The arbitration clause blocks every internal route; the regulator needs an admissible sample; the chemist is ordered to dilute and begins keeping a second set of numbers | The inspection is announced for a date the bypass can be closed for, and the only way to prove the discharge is to be at the river when the plant is not expecting it
ENDING: Nadia provides the sample and the schedule and loses her pension; the plant pays a fine and keeps operating with the valve sealed, which is a smaller outcome than she wanted and a real one.
PROMISES TO THE READER: an admissible sample will be taken or the case will die; the protagonist's own signature will matter; the announced inspection will be a turning point rather than a rescue.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Nadia finds the valve schedule, takes a sample improperly, and is offered a promotion for her diligence. The arbitration clause blocks every internal route; the regulator needs an admissible sample; the chemist is ordered to dilute and begins keeping a second set of numbers. The inspection is announced for a date the bypass can be closed for, and the only way to prove the discharge is to be at the river when the plant is not expecting it. Nadia provides the sample and the schedule and loses her pension; the plant pays a fine and keeps operating with the valve sealed, which is a smaller outcome than she wanted and a real one. Each becomes a pressure source, since a constraint the book respects generates plot.

Schedule the renewals of long threads the way scenes are scheduled, so that the middle of the book has obligations to service rather than only new material to generate.

Maintain a recovery schedule for physical and emotional damage. What the characters cannot do is as structural as what they can, and the schedule keeps the book's costs visible across acts.

Review the ledgers at act boundaries and use the review to plan the next act: what must be paid, what must be renewed, and what the accumulated state now makes possible.

Apply structural craft decisions as constraints during generation rather than as repairs afterward. A chapter drafted inside the style rules needs no corrective pass, and the reading experience stays even, which is what consistency actually means to a reader.

Keep unresolved threads and their intended resolutions visible in the working notes. A thread tracked only in memory is likely to be dropped, and a thread that disappears without recognition teaches the reader that the book's promises are unreliable.

Commit to the tracking systems as working documents and treat the book's accumulated state as the material of every later chapter. Continuity maintained this way stops being a correction and becomes an engine.

TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.

TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds rotating by section, past tense.

TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.

POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will understand the rules before any character states them; someone will be admitted who should not have been; the ferry will run one last time.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, present tense, two scientists.
PREMISE: At a monastery station studying a silence that behaves like a substance, two researchers discover the discipline that keeps them safe is the same discipline that has been feeding the phenomenon.
