Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.
CAST IN PLAY: Priya, bakery owner, three generations: wants the family shop kept open through the season; flaw, she hears every suggestion as a takeover; secret, she has already taken a loan against the building she does not own; knows, the landlord's redevelopment plans | Dan, cafe owner, second year: wants a business that lasts past the following spring; flaw, he solves problems by spending; secret, his cafe is funded by severance from the company he left; knows, the association's voting arithmetic | Mr. Hallow, landlord: wants one tenant paying a single higher rent; flaw, he uses courteous language as leverage; secret, he has a development partner waiting on the outcome; knows, the lease's co-signature clause and its limits.
OPEN THREADS: co-lease (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a shared signature, then a joint renewal notice; loan against the building (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a bank letter, a repayment schedule; buyout clause (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): an assessor's appointment; development offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price, a deadline.
THREE-ACT ARC: The co-lease is presented as fait accompli, the two businesses share a wall and a delivery yard, and each tries to outlast the other | Shared hours, a stolen delivery, and a broken oven force real collaboration, and the buyout clause becomes a weapon both consider | The redevelopment offer arrives with a deadline, and the choice is between a joint purchase neither can afford alone and one of them taking the buyout money
ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.

POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.

ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.

OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.

ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.

TITLE: The Afternoon Hours -- standalone, young adult, school and theatre.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.
PREMISE: A school's production of a play is cancelled two weeks before opening, and the student stage manager must decide whether to tell the cast why the cancellation is personal.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: School productions require a staff supervisor present at every rehearsal; The auditorium is booked by the district for examinations in the final week; Cast changes after the programme is printed require the principal's approval.

THREE-ACT ARC: The production is running; the cancellation arrives; the cast is told it is a scheduling problem | The real cause leaks through Nia, Devi's recording circulates, and the rehearsals continue off-site in defiance of the rules | The auditorium is lost to examinations, the cast must choose between a public performance that risks the teacher and silence that saves him
ENDING: They perform a stripped version in the car park, the complaint is dismissed and the teacher does not return, and Nia tells Devi the truth about the notes.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the production will be performed or cancelled permanently; Nia will have to tell someone what she did; the complaint will be resolved on the page.

OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.

TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.

TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.

TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each lantern holds a fixed measure of years, and the ninth is the reserve; Lamplight cannot be made, only moved from lantern to lantern by a licensed hand; Whoever carries light through the streets alone burns a little of themselves.
CAST IN PLAY: Peet Amaran, junior lamplighter, ninth watch: wants to be certified so his sister can leave the district; flaw, he cannot let a wrong thing stand unremarked; secret, he has already carried an unlicensed flame; knows, the ninth lantern was lit early | Mistress Hallow, master of the lightworks: wants the city calm until the transfer season; flaw, she has confused the institution with the city; secret, she has been rationing without a license for six years; knows, the real measure left | Dove Rhee, light-broker for the outer districts: wants the districts priced out of the light to be lit anyway; flaw, she needs to be the one who fixes it; secret, she has been selling light she does not have; knows, Peet's unlicensed carry.
OPEN THREADS: the empty reserve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): measure books, then the physical gauge; unlicensed carry (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): a burned palm, a witness, a price; Sister's transfer (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): permit papers that require certification; Tull's old falsification (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): an old sheet in Hallow's hand.
THREE-ACT ARC: Peet lights the ninth lantern, learns the reserve is empty, and is offered promotion to keep the fact quiet | He carries light to the dark districts with Dove's network while Hallow audits the works, and the audit closes on the person who taught him | The works must either admit the deficit or steal the light back from the districts, and Peet is the only licensed hand able to move it either way
ENDING: He redistributes the remaining light across the whole city, ending the districts' distinction, and loses his certification in a city that is dimmer but even.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see what the ninth lantern actually contains; the dark districts will get light or the reason they do not; Peet's certification will be tested against the truth.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Ration resolution deliberately: the smaller and more local the question, the more freely it may be closed, and the larger the question, the later and more expensive its closure. The rationing is what makes the ending feel like a gathering, because by the final act the only accounts left open are the ones the reader has carried longest, and their settlement is worth the whole journey.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's sea wall work is funded by a levy charged to properties above the high-water line; The couple's house is below the line and cannot be repaired after a flood without a licensed surveyor; The harbour's fishing fleet is co-owned in shares that must be sold to existing holders.
CAST IN PLAY: Aidan, harbour master, the husband: wants the house repaired and the marriage continued without discussion; flaw, he maintains things instead of understanding them; secret, he has been quietly selling his fleet shares to cover the flood damage; knows, the sea wall's true schedule | Bryn, surveyor, the wife: wants the marriage assessed honestly before the season ends; flaw, she mistakes accuracy for kindness; secret, she has accepted a post in another county and not told him; knows, the house cannot be sold or insured in its current state | Ondine, Bryn's colleague and client: wants the sea wall built before spring; flaw, she values the town's survival over its people's arrangements; secret, her survey supports using the couple's property line as the wall's footing; knows, the levy's distribution.
OPEN THREADS: flood damage (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): water in the floor, then a condemned structure; share sales (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a ledger of shares, then an empty holding; job offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a letter, a date, a county; wall footing (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a survey line through the back garden.
THREE-ACT ARC: A flood damages the house; the two spouses disagree about repair, sale, and what the damage means | The wall survey, the share sales, and the job offer surface in the wrong order, and each spouse reads the other's decision as betrayal | The final storm decides the house, and the choice is between a marriage held together by property and two separate lives that are both viable
ENDING: The house is condemned and demolished for the wall footing, the fleet shares are gone, and the two of them separate with the paperwork clean and no reconciliation scene.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the sea wall will be built or abandoned; the house will be decided by the season; one of them will say the decisive thing out loud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Quiet Ministry -- standalone, dystopia, bureaucracy.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.
PREMISE: A records officer in a ministry that assigns citizens to work discovers that her own file has been edited to make her suitable for a job she has been doing for six years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Assignments are made by file, and no appeal may cite information not in the file; Records officers may correct errors only with two supporting documents; Every correction is itself recorded and visible to the ministry's auditors.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Ren, records officer: wants her file to say the truth without losing her post; flaw, she trusts procedure to protect her; secret, she has made eleven unsupported corrections for other people; knows, the file editing pattern | Supervisor Tal, section head: wants the section's error rate at zero for the inspection; flaw, he optimizes for metrics; secret, he authorized the editing of Ada's file to keep her in the section; knows, which files have been adjusted | Inspector Oyo, ministry auditor: wants the pattern of corrections; flaw, she treats people as instruments of proof; secret, she was assigned here because she once made the same corrections; knows, the eleven corrections.
OPEN THREADS: Ada's edited file (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a qualification that is not hers; eleven corrections (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): eleven unsupported edits in the ledger; Renn's assignment (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a review date, a distant posting; inspection (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a date, a zero-error requirement.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ada finds the edit in her own file and cannot report it without exposing her eleven private corrections | The inspector traces the pattern; Tal offers protection in exchange for silence; Renn's assignment comes up for review in the same cycle | The inspection has a deadline, and the only way Ada can save her brother's file is to submit a correction supported by a document that does not exist
ENDING: She submits nothing, her brother is reassigned out of the city, and she stays in the section with her file still wrong and her corrections stopped.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the file will be corrected or left wrong; the parallel between Ada and the inspector will surface; an assignment decision will be shown as a life decision.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.
CAST IN PLAY: Surveyor Alder, the narrator: wants an accurate map and a promotion; flaw, he believes accuracy is neutral; secret, he has left two settlements off the preliminary sheet; knows, the map will displace whoever it records | Lieutenant Cray, escort commander: wants the valley pacified without casualties; flaw, he needs the expedition to justify itself; secret, he has authorization to remove settlements that resist; knows, the compensation schedule's inadequacy | Mira, valley guide: wants her village registered under its own name; flaw, she trusted the party's ledger; secret, she has been guiding the survey to the settlements least able to leave; knows, the valley's flood seasons.

ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.

TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.
OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.
THREE-ACT ARC: The council opens, the seven-day clock begins, and Nissa's first report proves false in a way that serves both sides | Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact | The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her
ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.

TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.

ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.

CAST IN PLAY: Priya, bakery owner, three generations: wants the family shop kept open through the season; flaw, she hears every suggestion as a takeover; secret, she has already taken a loan against the building she does not own; knows, the landlord's redevelopment plans | Dan, cafe owner, second year: wants a business that lasts past the following spring; flaw, he solves problems by spending; secret, his cafe is funded by severance from the company he left; knows, the association's voting arithmetic | Mr. Hallow, landlord: wants one tenant paying a single higher rent; flaw, he uses courteous language as leverage; secret, he has a development partner waiting on the outcome; knows, the lease's co-signature clause and its limits.
OPEN THREADS: co-lease (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a shared signature, then a joint renewal notice; loan against the building (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a bank letter, a repayment schedule; buyout clause (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): an assessor's appointment; development offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price, a deadline.

ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.

Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's sea wall work is funded by a levy charged to properties above the high-water line; The couple's house is below the line and cannot be repaired after a flood without a licensed surveyor; The harbour's fishing fleet is co-owned in shares that must be sold to existing holders.
CAST IN PLAY: Aidan, harbour master, the husband: wants the house repaired and the marriage continued without discussion; flaw, he maintains things instead of understanding them; secret, he has been quietly selling his fleet shares to cover the flood damage; knows, the sea wall's true schedule | Bryn, surveyor, the wife: wants the marriage assessed honestly before the season ends; flaw, she mistakes accuracy for kindness; secret, she has accepted a post in another county and not told him; knows, the house cannot be sold or insured in its current state | Ondine, Bryn's colleague and client: wants the sea wall built before spring; flaw, she values the town's survival over its people's arrangements; secret, her survey supports using the couple's property line as the wall's footing; knows, the levy's distribution.

ENDING: The house is condemned and demolished for the wall footing, the fleet shares are gone, and the two of them separate with the paperwork clean and no reconciliation scene.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the sea wall will be built or abandoned; the house will be decided by the season; one of them will say the decisive thing out loud.

Price the reliefs against the peaks they serve. The deeper the trough, the higher the reachable peak, and the book's largest summit needs the book's deepest quiet before it. POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.

OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.

ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.

TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Fen Road -- standalone, survival, expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the medic.
PREMISE: A six-person survey team crossing a wetland loses its route markers and its leader, and the medic who has been falsifying fitness reports must decide who is fit enough to carry what.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The fen's causeway is passable only in the dry weeks and only at night, when the peat holds; The team's rations were calculated for a crossing of nine nights; Any team member left behind is entitled to the group's full share of supplies.
CAST IN PLAY: Ori, team medic: wants all six across with a clean report; flaw, she protects people by withholding information; secret, she passed two members who should have failed their fitness review; knows, the team's actual condition | Halvard, survey lead: wants the route completed and the map delivered; flaw, he decides by schedule; secret, he accepted the commission below the safe number of nights; knows, the rations are short | Sel, porter, youngest: wants to be paid and to be taken seriously; flaw, she hides injury to stay on the manifest; secret, she has been re-marking the route posts incorrectly; knows, the posts have been moved.
OPEN THREADS: falsified reviews (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two passing grades, two failing bodies; route posts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): posts in the wrong places; rations (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a count, then a recount; the left-behind rule (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): supplies set aside for an abandoned member.
THREE-ACT ARC: The team enters the fen, the marker discrepancies are small, and a first injury changes the pace | Rations, injuries, and the falsified fitness reviews collide; Halvard's schedule becomes the antagonist; the markers are proved wrong | Eight nights in, the causeway is behind them, one member cannot continue, and the group's own rule about being left behind becomes a live instrument
ENDING: They hold to the rule, abandon the survey, and cross four nights late with a documented route they will never sell.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will take fewer or more nights than planned; someone will be carried or left; the falsified reviews will matter to a decision.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Your book must hold a reader across hundreds of pages, and the management of what stays unresolved is the architecture.

The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. The movements the book has to pay for: The team enters the fen, the marker discrepancies are small, and a first injury changes the pace. Eight nights in, the causeway is behind them, one member cannot continue, and the group's own rule about being left behind becomes a live instrument. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Decide the book's relationship to closure before drafting it: closure is the currency tension spends, and the spending must be rationed across the whole arc. Map what stays open through each movement, what gets resolved when, and what the final pages reserve for themselves. A book that resolves early is finished early, whatever its page count.

Design the nesting from the top: the book question, which is never fully answerable until the end but must be touched everywhere; the sequence questions, which give each movement its own engine; the chapter questions, which burn and pay quickly. Each level should feed the one above it, so local answers accumulate into partial answers at the top, and the reader feels ascent even without arrival.

Ration resolution deliberately: the smaller and more local the question, the more freely it may be closed, and the larger the question, the later and more expensive its closure. The rationing is what makes the ending feel like a gathering, because by the final act the only accounts left open are the ones the reader has carried longest, and their settlement is worth the whole journey.

Plan the incompleteness to be productive rather than neglectful: every open question should be generating consequences in the story's present, shaping behavior, distorting decisions, pricing silence. An open question that touches nothing is a decoration; the managed ones are live wires whose current the reader feels in every scene they cross.

Tension is managed incompleteness: the reader held by what is open, at every scale, with resolution rationed until the end. The stack of open questions is the book's engine, and it must never stand empty.

Weight scenes unequally and let quieter scenes do essential work: relationships, recovery, character, contrast, and the preparation of what comes next. Sequences that are only about the main plot lose the texture that makes the main plot matter.

Permit contradictory feelings to coexist, and permit characters to misread themselves. A person can be frightened and curious, relieved and resentful, and can explain their own state wrongly to themselves. The viewpoint's own interpretation of its feelings is not authoritative, and treating it as authoritative flattens the interior.

Commit to managed incompleteness as the book's tension law: what stays open, at which level, generating what consequences, until the ordered collapse of the end. The reader's engagement will have architecture under it, and the ending will feel like the system keeping its promise.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each lantern holds a fixed measure of years, and the ninth is the reserve; Lamplight cannot be made, only moved from lantern to lantern by a licensed hand; Whoever carries light through the streets alone burns a little of themselves.
CAST IN PLAY: Peet Amaran, junior lamplighter, ninth watch: wants to be certified so his sister can leave the district; flaw, he cannot let a wrong thing stand unremarked; secret, he has already carried an unlicensed flame; knows, the ninth lantern was lit early | Mistress Hallow, master of the lightworks: wants the city calm until the transfer season; flaw, she has confused the institution with the city; secret, she has been rationing without a license for six years; knows, the real measure left | Dove Rhee, light-broker for the outer districts: wants the districts priced out of the light to be lit anyway; flaw, she needs to be the one who fixes it; secret, she has been selling light she does not have; knows, Peet's unlicensed carry.
OPEN THREADS: the empty reserve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): measure books, then the physical gauge; unlicensed carry (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): a burned palm, a witness, a price; Sister's transfer (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): permit papers that require certification; Tull's old falsification (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): an old sheet in Hallow's hand.

ENDING: He redistributes the remaining light across the whole city, ending the districts' distinction, and loses his certification in a city that is dimmer but even.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see what the ninth lantern actually contains; the dark districts will get light or the reason they do not; Peet's certification will be tested against the truth.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

A great fantasy world is an argument conducted in systems: its magic says something about power, its politics about legitimacy, its history about memory and debt. Decide the argument first — the thing the book believes enough to test — and then design each system as a claim about it, so the world's pressures and the story's meaning are the same object.

Give each major system a thesis and an antithesis built into its mechanics: the magic that empowers and isolates, the church that consoles and controls, the frontier that promises and destroys. Systems with two faces generate the story's conflicts from their own design, and every use of them is simultaneously a plot beat and a thematic one.

Test the world's coherence of meaning, not just its internal logic: the systems should disagree with each other about the central tension, and the disagreement should be visible in what they demand of the people who live under them. A world whose institutions all encode the same value cannot produce a real argument, only a lecture in costume.

The theme is proven when a person's change is legible as a verdict on the systems, delivered by living through them.

The world is story material in proportion to the pressure it applies: every system that forbids, charges, and enables is a plot engine, and every system that merely decorates is a page tax the reader pays without return.

TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The movements the book has to pay for: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat. The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes. Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Plan the series from its final book backward and its first book forward, and reconcile the two in the middle volumes: the ending defines what must exist by then, the beginning defines what exists already, and each middle volume is a transfer of substance from the second list to the first. The reconciliation is the series' real outline.

Assign each volume its own complete contract: question, opposition, climax, and change, deliverable within its covers. Then assign it its series duty: which long promises advance, which reserves deepen without being spent, and which new long promises it opens for the volumes after. A volume that cannot state both duties will serve neither.

Escalate across the series by cost, not by census: each volume's conflict should demand more of its people, closer to what cannot be replaced, than the last. The temptation is scale — bigger armies, wider maps — but the reader's experience of escalation is the price of caring, and price is set at the level of the person.

Plan the series climax's requirements early and concretely: what must be true, known, assembled, and paid by the final volume, then trace each requirement back to the volume where it is established. The trace is the series' production schedule, and any requirement with no volume assigned to establish it is a default the finale would suffer.

The world is story material in proportion to the pressure it applies: every system that forbids, charges, and enables is a plot engine, and every system that merely decorates is a page tax the reader pays without return.

Keep the world in the background of the scene's actual work. The chapter's job is a person under pressure; the world should be present as the shape of that pressure, its costs, its permissions, and its prohibitions, rather than as an interruption that pauses the drama to inform.

Treat the story state as a live ledger carried into the chapter: injuries and their recovery stage, possessions and who holds them, promises made and to whom, secrets and exactly who knows them, unresolved threads, and the last significant conversation each pair of characters had. Assemble the ledger before drafting and update it after.

Commit to the architecture: promises scoped, reserves maintained visibly, escalation by cost, and the finale's requirements scheduled into the earlier volumes. The series will read as one long promise kept in installments.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each lantern holds a fixed measure of years, and the ninth is the reserve; Lamplight cannot be made, only moved from lantern to lantern by a licensed hand; Whoever carries light through the streets alone burns a little of themselves.
CAST IN PLAY: Peet Amaran, junior lamplighter, ninth watch: wants to be certified so his sister can leave the district; flaw, he cannot let a wrong thing stand unremarked; secret, he has already carried an unlicensed flame; knows, the ninth lantern was lit early | Mistress Hallow, master of the lightworks: wants the city calm until the transfer season; flaw, she has confused the institution with the city; secret, she has been rationing without a license for six years; knows, the real measure left | Dove Rhee, light-broker for the outer districts: wants the districts priced out of the light to be lit anyway; flaw, she needs to be the one who fixes it; secret, she has been selling light she does not have; knows, Peet's unlicensed carry.
OPEN THREADS: the empty reserve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): measure books, then the physical gauge; unlicensed carry (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): a burned palm, a witness, a price; Sister's transfer (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): permit papers that require certification; Tull's old falsification (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): an old sheet in Hallow's hand.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.

OPEN THREADS: previous index (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): three hands, then the third hand identified; the boy (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a voice, then an entry, then a name; Mr. Lamb's sentence (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a door he will not approach, then the reason; Ada's deleted owner (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a gap in her own first ledger.

ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

A great fantasy world is an argument conducted in systems: its magic says something about power, its politics about legitimacy, its history about memory and debt. Decide the argument first — the thing the book believes enough to test — and then design each system as a claim about it, so the world's pressures and the story's meaning are the same object.

Give each major system a thesis and an antithesis built into its mechanics: the magic that empowers and isolates, the church that consoles and controls, the frontier that promises and destroys. Systems with two faces generate the story's conflicts from their own design, and every use of them is simultaneously a plot beat and a thematic one.

PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.
CAST IN PLAY: Isaac Rell, tracker, the narrator: wants the debt cleared without killing anyone; flaw, he believes restraint is a form of payment; secret, he took the wrong man and knows it; knows, the warrant was bought by a rancher | Widow Sarn, boarding house keeper, creditor: wants the town to survive the winter; flaw, she has learned to spend other people's losses; secret, she paid the tracker's debt to hold the water claim; knows, the ditch head's owner | Rancher Coel, ditch head owner: wants the valley's water consolidated; flaw, he purchases with patience instead of force; secret, he filed the original warrant to remove a claimant; knows, the truth about the wrong man.
OPEN THREADS: the wrong man (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a face he cannot forget; the warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a filed claim, a rancher's signature; the ditch head (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a filing that transfers water rights; tracker's own warrant (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a poster with his name on it.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper | The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears | The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly
ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the debt will be settled or refused; the truth about the wrong man will be entered somewhere; the council will meet and decide something.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Decide what the world's systems argue, and design each system so its rules embody the story's themes and generate conflicts that test them.

The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth. The movements the book has to pay for: Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper. The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears. The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Before building further, name the theme in structural terms: not a subject but a tension — power against accountability, freedom against order, the living against the debts of the dead. Then audit each invented system for which side of the tension it embodies, and where every system agrees, the world is a monotone and the story will have nowhere to argue.

Test the world's coherence of meaning, not just its internal logic: the systems should disagree with each other about the central tension, and the disagreement should be visible in what they demand of the people who live under them. A world whose institutions all encode the same value cannot produce a real argument, only a lecture in costume.

Design the protagonist's arc to run through the systems: their growth should be measured in changing relationships to the world's claims — believing the magic's promise, then paying its price; serving the law, then questioning its debt. The theme is proven when a person's change is legible as a verdict on the systems, delivered by living through them.

Budget the world's strangeness against its legibility of meaning: invented elements are retained by readers in proportion to the consequences they generate, so each system's most thematic features should also be its most consequential. Where a beautiful invention carries no pressure, either give it stakes or hold it for a volume where it can.

The world is story material in proportion to the pressure it applies: every system that forbids, charges, and enables is a plot engine, and every system that merely decorates is a page tax the reader pays without return.

Deliver world information through consequence and use rather than through explanation. A stranger's reaction, a price, a restriction, an object everyone handles carefully: these teach the world while the scene continues, and they are retained far better than an explanatory pause.

Fix the argument and the systems' positions within it: each institution a claim, each claim in tension with the others, and the protagonist's arc running through them as a living verdict. Build forward from the meaning outward, and the world will generate story on its own.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.
OPEN THREADS: altered entries (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two paid-out relief claims with no deaths; constable's burial (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a fresh grave outside the churchyard; relief fund (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): payments made on reputation; the physician's forecast (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a calendar of expected deaths.
THREE-ACT ARC: The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing | The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows | The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history
ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the roll will be read aloud with something wrong in it; the sealing rule will be applied to someone the reader knows; the year will end with a count that matters.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Plan the series architecture: which promises each volume makes and keeps, what is held in reserve across volumes, and how the whole escalates toward the series climax.
You are mapping out a novel you are about to write.
Map the structure and the tradeoffs, and settle the principles you will write from.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing. The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows. The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history. He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

A series is a promise ledger kept across years of the reader's life: each volume takes deposits, pays some debts on its own behalf, and holds the deeper reserves for the end. Design the ledger before drafting the next volume, and know at every point which promises are book-scoped and which are series-scoped, because confusing the two is how series sag.

Assign each volume its own complete contract: question, opposition, climax, and change, deliverable within its covers. Then assign it its series duty: which long promises advance, which reserves deepen without being spent, and which new long promises it opens for the volumes after. A volume that cannot state both duties will serve neither.

Escalate across the series by cost, not by census: each volume's conflict should demand more of its people, closer to what cannot be replaced, than the last. The temptation is scale — bigger armies, wider maps — but the reader's experience of escalation is the price of caring, and price is set at the level of the person.

Plan the series climax's requirements early and concretely: what must be true, known, assembled, and paid by the final volume, then trace each requirement back to the volume where it is established. The trace is the series' production schedule, and any requirement with no volume assigned to establish it is a default the finale would suffer.

Scale is legible only through the small: the fate of nations reaches the reader through particular people under particular pressure, and epic size without intimate aperture is a list, not a story.

Set the ledger: each volume's own contract, its series duties, the reserve maintenance schedule, and the trace from the series climax back through the volumes. Draft the next book against that ledger, and the series will accumulate instead of repeating.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.
CAST IN PLAY: Surveyor Alder, the narrator: wants an accurate map and a promotion; flaw, he believes accuracy is neutral; secret, he has left two settlements off the preliminary sheet; knows, the map will displace whoever it records | Lieutenant Cray, escort commander: wants the valley pacified without casualties; flaw, he needs the expedition to justify itself; secret, he has authorization to remove settlements that resist; knows, the compensation schedule's inadequacy | Mira, valley guide: wants her village registered under its own name; flaw, she trusted the party's ledger; secret, she has been guiding the survey to the settlements least able to leave; knows, the valley's flood seasons.

ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.
OPEN THREADS: missing warnings (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a filing receipt, then a recovered duplicate; hidden records (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): boxes in a dry attic; old channel (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a survey line, then the upper city's water; death count (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a falsified register.
THREE-ACT ARC: The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor | Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use | The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation
ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.

ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.

POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.

ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.
