TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.

TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.

TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.

ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Mark which early expenditures are being held for late recall, and protect them from casual use.

By the climax, the reader should be able to state what each side is fighting for, what it has already spent, and what a loss would mean in the currency the story has taught them. The final conflict's power is the accumulated precision of that accounting, built stage by stage across the arc.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.
OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.
THREE-ACT ARC: Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged | Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds | Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public
ENDING: The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Quiet Ministry -- standalone, dystopia, bureaucracy.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.

CAST IN PLAY: Ada Ren, records officer: wants her file to say the truth without losing her post; flaw, she trusts procedure to protect her; secret, she has made eleven unsupported corrections for other people; knows, the file editing pattern | Supervisor Tal, section head: wants the section's error rate at zero for the inspection; flaw, he optimizes for metrics; secret, he authorized the editing of Ada's file to keep her in the section; knows, which files have been adjusted | Inspector Oyo, ministry auditor: wants the pattern of corrections; flaw, she treats people as instruments of proof; secret, she was assigned here because she once made the same corrections; knows, the eleven corrections.

ENDING: She submits nothing, her brother is reassigned out of the city, and she stays in the section with her file still wrong and her corrections stopped.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the file will be corrected or left wrong; the parallel between Ada and the inspector will surface; an assignment decision will be shown as a life decision.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Fen Road -- standalone, survival, expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the medic.
PREMISE: A six-person survey team crossing a wetland loses its route markers and its leader, and the medic who has been falsifying fitness reports must decide who is fit enough to carry what.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The fen's causeway is passable only in the dry weeks and only at night, when the peat holds; The team's rations were calculated for a crossing of nine nights; Any team member left behind is entitled to the group's full share of supplies.
CAST IN PLAY: Ori, team medic: wants all six across with a clean report; flaw, she protects people by withholding information; secret, she passed two members who should have failed their fitness review; knows, the team's actual condition | Halvard, survey lead: wants the route completed and the map delivered; flaw, he decides by schedule; secret, he accepted the commission below the safe number of nights; knows, the rations are short | Sel, porter, youngest: wants to be paid and to be taken seriously; flaw, she hides injury to stay on the manifest; secret, she has been re-marking the route posts incorrectly; knows, the posts have been moved.

ENDING: They hold to the rule, abandon the survey, and cross four nights late with a documented route they will never sell.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will take fewer or more nights than planned; someone will be carried or left; the falsified reviews will matter to a decision.

instruction:

TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.

TITLE: The Afternoon Hours -- standalone, young adult, school and theatre.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.

Opposition pressure is a budget, not a setting. A story that spends maximum pressure in every scene bankrupts itself by the middle; a story that hoards it starves. Plan the expenditure deliberately: where the antagonist's campaigns crest, where they merely continue, and where they are deliberately quiet.

Give the pressure a rhythm with reasons. Crests should follow buildup, and quiet periods should be explained by the opposition's own constraints, regroupings, or divided attention, so the reader experiences variation as the opponent's lifecycle rather than the author's breath. Mark the crest points and what each one is for.

Budget offstage pressure as carefully as staged confrontations. The moves the antagonist makes unseen, which the protagonist discovers as changed circumstances, cost page time but compound believability. Allocate a share of the opposition's campaign to the space between appearances, and let the protagonist find evidence of it.

Concentrate the final pressure deliberately. The endgame's confrontations should draw on budgets established earlier: the liability planted in the first act, the resource the antagonist has been conserving, the grudge that ripens into obsession. Decide what the endgame spends, and keep those notes unspent until the endgame arrives.

Conflict is a contest over something scarce and consequential; every other element is staging. Before writing any scene of struggle, be able to name the scarce thing, who wants it, what each side can spend, and what winning would actually mean.

Give major events aftermath. The consequences of an event are usually more interesting than the event, and skipping them costs the reader the payoff of the pressure they absorbed: how people are changed, what is now impossible, what has to be repaired or abandoned.

Let the reader arrive at the emotion before the text names it. Behavior, physical reaction, attention, dialogue, and choice carry an emotional state; naming is a fallback for moments where precision matters more than participation, and overuse converts the book into a report of feelings rather than an experience of them.

Set the budget: crest points, quiet periods with their in-story reasons, offstage expenditures, and the endgame's concentration. Draft the opposition as a campaign with finite means, and the contest will stay alive from first page to last.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.

ENDING: She writes the boy out of the index and lets the former owners back in, and leaves the house with the index unfinished and herself unrecorded.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the index controls; the boy will be accounted for; Ada will leave the house or be recorded into it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.

ENDING: The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged. Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds. Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public. The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts. Opposition pressure is a budget, not a setting. A story that spends maximum pressure in every scene bankrupts itself by the middle; a story that hoards it starves. Plan the expenditure deliberately: where the antagonist's campaigns crest, where they merely continue, and where they are deliberately quiet.

Give the pressure a rhythm with reasons. Crests should follow buildup, and quiet periods should be explained by the opposition's own constraints, regroupings, or divided attention, so the reader experiences variation as the opponent's lifecycle rather than the author's breath. Mark the crest points and what each one is for.

Concentrate the final pressure deliberately. The endgame's confrontations should draw on budgets established earlier: the liability planted in the first act, the resource the antagonist has been conserving, the grudge that ripens into obsession. Decide what the endgame spends, and keep those notes unspent until the endgame arrives.

Plan the protagonist's side of the ledger against it. Pressure is only legible against resistance: for each crest, know what the protagonist spends to absorb it, and what that expenditure makes impossible later. The two ledgers, pressure and resistance, are one system, and the story's fairness lives in their balance.

The reader's fear for a character is bounded by what the story has shown the character valuing. Stakes are built in scenes of attachment and spent in scenes of threat, and the exchange rate between them is set by the specificity of the attachment.

Do not resolve an emotion as soon as it appears. Emotional states should change gradually and leave residue: a chapter that closes an emotional movement completely must still let it alter behavior, decisions, or relationships in later chapters, or the reader learns that feelings in this book do not matter.

Let behavior shift with company. People perform differently for a superior, a sibling, a stranger, an old friend; the differences should be visible in speech, posture, and what they choose to admit, and the same person seen by two others should not look like one consistent image.

Set the budget: crest points, quiet periods with their in-story reasons, offstage expenditures, and the endgame's concentration. Draft the opposition as a campaign with finite means, and the contest will stay alive from first page to last.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.

ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.

OPEN THREADS: the altered sequence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): anomaly noticed, then dismissed, then provable; mother's medical debt (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): refinanced twice, then transferred; carter fire plot (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): accelerant cached, dates moved twice; Otte's grain payments (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): receipts referenced, never shown.

ENDING: She publishes the ledger, transfers her mother's seal to her own name, and stays in the archive she has just ruined, which is the only place the rebuilding can happen.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the ledger will be exposed or destroyed by the end; Ilsa's copying habit will cost her something specific; the poor's seals will be settled one way or the other.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year | The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route | Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day
ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately; the bond will be resolved, bought or broken.

Begin the planning with the terminal stake: what the protagonist is really fighting for at the end, which is usually a value, an identity, or a relationship that the opening conflict only disguised. Then design each earlier stage as a partial, distorted, or smaller version of that stake, so the whole arc reads as one continuous excavation.

Schedule the currency shifts. Practical stakes carry the opening; relational stakes should contaminate them by the middle; moral stakes should govern the end. Each shift is a scene-load: the moment the protagonist first has to pay in the new currency, and the moment they recognize the price has changed.

Plan the raises to revisit old wounds. The strongest escalation structure calls back earlier costs at higher denominations: the sacrifice of the first act returns in the last as the thing that decides whether the final choice is possible. Mark which early expenditures are being held for late recall, and protect them from casual use.

Escalation that matters changes the terms of the conflict: who is exposed, what victory would mean, what defeat now costs. Volume without a change of terms is repetition wearing a bigger costume.

Give each character an individual emotional signature rather than a shared repertoire of reactions. Surprise does not always widen the eyes; fear does not always shake; grief does not always produce tears. A reaction is characterization, so it should be as specific as the person having it.

Let behavior shift with company. People perform differently for a superior, a sibling, a stranger, an old friend; the differences should be visible in speech, posture, and what they choose to admit, and the same person seen by two others should not look like one consistent image.

Fix the ladder of meaning: the terminal stake, the staged redefinitions that excavate it, and the moments where the currency of cost changes. Draft every raise as a revelation of what the fight was always about.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year | The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route | Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day
ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately; the bond will be resolved, bought or broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.
Your story's opposition has finite means, and the distribution of those means across the arc is undecided.
Decide how opposition pressure is distributed across the whole book: where it is spent, where it is withheld, and how it compounds.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Give the structural reasoning only; the drafting will come later.
response:
The promises this book has already made are on the record: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year. The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route. Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day. She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Opposition pressure is a budget, not a setting. A story that spends maximum pressure in every scene bankrupts itself by the middle; a story that hoards it starves. Plan the expenditure deliberately: where the antagonist's campaigns crest, where they merely continue, and where they are deliberately quiet.

Give the pressure a rhythm with reasons. Crests should follow buildup, and quiet periods should be explained by the opposition's own constraints, regroupings, or divided attention, so the reader experiences variation as the opponent's lifecycle rather than the author's breath. Mark the crest points and what each one is for.

Budget offstage pressure as carefully as staged confrontations. The moves the antagonist makes unseen, which the protagonist discovers as changed circumstances, cost page time but compound believability. Allocate a share of the opposition's campaign to the space between appearances, and let the protagonist find evidence of it.

Concentrate the final pressure deliberately. The endgame's confrontations should draw on budgets established earlier: the liability planted in the first act, the resource the antagonist has been conserving, the grudge that ripens into obsession. Decide what the endgame spends, and keep those notes unspent until the endgame arrives.

Conflict is a contest over something scarce and consequential; every other element is staging. Before writing any scene of struggle, be able to name the scarce thing, who wants it, what each side can spend, and what winning would actually mean.

Enter scenes as late as seems possible and leave once the dramatic work is done, unless the material after the turn is exactly what the chapter is about. Summarize only what is genuinely uninteresting, and expand only what the story actually needs; neither motion is about reaching a word count.

Permit contradictory feelings to coexist, and permit characters to misread themselves. A person can be frightened and curious, relieved and resentful, and can explain their own state wrongly to themselves. The viewpoint's own interpretation of its feelings is not authoritative, and treating it as authoritative flattens the interior.

Commit to the paired ledgers: pressure allocated across the arc, resistance priced against it, and the endgame funded by everything withheld earlier. Write forward with the budget in hand, and let no scene of the conflict be unpriced.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.
OPEN THREADS: the cellar (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a search grid gap, then an excavation request; the object (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): carried then, kept now; sealed statement (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a transcript with an omission; second exit (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a plan, then a door under plaster.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.
Your novel has one dominant opposing force, and you must decide how its pressure is spent across the whole book.
Decide how opposition pressure is distributed across the whole book: where it is spent, where it is withheld, and how it compounds.
You are architecting a novel before drafting begins.
Set the load-bearing decisions down in full, so the draft has something solid to stand on.
response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar. The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life. Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit. Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Before drafting, treat the antagonist as a limited actor with limited means, and budget their pressure across the arc. The reader's sense of an alive opponent comes from seeing pressure arrive on schedule, escalate as its target adapts, and concentrate where it matters most.

Give the pressure a rhythm with reasons. Crests should follow buildup, and quiet periods should be explained by the opposition's own constraints, regroupings, or divided attention, so the reader experiences variation as the opponent's lifecycle rather than the author's breath. Mark the crest points and what each one is for.

Concentrate the final pressure deliberately. The endgame's confrontations should draw on budgets established earlier: the liability planted in the first act, the resource the antagonist has been conserving, the grudge that ripens into obsession. Decide what the endgame spends, and keep those notes unspent until the endgame arrives.

Plan the protagonist's side of the ledger against it. Pressure is only legible against resistance: for each crest, know what the protagonist spends to absorb it, and what that expenditure makes impossible later. The two ledgers, pressure and resistance, are one system, and the story's fairness lives in their balance.

The reader's fear for a character is bounded by what the story has shown the character valuing. Stakes are built in scenes of attachment and spent in scenes of threat, and the exchange rate between them is set by the specificity of the attachment.

Enter scenes as late as seems possible and leave once the dramatic work is done, unless the material after the turn is exactly what the chapter is about. Summarize only what is genuinely uninteresting, and expand only what the story actually needs; neither motion is about reaching a word count.

Permit contradictory feelings to coexist, and permit characters to misread themselves. A person can be frightened and curious, relieved and resentful, and can explain their own state wrongly to themselves. The viewpoint's own interpretation of its feelings is not authoritative, and treating it as authoritative flattens the interior.

Commit to the paired ledgers: pressure allocated across the arc, resistance priced against it, and the endgame funded by everything withheld earlier. Write forward with the budget in hand, and let no scene of the conflict be unpriced.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.
CAST IN PLAY: Surveyor Alder, the narrator: wants an accurate map and a promotion; flaw, he believes accuracy is neutral; secret, he has left two settlements off the preliminary sheet; knows, the map will displace whoever it records | Lieutenant Cray, escort commander: wants the valley pacified without casualties; flaw, he needs the expedition to justify itself; secret, he has authorization to remove settlements that resist; knows, the compensation schedule's inadequacy | Mira, valley guide: wants her village registered under its own name; flaw, she trusted the party's ledger; secret, she has been guiding the survey to the settlements least able to leave; knows, the valley's flood seasons.
OPEN THREADS: preliminary sheet (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a filed map, then a removal order; compensation schedule (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): payment per acre, assessed from the map; removal authorization (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a written power the surveyor must sign; flood season (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a road that closes for five months.
THREE-ACT ARC: The party enters the valley, the survey begins, and Alder's preliminary sheet is sent to the capital without his approval | Mira's guidance, Cray's authorization, and the compensation schedule intersect; the filed sheet's consequences reach the valley | The flood season closes the only road, the escort demands its authorization, and Alder must choose what the final map will say
ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning the novel described above, and the question below concerns the book's architecture rather than one scene.
You are planning a story whose conflicts will have to grow across hundreds of pages without exhausting themselves.
Plan the escalation of the whole story as a progression in meaning: how each stage of the conflict redefines what is truly at risk.
You are planning a novel.
Build the framework now, before any drafting begins.
response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. The party enters the valley, the survey begins, and Alder's preliminary sheet is sent to the capital without his approval. Mira's guidance, Cray's authorization, and the compensation schedule intersect; the filed sheet's consequences reach the valley. The flood season closes the only road, the escort demands its authorization, and Alder must choose what the final map will say. He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Escalation across a full arc is a change in what the conflict is about, not a growth in how loud it is. Plan the story's raises as a sequence of redefinitions, each one revealing that the fight was always also about something deeper than the previous stage admitted.

Begin the planning with the terminal stake: what the protagonist is really fighting for at the end, which is usually a value, an identity, or a relationship that the opening conflict only disguised. Then design each earlier stage as a partial, distorted, or smaller version of that stake, so the whole arc reads as one continuous excavation.

Schedule the currency shifts. Practical stakes carry the opening; relational stakes should contaminate them by the middle; moral stakes should govern the end. Each shift is a scene-load: the moment the protagonist first has to pay in the new currency, and the moment they recognize the price has changed.

Decide the endgame's accounting. By the climax, the reader should be able to state what each side is fighting for, what it has already spent, and what a loss would mean in the currency the story has taught them. The final conflict's power is the accumulated precision of that accounting, built stage by stage across the arc.

The reader's fear for a character is bounded by what the story has shown the character valuing. Stakes are built in scenes of attachment and spent in scenes of threat, and the exchange rate between them is set by the specificity of the attachment.

Keep emotional amplitude uneven across the book. If every chapter reaches the same intensity, the reader's calibration flattens and later events cannot exceed earlier ones. Decide where the chapter's emotional peak belongs, and let other chapters remain below it.

Allow characters to be wrong, selfish, and unwise without becoming stupid. Decisions must be reasonable from inside the character's knowledge and pressures, and the reader should be able to see why the choice looked correct at the moment it was made, even while seeing that it will cost.

Commit to the escalation plan: terminal stake first, currency shifts scheduled, early costs held for late recall. The story will now raise stakes by deepening them, and the reader will feel the ground move without the volume rising.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.
THREE-ACT ARC: Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates | Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate | Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth
ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.
Your materials center on one character's development, and the decision chain that expresses it is still unformed.
Plan the protagonist's decision arc across the whole book: how their pattern of choosing is established, tested, broken, and reformed.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Give the structural reasoning only; the drafting will come later.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting. Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates. Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate. Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth. The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

A character arc is a pattern of decisions that the story establishes, stresses, breaks, and rebuilds. Plan the arc as that pattern's biography: the early choices that show the default mode, the pressures that make the mode costly, the decision where it fails, and the choice that shows what has replaced it.

Schedule the stress tests. Through the middle, each major decision should raise the cost of the default pattern while leaving it technically viable, so the character can keep choosing it and the reader can keep dreading it. The arc's middle is a slow demonstration that the price compounds, delivered in decisions rather than observations.

Design the breaking choice. There must be one decision the old pattern cannot make correctly, where following it would destroy something the story has proven precious. The character's failure or refusal at this point is the arc's true midpoint, whatever page it lands on, and everything after is conducted under the new terms.

Plan the reformed pattern to be visible in a final decision of the same type as the founding ones. The reader recognizes change most clearly when the same kind of choice recurs with a different outcome: the earlier self's option visible and declined, at similar cost, for reasons the reader can now trace to everything between. Build the finale as that rhyme.

Every consequential choice needs three properties: options that are live, information that is incomplete, and time that is short. Remove any one and the choice becomes a demonstration; keep all three and it becomes a revelation.

Decide what each character wants in this chapter, what they are willing to risk for it, and what they will not do even to succeed. The boundary is where the character is legible, and it is the part of the design most often left implicit, which is why so many characters read as capable of anything.

Keep characters from explaining what they already know for the reader's benefit. Information in dialogue should be information someone has a reason to say aloud: a challenge, a correction, a lie, a question that conceals a different question. Where the reader needs a fact and no speaker would state it, move the fact out of the conversation entirely.

Commit to the arc's proof plan: which decisions establish, which stress, which break, which reform. Draft toward the breaking choice with the patience the middle requires, and let the final decision be the rhyme that convinces.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.
Your materials involve interlocking agendas, and the assignment of causal responsibility to each character is undecided.
Decide how agency is distributed across the cast: which characters drive which events, and how their initiatives interlock.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Set out how you will think about this across the whole arc.
response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient. The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating. The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her. Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Plan the cast as a system of intersecting initiatives rather than a hierarchy of importance. Each consequential character drives their own line of events from their own motives, and the plot is the space where those lines interfere. Decide the interference pattern now, and let every character's initiative have a price someone else pays.

Give the protagonist a monopoly on exactly one kind of causation, and distribute the rest. They might be the only one who can make a certain kind of sacrifice, see a certain kind of pattern, or refuse a certain kind of offer. The monopoly is what makes them necessary to the story; the distributed agency is what keeps the world from being their machinery.

Schedule the collisions of initiatives. The strongest plot beats occur where two characters' plans occupy the same ground: each acting reasonably from their own position, each making the other's situation worse. List the collisions the arc requires, and for each, trace the initiative back to the character and the want that produced it.

Budget the antagonist's agency above all. The opposition should cause at least as much of the plot as the protagonist does, and their initiatives should be aimed at their own ends rather than at testing the hero. If the antagonist only exists to respond, redistribute their agenda until their campaign could proceed with no hero in the book at all.

Every consequential choice needs three properties: options that are live, information that is incomplete, and time that is short. Remove any one and the choice becomes a demonstration; keep all three and it becomes a revelation.

Let relationships move slowly and unevenly, with friction inside affection and remembered history inside every exchange. Trust should be earned in visible increments, arguments should leave residue, and old disagreements should be able to resurface in a later scene with the same participants changed.

Dialogue is speech shaped by situation, relationship, and purpose, not prose wearing quotation marks. Fix what each speaker wants out of the exchange and what each is unwilling to say before writing the exchange, because those two facts generate the shape of the conversation more reliably than any line-by-line plan.

Commit to the distribution: who causes, who responds, who is mistaken about which they are doing. Write every major beat as an interference pattern between initiatives, and the story's power structure will be legible without explanation.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.

The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved. The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists. The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

A story's power structure is decided by who causes what. Before drafting, assign the causal responsibility: which character generates each major turn, who merely responds, and who is wrong about their own degree of control. The map of agency is the map of meaning, because readers read power through initiative.

Schedule the collisions of initiatives. The strongest plot beats occur where two characters' plans occupy the same ground: each acting reasonably from their own position, each making the other's situation worse. List the collisions the arc requires, and for each, trace the initiative back to the character and the want that produced it.

The opposition should cause at least as much of the plot as the protagonist does, and their initiatives should be aimed at their own ends rather than at testing the hero. If the antagonist only exists to respond, redistribute their agenda until their campaign could proceed with no hero in the book at all.

Decide which characters are wrong about their own control. The character who believes they are directing events while being used, and the one who believes themselves powerless while their choices drive the catastrophe, are where the story's irony lives. Assign the delusions deliberately, and let the reader see through them before the characters do.

Change in a character is only legible against a fixed pattern. Establish the default rigorously, stress it at rising cost, break it once at the right pressure, and rhyme it at the end: that is the entire architecture of an arc.

Build people from conflicting traits rather than assigned roles: generosity that coexists with vanity, competence that coexists with cowardice in one specific area. Contradiction is what produces decisions a reader cannot predict from a character's function in the plot.

Allow conversation to be inefficient. Interruptions, hesitations, subject changes, irrelevant remarks, corrections, unfinished thoughts, laughter at the wrong moment, and answers to questions nobody asked all belong, because efficiency is a property of written information transfer rather than of speech.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.
OPEN THREADS: the cellar (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a search grid gap, then an excavation request; the object (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): carried then, kept now; sealed statement (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a transcript with an omission; second exit (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a plan, then a door under plaster.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Through the middle, each major decision should raise the cost of the default pattern while leaving it technically viable, so the character can keep choosing it and the reader can keep dreading it. The arc's middle is a slow demonstration that the price compounds, delivered in decisions rather than observations.

The character's failure or refusal at this point is the arc's true midpoint, whatever page it lands on, and everything after is conducted under the new terms.

Decide what each character wants in this chapter, what they are willing to risk for it, and what they will not do even to succeed. The boundary is where the character is legible, and it is the part of the design most often left implicit, which is why so many characters read as capable of anything.

Let subtext and evasion do the work. Characters can lie, refuse, stall, deflect, answer a different question, or defend themselves against an attack that never came. The gap between what is said and what is happening is where dialogue becomes drama instead of transcription.

Set the decision arc in sequence: founding pattern, compounding stress, breaking choice, reformed rhyme. Every scene of the book now serves one of those four functions, and the ones that serve none are candidates for the knife.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.
CAST IN PLAY: Surveyor Alder, the narrator: wants an accurate map and a promotion; flaw, he believes accuracy is neutral; secret, he has left two settlements off the preliminary sheet; knows, the map will displace whoever it records | Lieutenant Cray, escort commander: wants the valley pacified without casualties; flaw, he needs the expedition to justify itself; secret, he has authorization to remove settlements that resist; knows, the compensation schedule's inadequacy | Mira, valley guide: wants her village registered under its own name; flaw, she trusted the party's ledger; secret, she has been guiding the survey to the settlements least able to leave; knows, the valley's flood seasons.
OPEN THREADS: preliminary sheet (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a filed map, then a removal order; compensation schedule (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): payment per acre, assessed from the map; removal authorization (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a written power the surveyor must sign; flood season (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a road that closes for five months.
THREE-ACT ARC: The party enters the valley, the survey begins, and Alder's preliminary sheet is sent to the capital without his approval | Mira's guidance, Cray's authorization, and the compensation schedule intersect; the filed sheet's consequences reach the valley | The flood season closes the only road, the escort demands its authorization, and Alder must choose what the final map will say
ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.

ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately; the bond will be resolved, bought or broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.

Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.

A story's power structure is decided by who causes what. Before drafting, assign the causal responsibility: which character generates each major turn, who merely responds, and who is wrong about their own degree of control. The map of agency is the map of meaning, because readers read power through initiative.

Give the protagonist a monopoly on exactly one kind of causation, and distribute the rest. They might be the only one who can make a certain kind of sacrifice, see a certain kind of pattern, or refuse a certain kind of offer. The monopoly is what makes them necessary to the story; the distributed agency is what keeps the world from being their machinery.
