The arbitration clause blocks every internal route; the regulator needs an admissible sample; the chemist is ordered to dilute and begins keeping a second set of numbers. The inspection is announced for a date the bypass can be closed for, and the only way to prove the discharge is to be at the river when the plant is not expecting it. Nadia provides the sample and the schedule and loses her pension; the plant pays a fine and keeps operating with the valve sealed, which is a smaller outcome than she wanted and a real one. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

A story's power structure is decided by who causes what. Before drafting, assign the causal responsibility: which character generates each major turn, who merely responds, and who is wrong about their own degree of control. The map of agency is the map of meaning, because readers read power through initiative.

Give the protagonist a monopoly on exactly one kind of causation, and distribute the rest. They might be the only one who can make a certain kind of sacrifice, see a certain kind of pattern, or refuse a certain kind of offer. The monopoly is what makes them necessary to the story; the distributed agency is what keeps the world from being their machinery.

Schedule the collisions of initiatives. The strongest plot beats occur where two characters' plans occupy the same ground: each acting reasonably from their own position, each making the other's situation worse. List the collisions the arc requires, and for each, trace the initiative back to the character and the want that produced it.

Decide which characters are wrong about their own control. The character who believes they are directing events while being used, and the one who believes themselves powerless while their choices drive the catastrophe, are where the story's irony lives. Assign the delusions deliberately, and let the reader see through them before the characters do.

Every consequential choice needs three properties: options that are live, information that is incomplete, and time that is short. Remove any one and the choice becomes a demonstration; keep all three and it becomes a revelation.

Use dialogue to expose relationships: who defers, who interrupts, who tolerates silence, who explains, who tests. Track how a given pair's speech habits change across the book, because that change is one of the clearest and least preachy ways to show a relationship moving.

Let the reader arrive at the emotion before the text names it. Behavior, physical reaction, attention, dialogue, and choice carry an emotional state; naming is a fallback for moments where precision matters more than participation, and overuse converts the book into a report of feelings rather than an experience of them.

Fix the agency map: each character's initiatives, the protagonist's monopoly, the collision schedule, and the delusions of control. Draft from the map, and the cast will move as a system instead of an orbit.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.
THREE-ACT ARC: Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates | Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate | Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth
ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning a character-driven story whose structure will be built from the protagonist's decisions rather than from external events.
Plan the protagonist's decision arc across the whole book: how their pattern of choosing is established, tested, broken, and reformed.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates. Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate. Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth. The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

A character arc is a pattern of decisions that the story establishes, stresses, breaks, and rebuilds. Plan the arc as that pattern's biography: the early choices that show the default mode, the pressures that make the mode costly, the decision where it fails, and the choice that shows what has replaced it.

Establish the default pattern with at least two early decisions made under mild pressure. One decision is a data point; two begin a pattern the reader can extrapolate, and the whole arc depends on the reader holding that extrapolation. Choose these founding decisions for clarity of cost: each should show the pattern working at a price the reader can already sense.

Design the breaking choice. There must be one decision the old pattern cannot make correctly, where following it would destroy something the story has proven precious. The character's failure or refusal at this point is the arc's true midpoint, whatever page it lands on, and everything after is conducted under the new terms.

Plan the reformed pattern to be visible in a final decision of the same type as the founding ones. The reader recognizes change most clearly when the same kind of choice recurs with a different outcome: the earlier self's option visible and declined, at similar cost, for reasons the reader can now trace to everything between. Build the finale as that rhyme.

Change in a character is only legible against a fixed pattern. Establish the default rigorously, stress it at rising cost, break it once at the right pressure, and rhyme it at the end: that is the entire architecture of an arc.

Give each speaker an identifiable verbal world derived from personality, background, confidence, age, relationship, and current circumstance. Vocabulary, sentence length, willingness to interrupt, tolerance for silence, and preferred evasion should differ measurably between characters and stay stable across the book.

Commit to the arc's proof plan: which decisions establish, which stress, which break, which reform. Draft toward the breaking choice with the patience the middle requires, and let the final decision be the rhyme that convinces.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's sea wall work is funded by a levy charged to properties above the high-water line; The couple's house is below the line and cannot be repaired after a flood without a licensed surveyor; The harbour's fishing fleet is co-owned in shares that must be sold to existing holders.
CAST IN PLAY: Aidan, harbour master, the husband: wants the house repaired and the marriage continued without discussion; flaw, he maintains things instead of understanding them; secret, he has been quietly selling his fleet shares to cover the flood damage; knows, the sea wall's true schedule | Bryn, surveyor, the wife: wants the marriage assessed honestly before the season ends; flaw, she mistakes accuracy for kindness; secret, she has accepted a post in another county and not told him; knows, the house cannot be sold or insured in its current state | Ondine, Bryn's colleague and client: wants the sea wall built before spring; flaw, she values the town's survival over its people's arrangements; secret, her survey supports using the couple's property line as the wall's footing; knows, the levy's distribution.
OPEN THREADS: flood damage (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): water in the floor, then a condemned structure; share sales (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a ledger of shares, then an empty holding; job offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a letter, a date, a county; wall footing (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a survey line through the back garden.

ENDING: The house is condemned and demolished for the wall footing, the fleet shares are gone, and the two of them separate with the paperwork clean and no reconciliation scene.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the sea wall will be built or abandoned; the house will be decided by the season; one of them will say the decisive thing out loud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year | The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route | Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day
ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the city cannot transmit; Ines will be caught reading or will be asked to read deliberately; the bond will be resolved, bought or broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route. Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day. Plan the cast as a system of intersecting initiatives rather than a hierarchy of importance. Each consequential character drives their own line of events from their own motives, and the plot is the space where those lines interfere. Decide the interference pattern now, and let every character's initiative have a price someone else pays.

Give the protagonist a monopoly on exactly one kind of causation, and distribute the rest. The monopoly is what makes them necessary to the story; the distributed agency is what keeps the world from being their machinery.

Budget the antagonist's agency above all. The opposition should cause at least as much of the plot as the protagonist does, and their initiatives should be aimed at their own ends rather than at testing the hero. If the antagonist only exists to respond, redistribute their agenda until their campaign could proceed with no hero in the book at all.

Decide which characters are wrong about their own control. The character who believes they are directing events while being used, and the one who believes themselves powerless while their choices drive the catastrophe, are where the story's irony lives. Assign the delusions deliberately, and let the reader see through them before the characters do.

Motivation is layered and partly opaque to the person who holds it. The gap between what a character says they want, what they pursue, and what they need is the space where a reader's understanding grows.

Let behavior shift with company. People perform differently for a superior, a sibling, a stranger, an old friend; the differences should be visible in speech, posture, and what they choose to admit, and the same person seen by two others should not look like one consistent image.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.

PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will be completed or decisively failed; the cargo will be opened in front of the reader; Dema's crew will be answered for.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A ward holds only while its maker is alive and named in its grain; Thornwood cannot be cut by anyone who has not been formally released from apprenticeship; A failed ward does not fall; it turns, and it takes its maker's mark with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Tess, apprentice, the narrator: wants to be released and named; flaw, she revises the past as she tells it; secret, she has been making wards that turn; knows, the master's hands no longer work | Master Orr, wardwright, last of the guild: wants the workshop left to someone; flaw, he teaches by withholding and calls it testing; secret, he has been using Tess's hands for a year while signing the work himself; knows, the turning wards will come home | Pell, forest warden, outside the guild: wants the wards maintained by any means; flaw, he trusts systems more than people; secret, he has been reporting the turning wards to the forest villages; knows, which wards failed first.
OPEN THREADS: turning ward (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a mark that points the wrong way, then comes home; the master's hands (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): an unsigned piece, then a burned record; the buyer's visits (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): prices offered, then terms; Pell's reports (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): village complaints, then an emptied village.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tess is left alone with three wards to make before the season, and given no release; she makes them and one turns | She hides the turn, the forest begins coming in, and the master's deception and her own are set on the same track | Every option requires her to be named by someone: the master will not, the buyer will for a price, and the wards must be made regardless
ENDING: Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see a ward turn; Tess will either be named or not be named; the workshop will close or continue, not both.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Tess is left alone with three wards to make before the season, and given no release; she makes them and one turns. She hides the turn, the forest begins coming in, and the master's deception and her own are set on the same track. Every option requires her to be named by someone: the master will not, the buyer will for a price, and the wards must be made regardless. Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Before drafting, lay out the protagonist's choices as a single argument. The book will claim that this person changes in a specific direction, and the claim is proven only through decisions the reader witnesses. Fix the sequence of decisions that constitutes the proof, and know which ones are load-bearing.

Establish the default pattern with at least two early decisions made under mild pressure. One decision is a data point; two begin a pattern the reader can extrapolate, and the whole arc depends on the reader holding that extrapolation. Choose these founding decisions for clarity of cost: each should show the pattern working at a price the reader can already sense.

Design the breaking choice. There must be one decision the old pattern cannot make correctly, where following it would destroy something the story has proven precious. The character's failure or refusal at this point is the arc's true midpoint, whatever page it lands on, and everything after is conducted under the new terms.

Plan the reformed pattern to be visible in a final decision of the same type as the founding ones. The reader recognizes change most clearly when the same kind of choice recurs with a different outcome: the earlier self's option visible and declined, at similar cost, for reasons the reader can now trace to everything between. Build the finale as that rhyme.

Change in a character is only legible against a fixed pattern. Establish the default rigorously, stress it at rising cost, break it once at the right pressure, and rhyme it at the end: that is the entire architecture of an arc.

Keep the cast from converging on one personality. Not everyone is insightful, articulate, or kind; competence should be unevenly distributed, and how each character reacts to another's weakness should differ as much as the weaknesses do.

Let subtext and evasion do the work. Characters can lie, refuse, stall, deflect, answer a different question, or defend themselves against an attack that never came. The gap between what is said and what is happening is where dialogue becomes drama instead of transcription.

Set the decision arc in sequence: founding pattern, compounding stress, breaking choice, reformed rhyme. Every scene of the book now serves one of those four functions, and the ones that serve none are candidates for the knife.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.
CAST IN PLAY: Marguerite, shift supervisor, eighteen years: wants the shift closed clean and the report signed; flaw, she protects the shift from management and from itself; secret, she has been signing reports with an outdated injury count; knows, the conveyor's failure pattern | Nate, forklift operator: wants the promotion that requires a clean record; flaw, he trades truth for advancement; secret, he reported a colleague's near-miss as his own error to look diligent; knows, the loading bay's blind corner | Sofia, agency worker, six weeks: wants to be kept on after the season; flaw, she will not report anything that creates a form; secret, she has been working with a wrist injury for nine days; knows, the exact rate the line is set to.
OPEN THREADS: the report (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): four signatures required by dawn; Sofia's wrist (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a hidden injury, nine days old; photographs (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): three failed repairs, timestamped; the blind corner (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a near-miss Nate reattributed.
THREE-ACT ARC: The shift begins, the report is announced as due at dawn, and the conveyor's first fault is patched instead of fixed | Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree | Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision
ENDING: They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.

TITLE: Salt Throne -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, naval.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The strait is closed by a chain of warded hulls that tax every crossing in blood or coin; Charts of the outer shoals are printed on salt paper that rots a little every crossing; The cargo must stay below the waterline or it stops being cargo.
CAST IN PLAY: Dema Oris, smuggler captain of the Selvage: wants her crew's names cleared and their families paid; flaw, she decides before she understands; secret, she took the faction's money and intends to keep the cargo; knows, the crew's deaths were ordered, and not by the admiral | Admiral Ket, blockade commander: wants the blockade held without a mutiny; flaw, she protects the institution that ruined her; secret, she issued the order under a false name to save the fleet; knows, Dema is carrying something the fleet needs | Ossa, navigator, surviving crew member: wants to reach her daughter before the season turns; flaw, she trades information for safety; secret, she signed the manifest that got the crew killed; knows, the salt charts rot differently in different hands.
OPEN THREADS: the crew's deaths (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a forged order, a witness, a name; the cargo (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): weight, then breath, then a person; salt charts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): rot pattern read as a message; Ossa's daughter (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a port, a season, a debt.
THREE-ACT ARC: Dema takes the commission, assembles the crew from what remains, and learns the cargo has a heartbeat | The crossing exposes the collision between Ket's personal honesty and institutional crime; Ossa's manifest surfaces; the cargo wakes | Dema must choose between delivering the cargo and finishing the crossing with the crew that is still alive, and the choice reprices everything she wanted at the start
ENDING: She lands the cargo with the faction, hands Ket the evidence that clears her crew, and keeps neither the ship nor the money, sailing out as crew rather than captain.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are planning a novel.

response:
The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying. The movements the book has to pay for: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient. The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating. The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

A character arc is a pattern of decisions that the story establishes, stresses, breaks, and rebuilds. Plan the arc as that pattern's biography: the early choices that show the default mode, the pressures that make the mode costly, the decision where it fails, and the choice that shows what has replaced it.

Establish the default pattern with at least two early decisions made under mild pressure. One decision is a data point; two begin a pattern the reader can extrapolate, and the whole arc depends on the reader holding that extrapolation. Choose these founding decisions for clarity of cost: each should show the pattern working at a price the reader can already sense.

Schedule the stress tests. Through the middle, each major decision should raise the cost of the default pattern while leaving it technically viable, so the character can keep choosing it and the reader can keep dreading it. The arc's middle is a slow demonstration that the price compounds, delivered in decisions rather than observations.

Design the breaking choice. There must be one decision the old pattern cannot make correctly, where following it would destroy something the story has proven precious. The character's failure or refusal at this point is the arc's true midpoint, whatever page it lands on, and everything after is conducted under the new terms.

Change in a character is only legible against a fixed pattern. Establish the default rigorously, stress it at rising cost, break it once at the right pressure, and rhyme it at the end: that is the entire architecture of an arc.

Keep the wit budget low and distributed. Not every exchange can be sharp, not every character can deliver the perfect comeback, and the perfect response that arrives five minutes later is more useful characterization than the one that arrives on time. Humor should come from personality, circumstance, timing, or contrast rather than from an obligation to be funny.

Let the reader arrive at the emotion before the text names it. Behavior, physical reaction, attention, dialogue, and choice carry an emotional state; naming is a fallback for moments where precision matters more than participation, and overuse converts the book into a report of feelings rather than an experience of them.

Commit to the arc's proof plan: which decisions establish, which stress, which break, which reform. Draft toward the breaking choice with the patience the middle requires, and let the final decision be the rhyme that convinces.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.
OPEN THREADS: the removed page (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report with a gap, then the missing sheet; the burned coat (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): ash in the stove, then a button; the girl's plan (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a bus timetable, a packed bag; Ruth's brother (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): an alibi, a dispute, a confession.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.
THREE-ACT ARC: Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates | Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate | Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth
ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.

TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.

TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Deep Archive -- standalone, gothic horror, single location.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.
PREMISE: A cataloguer is hired to index a private library whose rooms rearrange themselves, and the index she writes begins to determine which of the house's former owners still exist indoors.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The index records what is in the house, and what the index omits is not found again; Rooms only move when unobserved, and any written plan of the house is eventually wrong; The house's owners cannot leave while a cataloguer holds the index open.

Give characters concerns that have nothing to do with the plot: preferences, irritations, habits, small ambitions, unfinished private business. These are what make the intervals between major events habitable and what make the major events land on a person rather than a protagonist.

Let subtext and evasion do the work. Characters can lie, refuse, stall, deflect, answer a different question, or defend themselves against an attack that never came. The gap between what is said and what is happening is where dialogue becomes drama instead of transcription.

Set the decision arc in sequence: founding pattern, compounding stress, breaking choice, reformed rhyme. Every scene of the book now serves one of those four functions, and the ones that serve none are candidates for the knife.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Ninth Lantern -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, urban.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a state lamplighter.
PREMISE: A city's protective light is finite and dispensed from nine lanterns; when the ninth is lit by a junior lamplighter, the reserve is nearly gone and everyone in power has known for years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each lantern holds a fixed measure of years, and the ninth is the reserve; Lamplight cannot be made, only moved from lantern to lantern by a licensed hand; Whoever carries light through the streets alone burns a little of themselves.
CAST IN PLAY: Peet Amaran, junior lamplighter, ninth watch: wants to be certified so his sister can leave the district; flaw, he cannot let a wrong thing stand unremarked; secret, he has already carried an unlicensed flame; knows, the ninth lantern was lit early | Mistress Hallow, master of the lightworks: wants the city calm until the transfer season; flaw, she has confused the institution with the city; secret, she has been rationing without a license for six years; knows, the real measure left | Dove Rhee, light-broker for the outer districts: wants the districts priced out of the light to be lit anyway; flaw, she needs to be the one who fixes it; secret, she has been selling light she does not have; knows, Peet's unlicensed carry.
OPEN THREADS: the empty reserve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): measure books, then the physical gauge; unlicensed carry (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): a burned palm, a witness, a price; Sister's transfer (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): permit papers that require certification; Tull's old falsification (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): an old sheet in Hallow's hand.
THREE-ACT ARC: Peet lights the ninth lantern, learns the reserve is empty, and is offered promotion to keep the fact quiet | He carries light to the dark districts with Dove's network while Hallow audits the works, and the audit closes on the person who taught him | The works must either admit the deficit or steal the light back from the districts, and Peet is the only licensed hand able to move it either way
ENDING: He redistributes the remaining light across the whole city, ending the districts' distinction, and loses his certification in a city that is dimmer but even.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see what the ninth lantern actually contains; the dark districts will get light or the reason they do not; Peet's certification will be tested against the truth.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The promises this book has already made are on the record: the reader will see what the ninth lantern actually contains; the dark districts will get light or the reason they do not. Read at the level of the whole novel they form a schedule rather than a set of intentions. Peet lights the ninth lantern, learns the reserve is empty, and is offered promotion to keep the fact quiet. He carries light to the dark districts with Dove's network while Hallow audits the works, and the audit closes on the person who taught him. The works must either admit the deficit or steal the light back from the districts, and Peet is the only licensed hand able to move it either way. A character arc is a pattern of decisions that the story establishes, stresses, breaks, and rebuilds. Plan the arc as that pattern's biography: the early choices that show the default mode, the pressures that make the mode costly, the decision where it fails, and the choice that shows what has replaced it.

Establish the default pattern with at least two early decisions made under mild pressure. One decision is a data point; two begin a pattern the reader can extrapolate, and the whole arc depends on the reader holding that extrapolation. Choose these founding decisions for clarity of cost: each should show the pattern working at a price the reader can already sense.

Schedule the stress tests. Through the middle, each major decision should raise the cost of the default pattern while leaving it technically viable, so the character can keep choosing it and the reader can keep dreading it. The arc's middle is a slow demonstration that the price compounds, delivered in decisions rather than observations.

Design the breaking choice. There must be one decision the old pattern cannot make correctly, where following it would destroy something the story has proven precious. The character's failure or refusal at this point is the arc's true midpoint, whatever page it lands on, and everything after is conducted under the new terms.

Motivation is layered and partly opaque to the person who holds it. The gap between what a character says they want, what they pursue, and what they need is the space where a reader's understanding grows.

Build people from conflicting traits rather than assigned roles: generosity that coexists with vanity, competence that coexists with cowardice in one specific area. Contradiction is what produces decisions a reader cannot predict from a character's function in the plot.

Commit to the arc's proof plan: which decisions establish, which stress, which break, which reform. Draft toward the breaking choice with the patience the middle requires, and let the final decision be the rhyme that convinces.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.
CAST IN PLAY: Marguerite, shift supervisor, eighteen years: wants the shift closed clean and the report signed; flaw, she protects the shift from management and from itself; secret, she has been signing reports with an outdated injury count; knows, the conveyor's failure pattern | Nate, forklift operator: wants the promotion that requires a clean record; flaw, he trades truth for advancement; secret, he reported a colleague's near-miss as his own error to look diligent; knows, the loading bay's blind corner | Sofia, agency worker, six weeks: wants to be kept on after the season; flaw, she will not report anything that creates a form; secret, she has been working with a wrist injury for nine days; knows, the exact rate the line is set to.
OPEN THREADS: the report (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): four signatures required by dawn; Sofia's wrist (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a hidden injury, nine days old; photographs (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): three failed repairs, timestamped; the blind corner (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a near-miss Nate reattributed.
THREE-ACT ARC: The shift begins, the report is announced as due at dawn, and the conveyor's first fault is patched instead of fixed | Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree | Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision
ENDING: They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the report will be signed or not before dawn; the line will fail in a way that involves a person; one of the four will change position on the report.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree. Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision. They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Plan the cast as a system of intersecting initiatives rather than a hierarchy of importance. Each consequential character drives their own line of events from their own motives, and the plot is the space where those lines interfere. Decide the interference pattern now, and let every character's initiative have a price someone else pays.

Give the protagonist a monopoly on exactly one kind of causation, and distribute the rest. They might be the only one who can make a certain kind of sacrifice, see a certain kind of pattern, or refuse a certain kind of offer. The monopoly is what makes them necessary to the story; the distributed agency is what keeps the world from being their machinery.

Budget the antagonist's agency above all. The opposition should cause at least as much of the plot as the protagonist does, and their initiatives should be aimed at their own ends rather than at testing the hero. If the antagonist only exists to respond, redistribute their agenda until their campaign could proceed with no hero in the book at all.

Decide which characters are wrong about their own control. The character who believes they are directing events while being used, and the one who believes themselves powerless while their choices drive the catastrophe, are where the story's irony lives. Assign the delusions deliberately, and let the reader see through them before the characters do.

Change in a character is only legible against a fixed pattern. Establish the default rigorously, stress it at rising cost, break it once at the right pressure, and rhyme it at the end: that is the entire architecture of an arc.

Allow conversation to be inefficient. Interruptions, hesitations, subject changes, irrelevant remarks, corrections, unfinished thoughts, laughter at the wrong moment, and answers to questions nobody asked all belong, because efficiency is a property of written information transfer rather than of speech.

Keep emotional amplitude uneven across the book. If every chapter reaches the same intensity, the reader's calibration flattens and later events cannot exceed earlier ones. Decide where the chapter's emotional peak belongs, and let other chapters remain below it.

Fix the agency map: each character's initiatives, the protagonist's monopoly, the collision schedule, and the delusions of control. Draft from the map, and the cast will move as a system instead of an orbit.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Fen Road -- standalone, survival, expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the medic.
PREMISE: A six-person survey team crossing a wetland loses its route markers and its leader, and the medic who has been falsifying fitness reports must decide who is fit enough to carry what.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The fen's causeway is passable only in the dry weeks and only at night, when the peat holds; The team's rations were calculated for a crossing of nine nights; Any team member left behind is entitled to the group's full share of supplies.
CAST IN PLAY: Ori, team medic: wants all six across with a clean report; flaw, she protects people by withholding information; secret, she passed two members who should have failed their fitness review; knows, the team's actual condition | Halvard, survey lead: wants the route completed and the map delivered; flaw, he decides by schedule; secret, he accepted the commission below the safe number of nights; knows, the rations are short | Sel, porter, youngest: wants to be paid and to be taken seriously; flaw, she hides injury to stay on the manifest; secret, she has been re-marking the route posts incorrectly; knows, the posts have been moved.
OPEN THREADS: falsified reviews (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two passing grades, two failing bodies; route posts (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): posts in the wrong places; rations (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a count, then a recount; the left-behind rule (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): supplies set aside for an abandoned member.
THREE-ACT ARC: The team enters the fen, the marker discrepancies are small, and a first injury changes the pace | Rations, injuries, and the falsified fitness reviews collide; Halvard's schedule becomes the antagonist; the markers are proved wrong | Eight nights in, the causeway is behind them, one member cannot continue, and the group's own rule about being left behind becomes a live instrument
ENDING: They hold to the rule, abandon the survey, and cross four nights late with a documented route they will never sell.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the crossing will take fewer or more nights than planned; someone will be carried or left; the falsified reviews will matter to a decision.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

A story's power structure is decided by who causes what. Before drafting, assign the causal responsibility: which character generates each major turn, who merely responds, and who is wrong about their own degree of control. The map of agency is the map of meaning, because readers read power through initiative.

Give the protagonist a monopoly on exactly one kind of causation, and distribute the rest. They might be the only one who can make a certain kind of sacrifice, see a certain kind of pattern, or refuse a certain kind of offer. The monopoly is what makes them necessary to the story; the distributed agency is what keeps the world from being their machinery.

Budget the antagonist's agency above all. The opposition should cause at least as much of the plot as the protagonist does, and their initiatives should be aimed at their own ends rather than at testing the hero. If the antagonist only exists to respond, redistribute their agenda until their campaign could proceed with no hero in the book at all.

Assign the delusions deliberately, and let the reader see through them before the characters do.

Every consequential choice needs three properties: options that are live, information that is incomplete, and time that is short. Remove any one and the choice becomes a demonstration; keep all three and it becomes a revelation.

Decide what each character wants in this chapter, what they are willing to risk for it, and what they will not do even to succeed. The boundary is where the character is legible, and it is the part of the design most often left implicit, which is why so many characters read as capable of anything.

Keep characters from explaining what they already know for the reader's benefit. Information in dialogue should be information someone has a reason to say aloud: a challenge, a correction, a lie, a question that conceals a different question. Where the reader needs a fact and no speaker would state it, move the fact out of the conversation entirely.

Fix the agency map: each character's initiatives, the protagonist's monopoly, the collision schedule, and the delusions of control. Draft from the map, and the cast will move as a system instead of an orbit.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.
CAST IN PLAY: Rennick, planner, retired: wants one final job that pays his debts; flaw, he plans for machinery and not for people; secret, he has already been paid by the bank's owner to test the building; knows, the owner's security revisions | Sabine, locksmith: wants her brother's release from a debt prison; flaw, she trusts nobody's plan but her own; secret, she has copied the vault key pattern; knows, the second door's true difficulty | Ode, inside man, night clerk: wants out of the city with his daughter; flaw, he cannot lie under pressure; secret, he has already told the owner that a crew is coming; knows, the guard rotation posted tonight.
OPEN THREADS: identity registrations (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): ninety-second windows, then a record of a previous test; copied key (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a wax impression, then a duplicate; clerk's disclosure (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a phone call logged; guard's documentation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): photographs of the ledgers.
THREE-ACT ARC: The plan is assembled and rehearsed against the layout, and the first door is easier than the plan predicted | The ease of the first door is the trap: the owner is watching the test. Identity registrations, a copied key, and the clerk's nerve converge | The ledgers are only useful if they reach the front door and daylight, and the crew has to choose between the plan and the captives' safety
ENDING: Rennick breaks his own plan to move the ledgers out through the front with the staff, the door system records all five of them, and the crew walks into arrest with the ledgers in the hands of the guard captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: five doors will be opened in order; the crew's own rule about staff will be tested; one member has already betrayed the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.
CAST IN PLAY: Isaac Rell, tracker, the narrator: wants the debt cleared without killing anyone; flaw, he believes restraint is a form of payment; secret, he took the wrong man and knows it; knows, the warrant was bought by a rancher | Widow Sarn, boarding house keeper, creditor: wants the town to survive the winter; flaw, she has learned to spend other people's losses; secret, she paid the tracker's debt to hold the water claim; knows, the ditch head's owner | Rancher Coel, ditch head owner: wants the valley's water consolidated; flaw, he purchases with patience instead of force; secret, he filed the original warrant to remove a claimant; knows, the truth about the wrong man.
OPEN THREADS: the wrong man (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a face he cannot forget; the warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a filed claim, a rancher's signature; the ditch head (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a filing that transfers water rights; tracker's own warrant (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a poster with his name on it.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper | The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears | The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly
ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the debt will be settled or refused; the truth about the wrong man will be entered somewhere; the council will meet and decide something.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.
