instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Quiet Ministry -- standalone, dystopia, bureaucracy.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.
PREMISE: A records officer in a ministry that assigns citizens to work discovers that her own file has been edited to make her suitable for a job she has been doing for six years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Assignments are made by file, and no appeal may cite information not in the file; Records officers may correct errors only with two supporting documents; Every correction is itself recorded and visible to the ministry's auditors.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Ren, records officer: wants her file to say the truth without losing her post; flaw, she trusts procedure to protect her; secret, she has made eleven unsupported corrections for other people; knows, the file editing pattern | Supervisor Tal, section head: wants the section's error rate at zero for the inspection; flaw, he optimizes for metrics; secret, he authorized the editing of Ada's file to keep her in the section; knows, which files have been adjusted | Inspector Oyo, ministry auditor: wants the pattern of corrections; flaw, she treats people as instruments of proof; secret, she was assigned here because she once made the same corrections; knows, the eleven corrections.

THREE-ACT ARC: Ada finds the edit in her own file and cannot report it without exposing her eleven private corrections | The inspector traces the pattern; Tal offers protection in exchange for silence; Renn's assignment comes up for review in the same cycle | The inspection has a deadline, and the only way Ada can save her brother's file is to submit a correction supported by a document that does not exist
ENDING: She submits nothing, her brother is reassigned out of the city, and she stays in the section with her file still wrong and her corrections stopped.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the file will be corrected or left wrong; the parallel between Ada and the inspector will surface; an assignment decision will be shown as a life decision.

TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.

TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.

THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Use the character's expertise as a continuing descriptive resource across the book: the same trade or discipline supplies fresh attention at each stage, and its vocabulary can grow with the character's confidence, which gives the reader an economical signal of development.

One precise image and one strong sentence per page outlast a chapter of sustained brilliance, and a chapter that tries to be excellent everywhere has nowhere to go when something important happens.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

Maren and Torell meet at the stones, each prepared to withdraw, and both are prevented by a third event: the ward fails early and something gets through. Forced to work together to reseat the stones, each betrays the arrangement in ways the other detects and misreads; the border settlements become the currency. The thing behind the ward offers each heir exactly what they want in exchange for the covenant broken; both nearly accept, and the resolution is a choice neither wanted. They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

A book grounded in the physical has an advantage that abstract books do not: its changes are visible. Track the body across the book: injuries, exhaustion, illness, physical capacity. A body that remembers the previous act is one of the most reliable ways to make consequence real, and it converts action sequences from set pieces into entries in a ledger.

Let places change in ways the plot did not cause. Weather, decay, renovation, and crowding give the book a world that moves independently, which makes the protagonist's choices feel like interventions rather than like the only motion in the story.

Use the character's expertise as a continuing descriptive resource across the book: the same trade or discipline supplies fresh attention at each stage, and its vocabulary can grow with the character's confidence, which gives the reader an economical signal of development.

Concrete before abstract: give the reader the physical fact before the interpretation, and let the meaning be assembled rather than announced.

Lead with what is concretely there and let interpretation follow, when interpretation is needed at all. Concrete observation also keeps the metaphorical register honest: a comparison grounded in something the character can actually see is doing work, while a comparison floating above the scene is decoration.

Restraint before excess: fewer adjectives, fewer descriptions per object, fewer rhetorical flourishes. One precise image and one strong sentence per page outlast a chapter of sustained brilliance, and a chapter that tries to be excellent everywhere has nowhere to go when something important happens.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.
OPEN THREADS: missing warnings (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a filing receipt, then a recovered duplicate; hidden records (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): boxes in a dry attic; old channel (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a survey line, then the upper city's water; death count (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a falsified register.
THREE-ACT ARC: The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor | Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use | The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation
ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.
You are deciding how a story will show change in people who cannot articulate it.
How does behavior function as characterization across an entire book, and how does it change without breaking recognition?
You are mapping out a novel you are about to write.
Give the structural reasoning only; the drafting will come later.
response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor. Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use. The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation. The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Plan characterization as a set of pressures rather than a set of traits. What a person does under time pressure, under scrutiny, under obligation, and under boredom is four different kinds of information, and the contrast between them is what makes a character feel like a person rather than a type.

Let behavior vary by company. The same character should behave measurably differently with a superior, a sibling, a stranger, and someone they want to impress, and those differences should be visible in what they do rather than reported as a fact about them.

Stage the moments where a character acts against their own pattern, and make them cost something. A single deviation, prepared by circumstances the reader understands, does more for a character's depth than a chapter of explained contradiction.

Keep small behaviors attached to specific people across the book: what they do with their hands, what they check, what they refuse to touch. These are cheap to maintain, and their recurrence is how a reader recognizes a character in a scene without being told who is present.

Specific before generic: an incidental particular from this character's attention outlives any amount of transferred atmosphere.

Render emotion through behavior, body, attention, and choice rather than through labels. Anger has an object, a posture, a decision it tempts; nervousness has a habitual gesture and a direction of attention. Choose the behavior that belongs to this character, then let the reader complete the emotion.

Aim for prose that stays nearly invisible while the scene is working, and spend visible effort only where it buys something. Because every sentence can be made impressive, the discipline is deciding which sentences are permitted to be, and writing the rest plainly enough that the impressive ones still register.

Write the cast from behavioral constants under changing pressure, and let the story's evidence of change be a modification of conduct rather than a statement about personal growth. The reader will know the people by what they do and know the arc by what they stop doing.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Shift -- standalone, workplace drama, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: rotating close third among four night-shift staff, past tense.
PREMISE: Four night-shift staff in a warehouse fulfillment centre cover the same twelve hours on the night a safety report is due, and each of them is deciding whether to sign it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The safety report requires four staff signatures and cannot be filed late without triggering an inspection; Night shifts run with two fewer staff than the daytime schedule in the same building; Any injury requiring a hospital visit must be reported within twelve hours.
CAST IN PLAY: Marguerite, shift supervisor, eighteen years: wants the shift closed clean and the report signed; flaw, she protects the shift from management and from itself; secret, she has been signing reports with an outdated injury count; knows, the conveyor's failure pattern | Nate, forklift operator: wants the promotion that requires a clean record; flaw, he trades truth for advancement; secret, he reported a colleague's near-miss as his own error to look diligent; knows, the loading bay's blind corner | Sofia, agency worker, six weeks: wants to be kept on after the season; flaw, she will not report anything that creates a form; secret, she has been working with a wrist injury for nine days; knows, the exact rate the line is set to.
OPEN THREADS: the report (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): four signatures required by dawn; Sofia's wrist (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a hidden injury, nine days old; photographs (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): three failed repairs, timestamped; the blind corner (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a near-miss Nate reattributed.
THREE-ACT ARC: The shift begins, the report is announced as due at dawn, and the conveyor's first fault is patched instead of fixed | Sofia's wrist, Nate's promotion, and the escort photographs converge; the line's speed and the injury count disagree | Before dawn the conveyor fails with a person under a load, and the report's four signatures become the night's central decision
ENDING: They file a report with an accurate count and an incident attached, the client loses the contract, the staff keep their jobs under a new contractor, and Devon's photographs become the basis of the repair.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the report will be signed or not before dawn; the line will fail in a way that involves a person; one of the four will change position on the report.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Speed, weight, and processing load each have a natural sentence length; match them, and break any rhythm that has repeated three or four times, because an unnoticed pattern becomes the reader's main impression of the voice.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists | The service's original instructions prove obsolete and contradictory; the second generation becomes the deciding bloc; the missing previous crew surfaces | The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes
ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.
OPEN THREADS: missing warnings (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a filing receipt, then a recovered duplicate; hidden records (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): boxes in a dry attic; old channel (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a survey line, then the upper city's water; death count (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a falsified register.
THREE-ACT ARC: The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor | Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use | The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation
ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Give objects histories rather than meanings. An object that has been repaired, borrowed, stolen, lost, and returned carries more story than one whose significance is explained, and the accumulated states become available for later scenes at no cost to the narrative's speed.

TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.
OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.
THREE-ACT ARC: Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged | Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds | Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public
ENDING: The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged. Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds. Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public. The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Plan characterization as a set of pressures rather than a set of traits. What a person does under time pressure, under scrutiny, under obligation, and under boredom is four different kinds of information, and the contrast between them is what makes a character feel like a person rather than a type.

Decide which behaviors are stable and which are available for change. A person who tidies under stress may keep tidying for the whole book while their treatment of other people changes; the stable habit becomes the reader's recognizable anchor for the shifting material.

Let behavior vary by company. The same character should behave measurably differently with a superior, a sibling, a stranger, and someone they want to impress, and those differences should be visible in what they do rather than reported as a fact about them.

Stage the moments where a character acts against their own pattern, and make them cost something. A single deviation, prepared by circumstances the reader understands, does more for a character's depth than a chapter of explained contradiction.

Behavior before explanation: what a person does, avoids, and attends to carries their state more exactly than any statement about it.

When intensity rises, physical grounding should rise with it. The character should still be in contact with the room, still feel the chair, the strap, the cold, the weight in a pocket. Grounding is not decoration; it is what makes extreme situations legible and keeps the scene from floating into abstraction.

Write the cast from behavioral constants under changing pressure, and let the story's evidence of change be a modification of conduct rather than a statement about personal growth. The reader will know the people by what they do and know the arc by what they stop doing.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.

ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Design each major character with a small set of behavioral constants, habits of attention, ways of handling objects, ways of entering a room, ways of responding to disagreement, and then let the plot apply pressure to them, so that the reader learns the person by pattern and then learns the arc by how the pattern changes.

Keep small behaviors attached to specific people across the book: what they do with their hands, what they check, what they refuse to touch. These are cheap to maintain, and their recurrence is how a reader recognizes a character in a scene without being told who is present.

Specific before generic: an incidental particular from this character's attention outlives any amount of transferred atmosphere.

Write the cast from behavioral constants under changing pressure, and let the story's evidence of change be a modification of conduct rather than a statement about personal growth. The reader will know the people by what they do and know the arc by what they stop doing.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A ward holds only while its maker is alive and named in its grain; Thornwood cannot be cut by anyone who has not been formally released from apprenticeship; A failed ward does not fall; it turns, and it takes its maker's mark with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Tess, apprentice, the narrator: wants to be released and named; flaw, she revises the past as she tells it; secret, she has been making wards that turn; knows, the master's hands no longer work | Master Orr, wardwright, last of the guild: wants the workshop left to someone; flaw, he teaches by withholding and calls it testing; secret, he has been using Tess's hands for a year while signing the work himself; knows, the turning wards will come home | Pell, forest warden, outside the guild: wants the wards maintained by any means; flaw, he trusts systems more than people; secret, he has been reporting the turning wards to the forest villages; knows, which wards failed first.
OPEN THREADS: turning ward (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a mark that points the wrong way, then comes home; the master's hands (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): an unsigned piece, then a burned record; the buyer's visits (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): prices offered, then terms; Pell's reports (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): village complaints, then an emptied village.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tess is left alone with three wards to make before the season, and given no release; she makes them and one turns | She hides the turn, the forest begins coming in, and the master's deception and her own are set on the same track | Every option requires her to be named by someone: the master will not, the buyer will for a price, and the wards must be made regardless
ENDING: Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see a ward turn; Tess will either be named or not be named; the workshop will close or continue, not both.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Paper Mill -- standalone, thriller, corporate whistleblower.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the mid-level analyst.
PREMISE: An analyst discovers that her employer's celebrated water-recycling plant has been discharging into a river for a decade, and the only person who will believe her is the regulator she once helped discredit.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Regulatory inspections are announced four days in advance by statute; The company's severance agreements require arbitration and prohibit disclosure of process data; Discharge samples must be taken by a certified officer to be admissible.
CAST IN PLAY: Nadia Bell, process analyst: wants the discharge stopped without losing her pension; flaw, she documents everything and decides nothing; secret, she signed the original compliance report as a junior; knows, the plant's bypass valve schedule | Regulator Osei, environmental officer: wants an admissible sample; flaw, he needs to be right in public; secret, he leaked an earlier case to a journalist who burned him; knows, the company's legal exposure | Director Pike, plant director: wants the plant's award renewed and his retirement secured; flaw, he believes the discharge is acceptable accounting; secret, he authorized the bypass during a drought year and never restored it; knows, which documents prove authorization.

THREE-ACT ARC: Nadia finds the valve schedule, takes a sample improperly, and is offered a promotion for her diligence | The arbitration clause blocks every internal route; the regulator needs an admissible sample; the chemist is ordered to dilute and begins keeping a second set of numbers | The inspection is announced for a date the bypass can be closed for, and the only way to prove the discharge is to be at the river when the plant is not expecting it
ENDING: Nadia provides the sample and the schedule and loses her pension; the plant pays a fine and keeps operating with the valve sealed, which is a smaller outcome than she wanted and a real one.
PROMISES TO THE READER: an admissible sample will be taken or the case will die; the protagonist's own signature will matter; the announced inspection will be a turning point rather than a rescue.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Kingdom of Bells -- book one of a trilogy, political fantasy, succession.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.
PREMISE: A succession council must choose between two claimants in seven days, and the spy who supplies the deciding intelligence is the regent's own daughter, reporting to both sides.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.
CAST IN PLAY: Nissa Var, the regent's daughter, double agent: wants her mother's regency ended and her district unharmed; flaw, she optimizes for the survival of the arrangement; secret, she is reporting her mother's plans to the rival claimant; knows, both candidates' real intentions | Regent Var, Nissa's mother, acting ruler: wants the council to elect the candidate she can control; flaw, she has never distinguished her family from the state; secret, she has ordered a district's bell silenced; knows, her daughter is compromised and will not say so | Calind, rival claimant: wants the throne without a civil war; flaw, he outsources every hard decision to lawyers; secret, he has no legitimate claim and knows it; knows, the bells' ritual can be honored in the letter only.
OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.
THREE-ACT ARC: The council opens, the seven-day clock begins, and Nissa's first report proves false in a way that serves both sides | Each candidate is maneuvered into trading districts for votes while the silenced bell becomes the decisive fact | The bells must ring in one hour, and the only way to include the silenced district is for Nissa to carry the seal of a district that will not have her
ENDING: The bells ring, the elected ruler is neither candidate, the regency ends and Nissa leaves the city with a bell she has no right to carry.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the bells will ring or fail within one hour of the seventh day; Nissa's double reporting will be discovered by both parties; the council will not elect the candidate the regent wants.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Wren Halloway, night physician: wants her license intact and the death explained; flaw, she signs what she has not verified; secret, she signed three charts last month without seeing the patients; knows, the room's lock log was edited | Nurse Adeyemi, night charge nurse: wants the unit staffed and the investigation away from her floor; flaw, she protects the unit before the truth; secret, she removed a medication dose from the cabinet for a patient with no chart; knows, who was on the floor that night | Dr. Pell, senior consultant: wants the death recorded as cardiac and the unit reopened; flaw, he trusts systems and not people; secret, he countersigned the second patient's chart from a golf course; knows, the pharmacy discrepancy.
OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.

How does behavior function as characterization across an entire book, and how does it change without breaking recognition?

response:
Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient. The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating. The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her. Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Behavior is the most durable characterization instrument because it can be repeated, varied, and broken. Design each major character with a small set of behavioral constants, habits of attention, ways of handling objects, ways of entering a room, ways of responding to disagreement, and then let the plot apply pressure to them, so that the reader learns the person by pattern and then learns the arc by how the pattern changes.

Decide which behaviors are stable and which are available for change. A person who tidies under stress may keep tidying for the whole book while their treatment of other people changes; the stable habit becomes the reader's recognizable anchor for the shifting material.

Stage the moments where a character acts against their own pattern, and make them cost something. A single deviation, prepared by circumstances the reader understands, does more for a character's depth than a chapter of explained contradiction.

Keep small behaviors attached to specific people across the book: what they do with their hands, what they check, what they refuse to touch. These are cheap to maintain, and their recurrence is how a reader recognizes a character in a scene without being told who is present.

Concrete before abstract: give the reader the physical fact before the interpretation, and let the meaning be assembled rather than announced.

Watch for stretches where the writing has drifted entirely into abstraction, where decisions, meanings, and emotional states are discussed without any material anchor. Break such stretches with the concrete, and keep the abstract passage short enough to stay a movement within the scene rather than the scene's mode.

Vary sentence length and structure deliberately across the chapter, not randomly. Speed, weight, and processing load each have a natural sentence length; match them, and break any rhythm that has repeated three or four times, because an unnoticed pattern becomes the reader's main impression of the voice.

Write the cast from behavioral constants under changing pressure, and let the story's evidence of change be a modification of conduct rather than a statement about personal growth. The reader will know the people by what they do and know the arc by what they stop doing.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Cold Communion -- standalone, horror, isolated research station.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, present tense, two scientists.

ENDING: The researchers broadcast their measurements aloud, breaking the discipline and displacing the phenomenon out of the station, and the monastery is abandoned as a ruin full of unedited records.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what silence carries; the discipline will be broken or the station lost; the altered archive will be read aloud.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Long Evening -- standalone, quiet horror, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.
PREMISE: In a coastal retirement town, the recently dead take some time to notice, and the living have built a polite arrangement in which nobody mentions that the neighbours are thinning.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dead continue their routines until someone they know admits out loud that they died; Admission is irreversible, and the admitted person leaves immediately; The town's ferry does not run after the last admission of the season.
CAST IN PLAY: Marjorie Hale, retired postmistress: wants one more summer of ordinary conversation; flaw, she manages people instead of loving them; secret, she has known about her husband since April; knows, the arrangement's rules from practice | Alec Renner, retired ferryman: wants the boat's last season honored; flaw, he cannot refuse anyone an errand; secret, he has carried admissions the wrong way across the water; knows, who has been admitted and who has not | Dr. Olu, the last practicing physician: wants an honest end for her patients; flaw, she treats silence as a clinical tool; secret, she falsified a certificate in autumn to keep a family in the town; knows, the medical signs that precede admission.
OPEN THREADS: Marjorie's husband (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): his newspaper arrives, then his chair, then the admission; Olus's certificate (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a forged date, a family that stayed; the ferry season (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): schedule noted, then shortened, then final; Bea's telling (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a careless sentence that starts one neighbor's absence.

ENDING: Marjorie admits her husband in public, the ferry runs one time for those who want it, and the town continues the following year with fewer residents and the same courtesy.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will understand the rules before any character states them; someone will be admitted who should not have been; the ferry will run one last time.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Plan characterization as a set of pressures rather than a set of traits. instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.

ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Glasshouse City -- standalone, near-future science fiction, surveillance.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the compliance auditor.
PREMISE: A city scores every resident continuously, and an auditor whose job is to verify exemptions begins writing exemptions for strangers, one per week, until the pattern itself becomes the crime.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Residents below the compliance threshold lose housing, transport, and medical priority; Auditors can grant a single discretionary exemption per review cycle, and all grants are audited; The scoring model updates nightly and no auditor may see the update rules.
CAST IN PLAY: Rosa Bek, compliance auditor: wants her brother's score raised without a flag; flaw, she believes she is outside the system she administers; secret, she has written eleven discretionary exemptions she cannot justify; knows, the exemptions cluster by neighborhood | Timo Bek, her brother, delivery rider: wants to stop being scored at all; flaw, he takes offense at help; secret, he has already joined a group teaching score evasion; knows, his sister has been writing exemptions | Supervisor Ndiaye, audit supervisor: wants a clean discretionary record; flaw, she protects the model's reputation; secret, she has been granting exemptions to friends of the ministry; knows, the exemption anomaly and its author.
OPEN THREADS: eleven exemptions (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a weekly habit, then a pattern in a report; brother's score (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a threshold, a warning letter, a deadline; evasion group (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a meeting, then a distributed method; update history (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): nightly shifts, then a readable archive.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rosa grants a first unwarranted exemption, discovers how easy it is, and starts a weekly pattern she tells herself is mercy | The exemptions are noticed; her brother's evasion group makes her work a commodity; supervision closes in through the audit trail | Her final exemption must be spent on her brother or on the flaw in the model she has found, and either choice exposes the other
ENDING: She spends the exemption on a stranger and publishes the update history, losing her post and her brother's trust and leaving the model intact but publicly visible.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the score actually measures; Rosa's pattern will be discovered; the exemption budget will run out.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.
OPEN THREADS: the removed page (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report with a gap, then the missing sheet; the burned coat (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): ash in the stove, then a button; the girl's plan (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a bus timetable, a packed bag; Ruth's brother (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): an alibi, a dispute, a confession.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Behavior is the most durable characterization instrument because it can be repeated, varied, and broken. Design each major character with a small set of behavioral constants, habits of attention, ways of handling objects, ways of entering a room, ways of responding to disagreement, and then let the plot apply pressure to them, so that the reader learns the person by pattern and then learns the arc by how the pattern changes.

Character before description: choose whose attention the scene runs through and what they want from the room before deciding what the room contains. ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.
CAST IN PLAY: Kestrel Vane, captain of the wall: wants to hold until relief; flaw, she cannot admit relief is not coming; secret, she sent the relief request undelivered; knows, the gate's true weakness | Ferro Vane, her younger brother, quartermaster: wants the city fed through the siege; flaw, he keeps a private tally of who is worth feeding; secret, he has been trading grain to the besiegers' camp through a sanitation gate; knows, the besiegers' camp is starving too | Ambassador Senn, envoy who chose to stay: wants the terms signed before the fortieth dawn; flaw, she negotiates with herself more than with anyone else; secret, her own state wrote the original debt; knows, the besiegers' legal claim is valid.
OPEN THREADS: grain discrepancy (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a shortfall explained as spoilage, then as theft; foundation rhyme (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): children's rhyme, then the keeper's testimony; relief request (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a rider sent, a rider unaccounted for; the debt claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Senn's documents, then the council reading.
THREE-ACT ARC: Days one to ten: the siege settles in, the four threads establish their wants, and the grain ledger shows a discrepancy nobody investigates | Days eleven to thirty: rationing, a failed sortie, the legal claim surfaces, and the city learns the wall's foundation story from a child's rhyme that turns out to be accurate | Days thirty-one to forty: the gate, the terms, and the keeper's office converge, and each of the four must choose what the city is worth
ENDING: The wall opens from within on the fortieth dawn, the terms are signed in the besiegers' own language, and the city survives as a vassal rather than a ruin.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the foundation requires; the siege will end by agreement or by breach on the fortieth day; one of the four will open the gate or refuse to.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

OPEN THREADS: second chart (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a signature she cannot recall, then a name; lock log (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): an edit at 03:14; pharmacy count (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing dose, then a weekly reconciliation; trial protocol (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): consent forms, then an unapproved admission.
THREE-ACT ARC: The death is recorded as cardiac; Wren notices a second chart with her signature on it and no memory of the patient | The lock logs, the pharmacy reconciliation, and the trial protocol intersect; the unit closes; Adeyemi stops cooperating | The weekly reconciliation falls on the fourth night, and the only way to prove the second patient exists is to open the trial's records, which implicates the person helping her
ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes. The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford. instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.
OPEN THREADS: altered entries (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two paid-out relief claims with no deaths; constable's burial (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a fresh grave outside the churchyard; relief fund (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): payments made on reputation; the physician's forecast (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a calendar of expected deaths.
THREE-ACT ARC: The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing | The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows | The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history
ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the roll will be read aloud with something wrong in it; the sealing rule will be applied to someone the reader knows; the year will end with a count that matters.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

How does behavior function as characterization across an entire book, and how does it change without breaking recognition?
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.

The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows. The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Behavior is the most durable characterization instrument because it can be repeated, varied, and broken. Design each major character with a small set of behavioral constants, habits of attention, ways of handling objects, ways of entering a room, ways of responding to disagreement, and then let the plot apply pressure to them, so that the reader learns the person by pattern and then learns the arc by how the pattern changes.

Decide which behaviors are stable and which are available for change. A person who tidies under stress may keep tidying for the whole book while their treatment of other people changes; the stable habit becomes the reader's recognizable anchor for the shifting material.

Let behavior vary by company. The same character should behave measurably differently with a superior, a sibling, a stranger, and someone they want to impress, and those differences should be visible in what they do rather than reported as a fact about them.

Keep small behaviors attached to specific people across the book: what they do with their hands, what they check, what they refuse to touch. These are cheap to maintain, and their recurrence is how a reader recognizes a character in a scene without being told who is present.

Specific before generic: an incidental particular from this character's attention outlives any amount of transferred atmosphere.

Render emotion through behavior, body, attention, and choice rather than through labels. Anger has an object, a posture, a decision it tempts; nervousness has a habitual gesture and a direction of attention. Choose the behavior that belongs to this character, then let the reader complete the emotion.

Prefer simple, precise diction. Plain words used exactly outperform elaborate words used approximately, and the elaborate register invites the reader to notice the writing rather than the scene. When a fancier word is tempting, the useful test is whether it adds information the plain word lacks.

Write the cast from behavioral constants under changing pressure, and let the story's evidence of change be a modification of conduct rather than a statement about personal growth. The reader will know the people by what they do and know the arc by what they stop doing.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both leads, past tense.
PREMISE: Two competing owners of failing businesses on the same street are forced into a joint lease by a landlord who wants them both gone, and their partnership outlasts the rivalry before either admits it.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lease requires both tenants to co-sign renewals, and the landlord may not evict while both sign; The street's business association sets shared opening hours by majority vote; Either business may buy out the other's share at a valuation set by an outside assessor.
CAST IN PLAY: Priya, bakery owner, three generations: wants the family shop kept open through the season; flaw, she hears every suggestion as a takeover; secret, she has already taken a loan against the building she does not own; knows, the landlord's redevelopment plans | Dan, cafe owner, second year: wants a business that lasts past the following spring; flaw, he solves problems by spending; secret, his cafe is funded by severance from the company he left; knows, the association's voting arithmetic | Mr. Hallow, landlord: wants one tenant paying a single higher rent; flaw, he uses courteous language as leverage; secret, he has a development partner waiting on the outcome; knows, the lease's co-signature clause and its limits.
OPEN THREADS: co-lease (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a shared signature, then a joint renewal notice; loan against the building (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a bank letter, a repayment schedule; buyout clause (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): an assessor's appointment; development offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price, a deadline.
THREE-ACT ARC: The co-lease is presented as fait accompli, the two businesses share a wall and a delivery yard, and each tries to outlast the other | Shared hours, a stolen delivery, and a broken oven force real collaboration, and the buyout clause becomes a weapon both consider | The redevelopment offer arrives with a deadline, and the choice is between a joint purchase neither can afford alone and one of them taking the buyout money
ENDING: They buy the building together, fail to settle the rivalry, and the partnership holds as a working arrangement with an unspoken remainder.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the building will be decided by the end of the season; the two of them will work together before they stop competing; someone will take the buyout or refuse it in a scene.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Plan characterization as a set of pressures rather than a set of traits. What a person does under time pressure, under scrutiny, under obligation, and under boredom is four different kinds of information, and the contrast between them is what makes a character feel like a person rather than a type.

Stage the moments where a character acts against their own pattern, and make them cost something. A single deviation, prepared by circumstances the reader understands, does more for a character's depth than a chapter of explained contradiction.

Behavior before explanation: what a person does, avoids, and attends to carries their state more exactly than any statement about it.

Vary sentence length and structure deliberately across the chapter, not randomly. Speed, weight, and processing load each have a natural sentence length; match them, and break any rhythm that has repeated three or four times, because an unnoticed pattern becomes the reader's main impression of the voice.

Write the cast from behavioral constants under changing pressure, and let the story's evidence of change be a modification of conduct rather than a statement about personal growth. The reader will know the people by what they do and know the arc by what they stop doing.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the smuggler captain.
PREMISE: A smuggler captain is forced to run a blockade for the faction that executed her crew, carrying a cargo she has been paid not to open, while the admiral hunting her is the only person who knows why her crew died.

instruction:

TITLE: Five Doors -- standalone, heist thriller, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by section, past tense.
PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.

Plan characterization as a set of pressures rather than a set of traits. What a person does under time pressure, under scrutiny, under obligation, and under boredom is four different kinds of information, and the contrast between them is what makes a character feel like a person rather than a type.

Decide which behaviors are stable and which are available for change. A person who tidies under stress may keep tidying for the whole book while their treatment of other people changes; the stable habit becomes the reader's recognizable anchor for the shifting material.

Let behavior vary by company. The same character should behave measurably differently with a superior, a sibling, a stranger, and someone they want to impress, and those differences should be visible in what they do rather than reported as a fact about them.

Keep small behaviors attached to specific people across the book: what they do with their hands, what they check, what they refuse to touch. These are cheap to maintain, and their recurrence is how a reader recognizes a character in a scene without being told who is present.

Specific before generic: an incidental particular from this character's attention outlives any amount of transferred atmosphere.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
