Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.
OPEN THREADS: the cellar (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a search grid gap, then an excavation request; the object (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): carried then, kept now; sealed statement (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a transcript with an omission; second exit (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a plan, then a door under plaster.

Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit

Design the inventory before drafting: the major loops, their planting scenes, their renewal touches, and their collection points, so the promises are never improvised and the collections never defaulted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.
OPEN THREADS: altered entries (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two paid-out relief claims with no deaths; constable's burial (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a fresh grave outside the churchyard; relief fund (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): payments made on reputation; the physician's forecast (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a calendar of expected deaths.
THREE-ACT ARC: The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing | The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows | The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history
ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a sixteen-year-old stage manager.
PREMISE: A school's production of a play is cancelled two weeks before opening, and the student stage manager must decide whether to tell the cast why the cancellation is personal.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: School productions require a staff supervisor present at every rehearsal; The auditorium is booked by the district for examinations in the final week; Cast changes after the programme is printed require the principal's approval.
CAST IN PLAY: Nia, stage manager, sixteen: wants the production to open; flaw, she manages other people's feelings instead of stating her own; secret, she gave the supervisor's notes to the principal; knows, the supervisor's medical leave | Mr. Okafor, drama teacher and supervisor: wants the cast protected from the reason he is being investigated; flaw, he handles accusation by going quiet; secret, a complaint has been filed against him and he has not told the students; knows, the cancellation's real cause | Devi, lead actor, Nia's best friend: wants the play and the audition tape that will get her out of this town; flaw, she reads every delay as a personal insult; secret, she recorded a rehearsal to use as an audition tape; knows, the recording exists.
OPEN THREADS: the notes (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): copied pages, then a principal's drawer; the recording (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a phone, a rehearsal, a file; the complaint (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a filed document with no evidence; auditorium booking (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a calendar, an exam week.
THREE-ACT ARC: The production is running; the cancellation arrives; the cast is told it is a scheduling problem | The real cause leaks through Nia, Devi's recording circulates, and the rehearsals continue off-site in defiance of the rules | The auditorium is lost to examinations, the cast must choose between a public performance that risks the teacher and silence that saves him
ENDING: They perform a stripped version in the car park, the complaint is dismissed and the teacher does not return, and Nia tells Devi the truth about the notes.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the production will be performed or cancelled permanently; Nia will have to tell someone what she did; the complaint will be resolved on the page.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. The book's loop system is its deepest architecture: every plant is a promise, every payoff a keeping, and the reader's trust in the story's world is the balance between them. Design the inventory before drafting: the major loops, their planting scenes, their renewal touches, and their collection points, so the promises are never improvised and the collections never defaulted.

Classify the loops by register and weight: material loops, objects, skills, facts, and emotional loops, promises, wounds, grudges, loves, each at minor and major scale. The book needs a spread across all four cells, because material-only systems feel mechanical and emotional-only systems feel vague. Assign every major moment of the ending a loop of each register supporting it.

Distribute the collection points along the book's spine. A system that pays everything at the climax overloads the ending; a system that pays too early leaves the final act insolvent. Schedule the collections to escalate: minor loops through the middle, senior loops in the late middle, and the majors held for the climax, where the story's full credit is cashed at once.

Stress-test the inventory for dependency: which payoffs depend on other payoffs, and what happens to the ending if any single loop fails. The load-bearing loops, those whose collapse would flatten the ending, need redundancy: a second plant, an alternate path, a scene that establishes the same truth from another angle. Concentration of dependency is where endings break.

Every plant is a promise and every payoff is a keeping: the reader's trust is a balance sheet, and the book's authority rests on its solvency at the end.

Do not rewrite plot events, invent character arcs that compete with the planned ones, alter established relationships, or adjust world rules because the current scene would be easier. Any genuine problem with the plan is a planning problem, and it is solved before drafting rather than silently at the page.

Carry consequences forward across chapters rather than resetting to a neutral baseline. Fatigue, resentment, trust, debt, and reputation should all reflect what has happened, and the gradual accumulation of that reflection is what makes a long book feel cumulative rather than episodic.

Commit to the system: both lists reconciled, the escalation schedule fixed, the load-bearing loops made redundant. The book's promises are now structured debts, and the ending will gather what the beginning actually planted.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Seventh Crew -- standalone, science fiction, time dilation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the relief pilot.
PREMISE: A relief crew arrives at a research station after a one-year transit to find that thirty years have passed inside, and the station's surviving staff have built a society that does not want to be relieved.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The station's orbit causes time dilation that grows with each service ring; Relief crews may only depart on a launch window that opens every fourteen months, station-time; Station law is made by the staff who have lived there longest, weighted by years served.
CAST IN PLAY: Pilot Dene, relief crew commander, one year older than she was: wants the handover completed and her crew home; flaw, she enforces procedure to avoid thinking; secret, her crew was selected because they have no families to return to; knows, the launch window closes in nine days | Warden Strell, station governor, forty years served: wants the station's independence recognized; flaw, he has become the institution he was sent to staff; secret, he has not sent a status report in six years; knows, the station's stock of parts is nearly exhausted | Tech Amsel, born on station, second generation, sixteen: wants to see the surface of any world; flaw, she trusts the relief crew because they are new; secret, she has been listening to the service channel without authorization; knows, the previous relief crew never departed.
OPEN THREADS: previous crew (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a docked launch no one mentions, then a manifest; untended reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): six years of silence, then the reason; Amsel's listening (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): service traffic, then a real order; governor's illness (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): slowed decline, then the ledger.
THREE-ACT ARC: The relief crew docks, learns the time that has passed, and begins a handover the station quietly resists | The service's original instructions prove obsolete and contradictory; the second generation becomes the deciding bloc; the missing previous crew surfaces | The launch window arrives with insufficient seats and a station that will not accept relief; Dene must decide what the service's order actually authorizes
ENDING: Dene leaves three of her crew as the station's new staff, returns with the station's surplus population, and the service's authority over the station ends by the station's own vote.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the previous crew did; the launch window will be decisive; someone will be left behind or the station's population carried away.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

An ending is a solvent enterprise or it is nothing: it can only pay what the story deposited, and it must pay enough that the reader feels completion rather than abandonment. Design the economy deliberately: the deposit schedule, the collection budget, and the exchange rate between what is resolved and what the reader experiences as resolved.

Rank the reader's open questions by emotional carrying weight, not by plot importance. The questions weighted with feeling, will they reconcile, what happened to the one who left, must be collected or explicitly honored; the merely factual ones can be resolved in a clause or released. The ending's budget goes to the heavy entries first.

Decide the deliberate remainders: what the story will leave open, and how the leaving is framed so it reads as chosen rather than forgotten. The open residue should be either thematically eloquent, the one debt the story refuses to cheapen by paying, or structurally invisible, small enough that only the inventory notices. Write the remainders into the plan with the same care as the collections.

Schedule the final pages' density. The last sequence of the book should carry the highest concentration of collections in the story, escalating as it goes, so the reader experiences acceleration toward completeness. The rhythm of the ending is set by the spacing of those collections, and the last page should land on either the final payoff or the deliberate remainder, never on unmanaged residue.

Every plant is a promise and every payoff is a keeping: the reader's trust is a balance sheet, and the book's authority rests on its solvency at the end.

Do not rewrite plot events, invent character arcs that compete with the planned ones, alter established relationships, or adjust world rules because the current scene would be easier. Any genuine problem with the plan is a planning problem, and it is solved before drafting rather than silently at the page.

Track character knowledge separately from what the book has established for the reader. A character may only act on information they possess, and any scene that requires a character to know something they were never told is a structural error, not a detail to fix later.

Commit to the solvent ending: the collections ranked by carrying weight, the signals placed, the residue deliberate. The book will close its accounts in the reader's memory, and the balance will read as design.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Glass Ledger -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, city-state political.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the archivist.
PREMISE: A city-state's debts are bound with glass seals that make every obligation physically real to the debtor, and the archivist who keeps the ledgers discovers the seals have been quietly re-ordered to enslave a generation of the poor.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A sealed debt draws heat and weight from the debtor's body until it is paid or transferred; Seals may only be altered by the hand that carries the registrar's mark; Destroying a seal kills the debtor's obligation and the debtor with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Ilsa Verrane, junior archivist: wants to keep her post and her mother's medical debt off the block; flaw, she edits what she cannot face; secret, she has been copying sealed pages for two years; knows, the seal sequence changed after the flood | Registrar Otte, keeper of the seals: wants to hold the city together through one more winter; flaw, he treats people as accounts; secret, he ordered the re-sequencing himself to pay for grain; knows, the grain ships never arrived | Cassian Rhee, debt collector for the merchant floor: wants his brother's seal released; flaw, violence is his first fluent language; secret, he owes the register more than his brother does; knows, Ilsa copies pages.
OPEN THREADS: the altered sequence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): anomaly noticed, then dismissed, then provable; mother's medical debt (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): refinanced twice, then transferred; carter fire plot (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): accelerant cached, dates moved twice; Otte's grain payments (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): receipts referenced, never shown.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ilsa finds the anomaly in the sequence, tests it, and is caught copying by Cassian, who uses her instead of reporting her | The two of them trace the re-sequencing to Otte while the carters plan a fire; Ilsa's mother's seal comes up for transfer and the market price of mercy collapses | Ilsa must choose between publishing the true ledger, which would free the poor but strip the city's grain credit, and burning the register, which would kill thousands of sealed debtors including her mother
ENDING: She publishes the ledger, transfers her mother's seal to her own name, and stays in the archive she has just ruined, which is the only place the rebuilding can happen.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the ledger will be exposed or destroyed by the end; Ilsa's copying habit will cost her something specific; the poor's seals will be settled one way or the other.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Plan the payoff economy from the reader's ledger rather than the plot's: which questions, once answered, will make the reader feel the story was whole, and which open details they will not miss. The two lists are never the same length, and the craft is in spending the ending's limited pages on the entries the reader is actually carrying.

Design the exchange rates: what a small collection buys when placed at the right moment. A minor detail resolved in the final pages, in passing, can signal that the story's whole fabric was woven deliberately, and the reader extrapolates the diligence to everything. Spend two or three of these signal collections deliberately; they are the cheapest completeness the book can buy.

Decide the deliberate remainders: what the story will leave open, and how the leaving is framed so it reads as chosen rather than forgotten. The open residue should be either thematically eloquent, the one debt the story refuses to cheapen by paying, or structurally invisible, small enough that only the inventory notices. Write the remainders into the plan with the same care as the collections.

The last sequence of the book should carry the highest concentration of collections in the story, escalating as it goes, so the reader experiences acceleration toward completeness. The rhythm of the ending is set by the spacing of those collections, and the last page should land on either the final payoff or the deliberate remainder, never on unmanaged residue.

Fairness is the payoff system's law: the trail must exist in the text the reader already read, and surprise is only legitimate when its inevitability is visible in hindsight.

The outline is a constraint, not a suggestion. Every planned beat in this chapter must survive into the draft in a recognizable form; where a beat resists dramatization, the correct response is to find the staging that makes it work rather than to substitute a different event that happens to write more easily.

Keep unresolved threads and their intended resolutions visible in the working notes. A thread tracked only in memory is likely to be dropped, and a thread that disappears without recognition teaches the reader that the book's promises are unreliable.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.

ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Each renewal should add a shade of meaning, a new context for the same detail, so the loop compounds rather than repeats, and the final collection feels like the last term of a series the reader has been watching converge.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Cold Communion -- standalone, horror, isolated research station.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, present tense, two scientists.
PREMISE: At a monastery station studying a silence that behaves like a substance, two researchers discover the discipline that keeps them safe is the same discipline that has been feeding the phenomenon.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The phenomenon occupies measured silence and can be displaced by noise, but it returns to any space left quiet; The station's rule forbids speech outside the chanting hours; Every recorded measurement taken during the silence has been altered before it reaches the archive.
CAST IN PLAY: Dr. Ilse Ko, acoustics researcher: wants a publishable measurement and an exit; flaw, she measures instead of protecting; secret, she falsified a baseline to get funded; knows, the archive has been edited | Brother Anton, station's chanting master: wants the discipline kept; flaw, he would rather lose a person than a rule; secret, he has been altering the archive at the order's instruction; knows, the silence grows where people stop speaking | Dr. Piedra, geologist, second researcher: wants the station closed and everyone out; flaw, she advocates with contempt; secret, she has stopped sleeping in her own room and will not say why; knows, the measured silence does not obey containment.
OPEN THREADS: edited archive (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a warm number in a cold month, then the order's instruction; falsified baseline (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a funding timeline, then a confession read into the record; Piedra's room (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a room she avoids, a recorded hum; the missing year (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): Ren's memory, then the chant book's blank pages.
THREE-ACT ARC: The researchers arrive, learn the discipline, and record the first anomaly during a chant | Measurements diverge from the archive, the silence begins to occupy rooms that people leave, and the two researchers split on whether to publish or flee | Publishing requires speech, and the station's rule makes speech a weapon; the order must choose between the archive and the building
ENDING: The researchers broadcast their measurements aloud, breaking the discipline and displacing the phenomenon out of the station, and the monastery is abandoned as a ruin full of unedited records.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what silence carries; the discipline will be broken or the station lost; the altered archive will be read aloud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Cold Communion -- standalone, horror, isolated research station.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, present tense, two scientists.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.
CAST IN PLAY: Isaac Rell, tracker, the narrator: wants the debt cleared without killing anyone; flaw, he believes restraint is a form of payment; secret, he took the wrong man and knows it; knows, the warrant was bought by a rancher | Widow Sarn, boarding house keeper, creditor: wants the town to survive the winter; flaw, she has learned to spend other people's losses; secret, she paid the tracker's debt to hold the water claim; knows, the ditch head's owner | Rancher Coel, ditch head owner: wants the valley's water consolidated; flaw, he purchases with patience instead of force; secret, he filed the original warrant to remove a claimant; knows, the truth about the wrong man.

THREE-ACT ARC: Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper | The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears | The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly
ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the debt will be settled or refused; the truth about the wrong man will be entered somewhere; the council will meet and decide something.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly. He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Plan the loops from both ends at once. From the start: what the story will establish in its early pages, under cover of ordinary business. From the end: what the climax and resolution need already to exist. The inventory is the reconciliation of those two lists, and every loop that appears on only one side is a design flaw waiting for a reader to find.

Classify the loops by register and weight: material loops, objects, skills, facts, and emotional loops, promises, wounds, grudges, loves, each at minor and major scale. The book needs a spread across all four cells, because material-only systems feel mechanical and emotional-only systems feel vague. Assign every major moment of the ending a loop of each register supporting it.

Distribute the collection points along the book's spine. A system that pays everything at the climax overloads the ending; a system that pays too early leaves the final act insolvent. Schedule the collections to escalate: minor loops through the middle, senior loops in the late middle, and the majors held for the climax, where the story's full credit is cashed at once.

Design the renewal schedule for every long loop: the touches in passing, spaced across the middle, that keep the promise warm without spending it. Each renewal should add a shade of meaning, a new context for the same detail, so the loop compounds rather than repeats, and the final collection feels like the last term of a series the reader has been watching converge.

Plant under cover of ordinary business, renew in passing, collect at consequence: the three-stage life of a long loop, and the discipline of each stage is what the other two depend on.

Keep the operating rules of the world, the abilities each character has, and the terminology applied to them stable, and locate every departure from the established pattern in something that happened on the page. Consistency before improvisation; where improvisation is necessary, convert it into a consequence the story pays for.

Trust the reader to assemble meaning. Once something has been shown through behavior, event, or consequence, the text owes no immediate explanation of it, and explanation at that moment converts an experience into a lesson while signaling that the reader could not otherwise have kept up.

Set the inventory: loops classified by register and weight, collections scheduled along the spine, renewals designed, dependencies stressed. Draft from the inventory, and every plant will carry a destination from the day it is written.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

TITLE: Hollow Crown -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, siege.
POV AND DISTANCE: four close thirds, rotating by chapter, past tense.
PREMISE: A city under a forty-day siege discovers its walls were built on a debt owed to the people who now besiege it, and the four people holding the city each believe a different version of why they are fighting.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The wall's foundation requires a keeper present at every dawn, and only four families can supply one; Siege engines cannot breach the wall, but the wall's outer gate can be opened from within; The besiegers' terms expire at dawn on the fortieth day.

TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.

Classify the loops by register and weight: material loops, objects, skills, facts, and emotional loops, promises, wounds, grudges, loves, each at minor and major scale. ENDING: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.

Write the remainders into the plan with the same care as the collections.

The last sequence of the book should carry the highest concentration of collections in the story, escalating as it goes, so the reader experiences acceleration toward completeness. The rhythm of the ending is set by the spacing of those collections, and the last page should land on either the final payoff or the deliberate remainder, never on unmanaged residue.

Fairness is the payoff system's law: the trail must exist in the text the reader already read, and surprise is only legitimate when its inevitability is visible in hindsight.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the cataloguer.

POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.

OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.

POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.

ENDING: He files a map marking the valley as unregistered and uninhabitable for works, the state abandons the project, and the settlements remain unrecorded and unserviced.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the map will be filed and someone will act on it; the surveyor's endorsement will be required for something he opposes; the valley will be recorded or left off the record.

PREMISE: Five thieves must open five doors in one night inside a bank that has been designed so that each door requires the person before it to have already passed, and one of them has been employed by the owner.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.
CAST IN PLAY: Rennick, planner, retired: wants one final job that pays his debts; flaw, he plans for machinery and not for people; secret, he has already been paid by the bank's owner to test the building; knows, the owner's security revisions | Sabine, locksmith: wants her brother's release from a debt prison; flaw, she trusts nobody's plan but her own; secret, she has copied the vault key pattern; knows, the second door's true difficulty | Ode, inside man, night clerk: wants out of the city with his daughter; flaw, he cannot lie under pressure; secret, he has already told the owner that a crew is coming; knows, the guard rotation posted tonight.
OPEN THREADS: identity registrations (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): ninety-second windows, then a record of a previous test; copied key (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a wax impression, then a duplicate; clerk's disclosure (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a phone call logged; guard's documentation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): photographs of the ledgers.
THREE-ACT ARC: The plan is assembled and rehearsed against the layout, and the first door is easier than the plan predicted | The ease of the first door is the trap: the owner is watching the test. Identity registrations, a copied key, and the clerk's nerve converge | The ledgers are only useful if they reach the front door and daylight, and the crew has to choose between the plan and the captives' safety
ENDING: Rennick breaks his own plan to move the ledgers out through the front with the staff, the door system records all five of them, and the crew walks into arrest with the ledgers in the hands of the guard captain.
PROMISES TO THE READER: five doors will be opened in order; the crew's own rule about staff will be tested; one member has already betrayed the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: A Marriage of Weather -- standalone, literary, marriage and a coastal town.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, both spouses, past tense.
PREMISE: A marriage ends across one storm season in a coastal town that is also losing its beach, and both spouses are right about what went wrong.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's sea wall work is funded by a levy charged to properties above the high-water line; The couple's house is below the line and cannot be repaired after a flood without a licensed surveyor; The harbour's fishing fleet is co-owned in shares that must be sold to existing holders.
CAST IN PLAY: Aidan, harbour master, the husband: wants the house repaired and the marriage continued without discussion; flaw, he maintains things instead of understanding them; secret, he has been quietly selling his fleet shares to cover the flood damage; knows, the sea wall's true schedule | Bryn, surveyor, the wife: wants the marriage assessed honestly before the season ends; flaw, she mistakes accuracy for kindness; secret, she has accepted a post in another county and not told him; knows, the house cannot be sold or insured in its current state | Ondine, Bryn's colleague and client: wants the sea wall built before spring; flaw, she values the town's survival over its people's arrangements; secret, her survey supports using the couple's property line as the wall's footing; knows, the levy's distribution.
OPEN THREADS: flood damage (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): water in the floor, then a condemned structure; share sales (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a ledger of shares, then an empty holding; job offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a letter, a date, a county; wall footing (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a survey line through the back garden.
THREE-ACT ARC: A flood damages the house; the two spouses disagree about repair, sale, and what the damage means | The wall survey, the share sales, and the job offer surface in the wrong order, and each spouse reads the other's decision as betrayal | The final storm decides the house, and the choice is between a marriage held together by property and two separate lives that are both viable
ENDING: The house is condemned and demolished for the wall footing, the fleet shares are gone, and the two of them separate with the paperwork clean and no reconciliation scene.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the sea wall will be built or abandoned; the house will be decided by the season; one of them will say the decisive thing out loud.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Tidewater -- standalone, science fiction, colony disaster.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense, administrator and engineer.
PREMISE: After a tidal surge destroys a colony's lower city, the administrator and the engineer who predicted the surge must divide one working pump between two neighborhoods.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The lower city floods on a six-day cycle and only one pump remains functional; The colony charter requires equal allocation of critical infrastructure; Salvage from the flood belongs to whoever recovers it, which makes recovery a form of property.
CAST IN PLAY: Administrator Yew, colonial administrator: wants the charter honored and the colony recognized by the home office; flaw, he confuses legal process with legitimacy; secret, he suppressed the engineer's surge warning to protect the harvest season; knows, the home office will not send aid | Engineer Sanai, hydraulics chief: wants the pump used where the water does the most damage; flaw, she despises the people she is trying to save; secret, her warning was filed twice and both copies are missing; knows, the upper city is built over an old channel | Kes, salvage boss of the flooded district: wants her neighborhood's recovery recognized as a claim; flaw, she converts grief into negotiating positions; secret, she has been recovering the drowned houses' records and hiding them; knows, which houses are still structurally sound.
OPEN THREADS: missing warnings (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a filing receipt, then a recovered duplicate; hidden records (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): boxes in a dry attic; old channel (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a survey line, then the upper city's water; death count (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a falsified register.
THREE-ACT ARC: The surge recedes, the pump is shared unevenly under emergency discretion, and the missing warnings surface as rumor | Salvage becomes the economy; the records Kes hides prove the surge was predicted; the engineer trades her knowledge for the pump's use | The next cycle will flood one district, the charter cannot be honored, and the administrator must choose which document matters more: the warning or the allocation
ENDING: The pump is moved to the lower city permanently, the charter is amended rather than honored, and Yew resigns to run the recovery he failed to prevent.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see the next tide arrive; the suppressed warning will be found; one district will be saved at the other's expense or the rule will be broken.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the fire was; the ritual obligation will be performed once more or ended; each generation's silence will be visible to the others.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The architecture is fixed at the level of the outline, and the question below concerns the whole of it. Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing. The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register. The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Plan the chapter as the reader's basic unit of experience: the span they read in one sitting, the arc they remember between sittings. Decide what each span must contain, an engaged question, a meaningful shift, a reason to continue, and hold every chapter to that minimum, because the book's reputation is assembled from these units.

Define the turn standard: by the chapter's end, something is different that the next chapter's business depends on, in knowledge, position, intention, or relationship. The turn can be large or small, but it must be specific enough to name, and the naming is the discipline: a chapter whose turn cannot be stated in a sentence has not turned.

Set the exit standard: the chapter's final beat leaves live pressure drawn from its own material, in a register chosen against the neighboring chapters. The standard is not suspense in general but specificity: a reader who cannot say what the chapter left open has been given a rest stop, and the sequence's momentum pays for it.

Make the contract self-enforcing by auditing each finished chapter against its three clauses: promise engaged by page one, turn delivered by the end, pressure live across the boundary. Chapters that fail one clause get repaired or absorbed; chapters that pass become the book's verified units, and the sequence can be composed from them with confidence.

A chapter is the reader's unit of experience: promise at the opening, turn by the end, pressure across the boundary. The book's pace is the sum of its kept contracts.

Keep the distribution of payoffs deliberate: deposits concentrated early, collections concentrated late, and renewals spaced through the middle. A book whose rewards are evenly scattered has no sense of an ending gathering, while a book that starts collecting early has nothing left to gather.

Hold the style steady across the whole book rather than establishing it in the opening chapters. Drift is cumulative and quiet, and by the middle of a long book a voice that has relaxed toward the model's statistical default is unrecoverable without a full pass.

Adopt the contract: promise by page one, named turn by the end, live pressure across the boundary, audited after every chapter. Draft each unit to the standard, and the book's architecture will be built from parts that hold.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

TITLE: The Long Evening -- standalone, quiet horror, ensemble.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with wide and narrowing distance, past tense.
PREMISE: In a coastal retirement town, the recently dead take some time to notice, and the living have built a polite arrangement in which nobody mentions that the neighbours are thinning.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dead continue their routines until someone they know admits out loud that they died; Admission is irreversible, and the admitted person leaves immediately; The town's ferry does not run after the last admission of the season.
CAST IN PLAY: Marjorie Hale, retired postmistress: wants one more summer of ordinary conversation; flaw, she manages people instead of loving them; secret, she has known about her husband since April; knows, the arrangement's rules from practice | Alec Renner, retired ferryman: wants the boat's last season honored; flaw, he cannot refuse anyone an errand; secret, he has carried admissions the wrong way across the water; knows, who has been admitted and who has not | Dr. Olu, the last practicing physician: wants an honest end for her patients; flaw, she treats silence as a clinical tool; secret, she falsified a certificate in autumn to keep a family in the town; knows, the medical signs that precede admission.

TITLE: Quiet Ministry -- standalone, dystopia, bureaucracy.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.
PREMISE: A records officer in a ministry that assigns citizens to work discovers that her own file has been edited to make her suitable for a job she has been doing for six years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Assignments are made by file, and no appeal may cite information not in the file; Records officers may correct errors only with two supporting documents; Every correction is itself recorded and visible to the ministry's auditors.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Ren, records officer: wants her file to say the truth without losing her post; flaw, she trusts procedure to protect her; secret, she has made eleven unsupported corrections for other people; knows, the file editing pattern | Supervisor Tal, section head: wants the section's error rate at zero for the inspection; flaw, he optimizes for metrics; secret, he authorized the editing of Ada's file to keep her in the section; knows, which files have been adjusted | Inspector Oyo, ministry auditor: wants the pattern of corrections; flaw, she treats people as instruments of proof; secret, she was assigned here because she once made the same corrections; knows, the eleven corrections.
OPEN THREADS: Ada's edited file (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a qualification that is not hers; eleven corrections (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): eleven unsupported edits in the ledger; Renn's assignment (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a review date, a distant posting; inspection (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a date, a zero-error requirement.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ada finds the edit in her own file and cannot report it without exposing her eleven private corrections | The inspector traces the pattern; Tal offers protection in exchange for silence; Renn's assignment comes up for review in the same cycle | The inspection has a deadline, and the only way Ada can save her brother's file is to submit a correction supported by a document that does not exist
ENDING: She submits nothing, her brother is reassigned out of the city, and she stays in the section with her file still wrong and her corrections stopped.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A ward holds only while its maker is alive and named in its grain; Thornwood cannot be cut by anyone who has not been formally released from apprenticeship; A failed ward does not fall; it turns, and it takes its maker's mark with it.

OPEN THREADS: turning ward (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a mark that points the wrong way, then comes home; the master's hands (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): an unsigned piece, then a burned record; the buyer's visits (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): prices offered, then terms; Pell's reports (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): village complaints, then an emptied village.

ENDING: Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see a ward turn; Tess will either be named or not be named; the workshop will close or continue, not both.

Check the chapter against explicit style rules before accepting it, and where two preferences conflict, give the explicit rule priority. The rules exist precisely to be the tiebreaker in the moments when one construction feels better than it is.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.

TITLE: Terms of the Truce -- standalone, romance, rivals to partners.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.
OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.

ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.

ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.

PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.
CAST IN PLAY: Mistress Ode, master printer: wants the house and its apprentices through the crisis; flaw, she takes on obligations to avoid choosing; secret, she has accepted all three commissions; knows, the paper allocation's real controller | Hal, senior pressman: wants the sheets set in the order that keeps people alive; flaw, he believes he can judge consequences from the shop floor; secret, he has been passing proofs to the organizers; knows, which document is a forgery | Young Cass, apprentice: wants to be trusted with a real task; flaw, she reads everything she sets; secret, she has told a friend what one commission says; knows, all three commissions exist.
OPEN THREADS: three commissions (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a levy notice, a denunciation, a committee's address; forgery (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a signature on a document nobody in the shop wrote; leaked proofs (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a friend, a copied page; warrant timetable (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): three days, one magistrate.
THREE-ACT ARC: Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority | One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock | The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first
ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.
PROMISES TO THE READER: all three documents will be printed or refused; the house's mark will be used against it; the apprentice's leak will reach the street.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Paper Mill -- standalone, thriller, corporate whistleblower.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the mid-level analyst.
PREMISE: An analyst discovers that her employer's celebrated water-recycling plant has been discharging into a river for a decade, and the only person who will believe her is the regulator she once helped discredit.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Regulatory inspections are announced four days in advance by statute; The company's severance agreements require arbitration and prohibit disclosure of process data; Discharge samples must be taken by a certified officer to be admissible.
CAST IN PLAY: Nadia Bell, process analyst: wants the discharge stopped without losing her pension; flaw, she documents everything and decides nothing; secret, she signed the original compliance report as a junior; knows, the plant's bypass valve schedule | Regulator Osei, environmental officer: wants an admissible sample; flaw, he needs to be right in public; secret, he leaked an earlier case to a journalist who burned him; knows, the company's legal exposure | Director Pike, plant director: wants the plant's award renewed and his retirement secured; flaw, he believes the discharge is acceptable accounting; secret, he authorized the bypass during a drought year and never restored it; knows, which documents prove authorization.
OPEN THREADS: bypass valve (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a maintenance schedule, then a physical seal; signed report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 9): her signature, then the amended version; diluted samples (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): two sets of numbers; leaked case (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a journalist's name, a burned source.
THREE-ACT ARC: Nadia finds the valve schedule, takes a sample improperly, and is offered a promotion for her diligence | The arbitration clause blocks every internal route; the regulator needs an admissible sample; the chemist is ordered to dilute and begins keeping a second set of numbers | The inspection is announced for a date the bypass can be closed for, and the only way to prove the discharge is to be at the river when the plant is not expecting it
ENDING: Nadia provides the sample and the schedule and loses her pension; the plant pays a fine and keeps operating with the valve sealed, which is a smaller outcome than she wanted and a real one.
PROMISES TO THE READER: an admissible sample will be taken or the case will die; the protagonist's own signature will matter; the announced inspection will be a turning point rather than a rescue.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. Nadia finds the valve schedule, takes a sample improperly, and is offered a promotion for her diligence. The arbitration clause blocks every internal route; the regulator needs an admissible sample; the chemist is ordered to dilute and begins keeping a second set of numbers. The inspection is announced for a date the bypass can be closed for, and the only way to prove the discharge is to be at the river when the plant is not expecting it. Nadia provides the sample and the schedule and loses her pension; the plant pays a fine and keeps operating with the valve sealed, which is a smaller outcome than she wanted and a real one. Plan the book's middle as a series of sequences, each a group of chapters with its own pressure contour: a rise, a sustained stretch, a crest, and a controlled fall into the next sequence. The sequence, not the chapter, is the book's true rhythmic unit, and composing at that level is what separates a shaped middle from a long one.

Place the rests deliberately and defend them. A sequence without a low stretch flattens the reader's sensitivity before the crest arrives, and the crest lands on an exhausted nervous system. The rest chapters carry attachment, comprehension, and the quiet assembly of the next pressure, and they are where the reader's investment is actually made.

Design the crests to escalate across sequences. Each sequence's peak should reach further or cost more than the last, so the book's trajectory is a staircase rather than a sawtooth, and the reader's sense of mounting consequence accumulates. Decide the relative heights early, and let no early crest outshine the ones the structure owes later.

Manage the seams between sequences. A crest that falls directly into the next sequence's opening gives the book forward roll; a fall that lands in a distinct low chapter gives the reader recovery and a fresh start. Alternate the seam types across the book, because the same seam repeated becomes another metronome.

Length is emphasis: give pages to what must carry weight, and compress what must only connect. The reader feels your time allocations as judgments before they can articulate them.

Treat the voice as a property of the entire book, which means a passage is only good if it does not cost the surrounding pages. A brilliant paragraph that breaks the register is a net loss, and the same material delivered inside the register will usually carry further.

Treat the story state as a live ledger carried into the chapter: injuries and their recovery stage, possessions and who holds them, promises made and to whom, secrets and exactly who knows them, unresolved threads, and the last significant conversation each pair of characters had. Assemble the ledger before drafting and update it after.

Compose the sequence: unifying question, deliberate rests, escalating crests, and a chosen seam into the next movement. Set the contour on paper before drafting, and let each chapter's job come from the shape.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Each door registers the identity of the last person through it for ninety seconds; The vault's ledgers are physical and cannot leave the building except through the front; Staff may not be harmed, and the crew's agreement voids the contract if anyone is.
CAST IN PLAY: Rennick, planner, retired: wants one final job that pays his debts; flaw, he plans for machinery and not for people; secret, he has already been paid by the bank's owner to test the building; knows, the owner's security revisions | Sabine, locksmith: wants her brother's release from a debt prison; flaw, she trusts nobody's plan but her own; secret, she has copied the vault key pattern; knows, the second door's true difficulty | Ode, inside man, night clerk: wants out of the city with his daughter; flaw, he cannot lie under pressure; secret, he has already told the owner that a crew is coming; knows, the guard rotation posted tonight.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Vale Inquiry -- standalone, crime, missing person, mountain town.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the searcher, unreliable by omission.
PREMISE: A searcher hired to find a missing teenager in a mountain town discovers the town has agreed on a story, and that the story protects the searcher's own brother.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The town's search protocol requires the sheriff's sign-off for cadaver dogs and helicopters; The pass road closes with the first heavy snow, ending any search above the tree line; Searchers are paid by the day, which makes persistence and self-interest the same action.
CAST IN PLAY: Ruth Ansel, private searcher, the narrator: wants the fee and a clean result; flaw, she investigates by confirming what she already suspects; secret, her brother was the last person seen with the missing girl; knows, the town's story has three versions | Sheriff Dunmore, county sheriff: wants the search closed before the snow; flaw, he manages outcomes instead of facts; secret, he removed a page from the initial report; knows, the brother's alibi is false | Willa Ansel, Ruth's sister-in-law: wants her husband cleared; flaw, loyalty priced above truth; secret, she burned a coat; knows, where the coat came from.
OPEN THREADS: the removed page (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report with a gap, then the missing sheet; the burned coat (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): ash in the stove, then a button; the girl's plan (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a bus timetable, a packed bag; Ruth's brother (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): an alibi, a dispute, a confession.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ruth arrives, takes the town's story at face value, and runs a professional search over four days | Contradictions accumulate: a version of the night, a coat, a page, a plan to leave; her brother's involvement hardens from suspicion into certainty | Snow closes the search, the town offers a culprit, and Ruth must decide whether to deliver the brother her client will pay to convict someone else for
ENDING: She delivers her brother, the girl is found below the pass by her own route out of town, and Ruth keeps no fee and no family.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what happened on the night in question; the snow will end the search; the narrator's family connection will be exposed.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Boundaries are instruments: every cut buys something, urgency, dread, withheld knowledge, anticipated consequence, and a boundary that buys nothing is a leak in the book's momentum.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Plague Ledger -- standalone, historical, an epidemic year.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, a parish clerk.
PREMISE: A parish clerk keeping the mortality rolls during an epidemic year must decide which deaths to record accurately, knowing the rolls will determine which households are quarantined and which are spared.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Households listed as infected are sealed for forty days by the constable; The parish's relief fund pays only for deaths recorded in the roll; The clerk's roll is read aloud each Sunday and is the only public record the parish trusts.
CAST IN PLAY: Elias Ware, parish clerk: wants the roll kept and his own household unsealed; flaw, he believes accurate records are the same as mercy; secret, he has altered two entries to spare families; knows, which households have unreported dead | Constable Pike, enforcer of the sealing: wants the parish sealed properly and the sickness stopped; flaw, he equates enforcement with protection; secret, he buried a member of his own household without a roll entry; knows, the footpaths between the outlying farms | Goodwife Sarn, relief fund keeper: wants money spent where it keeps people alive; flaw, she decides by household reputation; secret, she has been paying relief to households with no recorded deaths; knows, which families are starving.
OPEN THREADS: altered entries (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two paid-out relief claims with no deaths; constable's burial (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a fresh grave outside the churchyard; relief fund (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): payments made on reputation; the physician's forecast (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a calendar of expected deaths.
THREE-ACT ARC: The epidemic arrives, the roll begins, and Elias's first accurate entry seals a household that does not survive the sealing | The rolls and the relief fund diverge; the constable's private burial is discovered by Elias; each accurate entry costs someone he knows | The epidemic peaks, the roll is to be read aloud with a false count, and Elias must decide which version of the parish becomes the official history
ENDING: He reads the true count, the parish's relief fund collapses and the constable is removed, and the roll survives as the record of a year that people would rather not have.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the roll will be read aloud with something wrong in it; the sealing rule will be applied to someone the reader knows; the year will end with a count that matters.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.

ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.

TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.

TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.

Novel outline:
