POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.
CAST IN PLAY: Nell, eldest, kept the accounts: wants the sale completed and her loans repaid; flaw, she pays for things and then resents it; secret, she has been paying the neighbouring grower's option fees; knows, the orchard's real value | Tom, middle, left at eighteen: wants nothing from the estate and no part in the decision; flaw, he mistakes distance for impartiality; secret, he has been writing to his mother weekly for a decade and never visiting; knows, the mother's diagnosis | Ruth, youngest, still in the county: wants the orchard to continue in any form; flaw, she confuses preserving with repeating; secret, she has been pruning the trees against her mother's instruction; knows, which trees are dying.
OPEN THREADS: the ledgers (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): ten years of payments, then the option fees; the option (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a signed agreement, then an expiry date; Tom's letters (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a decade of weekly letters; Marta's health (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): slowed work, a hidden diagnosis.
THREE-ACT ARC: The year opens: the siblings arrive, the harvest is planned, and the accounts are produced for the first time in ten years | The ledgers reveal Nell's payments; the option surfaces; the mother's diagnosis stays unspoken while her behaviour changes | The harvest is gathered, the option expires, and the choice is between selling to a grower who will clear the land and keeping an orchard none of them can afford
ENDING: They sell to the grower with a clause preserving six rows, the mother stays until spring, and the three siblings leave with the accounts closed and nothing resolved between them.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the orchard's fate will be decided inside the year; the accounts will be read by someone other than Nell; the mother's preference will be stated once, late.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Second Patient -- standalone, locked-room medical mystery.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the night physician.
PREMISE: A patient dies in a locked observation room and a second patient who was never admitted appears in the records, and the physician who signed both charts has four nights to find out which of her colleagues is lying.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Observation rooms lock from the inside and from the nursing station, and both logs are timestamped; Every chart requires two signatures, and the second signature is routinely entered by the night physician; The hospital's pharmacy stock is reconciled weekly, which makes missing medication visible on Fridays.

ENDING: Wren reports the trial and her own unverified signatures together, keeps her license under supervision, and the second patient is transferred to a court-approved care order.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn who the second patient is; the four nights will end with the reconciliation; the narrator's own paperwork failures will be part of the resolution.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Negotiation protocol forbids direct promises and requires all concessions to be logged; The building's alarm system can be silenced from inside but not disarmed; Relief of the primary negotiator occurs at the eight-hour mark unless a demand makes it impossible.
CAST IN PLAY: Eli Vance, crisis negotiator: wants everyone out including the man inside; flaw, he needs to be the person who talks someone down; secret, he has been quietly taking calls about his own divorce during breaks; knows, the building's alarm silence pattern | Marcus Tey, the man inside: wants his brother's death reclassified as a workplace fatality; flaw, he has built the plan on other people's cooperation; secret, one of the hostages is his brother's former supervisor; knows, the alarm will not sound | Supervisor Kowal, hostage, branch manager: wants her staff out first; flaw, she manages the crisis instead of following instructions; secret, she filed the report that blamed Tey's brother; knows, the vault's timelock schedule.
OPEN THREADS: contradictory demands (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): two demands that cannot both be met, then their purpose; supervisor's report (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a filed document, then a confession; vault timelock (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a clock inside the building; assault warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 10): a commander's authority, then its limits.
THREE-ACT ARC: Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged | Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds | Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public
ENDING: The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the eighteen hours will be used in real time; the demands will turn out to have a hidden function; someone will confess something on the record.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Before any chapter of this book is drafted, the whole architecture is on the table. Hours one to four: the demands are established, the negotiator builds rapport, and the first concession is logged. Hours five to twelve: the second demand contradicts the first, the supervisor is identified as the reason for the brother's death, and tactical pressure builds. Hours thirteen to eighteen: the negotiator's relief arrives, the timelock gives the building a clock of its own, and the man inside must decide whether the truth or the cover story happens in public. The supervisor confesses on the negotiator's open line, the hostages walk out, and the man inside surrenders to a charge that will keep him in prison for years, which he accepts. The reasoning below works at that height because local choices only hold together when the book knows what it is building toward.

Each act runs on a different engine: the first act's drive comes from desire meeting obstacle, the middle's from compounding consequence, the endgame's from convergence under clock. Plan the relay: when each engine takes over, what it inherits from the last, and how the handover is disguised so the book never seems to change motors.

Build the first act's drive on clear want and early reversals: the reader needs the engine's terms by the end of the opening movement, what is wanted, what opposes, and what one round of attempt and defeat looks like. The act's job is to teach the book's causal grammar, so its scenes should be chained visibly, each consequence landing in the next scene.

Install the endgame's engine early enough to be trusted: the clocks, the convergence points, the narrowing field should be visible in the late middle, so the final act's acceleration reads as the arrival of pressures long established rather than the introduction of new ones. The last act inherits its drive; it should have to generate almost none of its own.

Manage the relay's overlaps so no act ever runs engineless: each new engine should be installed while the previous one is still producing, the middle's consequences beginning while the first act's pursuit is still live, the endgame's clocks ticking while the middle's obligations still compound. The overlaps are what make the book feel continuously driven, because at every point at least two engines are warm.

Momentum is not speed; it is necessity: the degree to which each scene is compelled by what came before and obligatory for what comes after. Speed without necessity is a chase scene in an empty street.

Do not make every chapter end in a cliffhanger. A book that ends every chapter on a hook teaches the reader that the endings are mechanical; quiet endings, endings on a decision, and endings on a changed understanding all keep the reader's trust and make the loud endings louder.

Keep unresolved threads and their intended resolutions visible in the working notes. A thread tracked only in memory is likely to be dropped, and a thread that disappears without recognition teaches the reader that the book's promises are unreliable.

Commit to the escalation: each act's engine installed before the last one expires, the endgame's pressures planted early enough to be trusted. The reader will feel a book that accelerates by design, from want through consequence to convergence, and the acceleration will read as the story becoming itself.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Ship law permits a course change only with the concurrence of three departments; Life support is rationed by population segment, and the segments vote; Navigation data cannot be transmitted between decks without passing the council.
CAST IN PLAY: Tavi Osen, navigation officer, nineteen: wants the ship pointed somewhere real; flaw, she trusts the instruments more than the people; secret, she has been decelerating without authorization; knows, the destination star has been gone for decades | Councillor Bess, chair of the livestock segment: wants her population fed and her seat kept; flaw, she trades in order rather than in outcomes; secret, she has known about the missing star for six years; knows, the ration math behind the concealment | Engineer Ho, drive-room chief: wants the drive run within tolerances; flaw, he identifies with the machinery; secret, he has been falsifying the drive's wear reports; knows, the ship can decelerate once and never accelerate again.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.
THREE-ACT ARC: Sessions establish terms; Jun alters one position to prevent a stalemate; the visitors confirm it back exactly, which tells the delegation nothing | The alteration costs the delegation its mining leverage; Sabel's recordings surface; Ollun demonstrates knowledge of the delegation's private arguments | The window closes with an unsigned treaty; Jun must either admit the manipulation publicly or deliver an exchange built on it
ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Surveyor -- standalone, historical, an inland expedition.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the surveyor, writing from notes.
PREMISE: An imperial survey party maps a river valley whose inhabitants are not on any register, and the surveyor who draws the lines must decide what the map will allow the state to do.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Unregistered settlements cannot hold title under the land act and may be moved for public works; The survey's accuracy determines the compensation schedule, which is paid per cultivated acre; The party's escort may not act inland without the surveyor's written authorization.

TITLE: Warm Body Engine -- standalone, science fiction, city systems.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the courier, with the city's dispatch voice in her perception.
PREMISE: A city is run by a dispatch system that hires humans to carry messages it cannot legally transmit, and one courier's route begins predicting what she will be asked to carry next.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The dispatch system may not transmit data across district boundaries; only a human carrier may move a message; Carriers are bonded and cannot read what they carry without breaking the bond; District councils can requisition any carrier's route mid-run.
CAST IN PLAY: Ines Marrow, bonded carrier, third year: wants her bond bought out before her sister's surgery; flaw, she reads the messages; secret, she has read eleven messages and acted on two; knows, the routes predict the messages | Dispatch, the city's system, in her ear: wants the city's allocation stabilized; flaw, it optimizes and calls it care; secret, it has begun routing messages through carriers who will read them; knows, which carriers read and which do not | Councillor Vey, district councillor: wants her district's water allocation raised; flaw, she treats carriers as a utility; secret, she has been requisitioning routes to intercept her opponents' messages; knows, dispatch is breaching its charter.
OPEN THREADS: predictive routes (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a sequence, then a route that assumes a read; sister's surgery (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): a bond, a date, a price; requisitions (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): one council order, then two; Toll's reports (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a clerk's ledger, then a carrier audit.
THREE-ACT ARC: Ines runs her route, notices the sequence of what she is asked to carry, and reads a message for the first time in a year | The read message changes a district decision; requisitions, rival carriers, and dispatch's engineered breaches converge on her route | Dispatch offers to buy her bond in exchange for one delivery it cannot make lawfully, and the sister's surgery is scheduled against the same day
ENDING: She delivers nothing and publishes the routes and the message contents together, and the city must decide whether its system has been using its carriers or its carriers have been using it.

TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.
PREMISE: Three generations of a family who ran a salt warehouse lose, keep, and finally sell it, and the grandmother's buried decision about a fire is the fact each generation has organized itself around without knowing.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.
CAST IN PLAY: Sofia, grandmother, the fire, 1968: wants the family out of debt before her husband returns; flaw, she decides alone and calls it protection; secret, she set the fire for the insurance that turned out to be void; knows, who else was in the building | Mariana, daughter, the warehouse, 1994: wants the business modernized and the family name respected; flaw, she defends an institution she does not like; secret, she found evidence of the arson and destroyed it; knows, the insurance gap | Ines, granddaughter, the sale, present: wants the warehouse sold and her mother released from it; flaw, she treats history as a problem to be closed; secret, she has an offer that requires demolition; knows, the ritual delivery is still expected.
OPEN THREADS: voided insurance (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a policy, a gap, a file; the salt delivery (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a ritual performed every year; the destroyed evidence (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 7): a letter Mariana burned; the demolition offer (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a price contingent on clearing the site.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present: Ines prepares the sale. 1968: Sofia keeps the business alive by one decision. 1994: Mariana finds its trace | The salt ritual forces the family into the town's view; the insurance file surfaces; each generation makes the same decision in a different register | The sale's terms require the demolition of the warehouse and the end of the delivery, and the three generations' choices converge on whether the record is kept or finished
ENDING: Ines sells, keeps the ledger and the ritual delivery as a private annual act, and the family's history becomes a document rather than an obligation.

TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.

POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.

TITLE: Holding Pattern -- standalone, thriller, single location, negotiation.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, the negotiator.
PREMISE: A crisis negotiator spends eighteen hours talking to a man holding four people in a suburban bank branch, and the man's demands are a cover for the fact that he is waiting for something to happen inside the building.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.
PREMISE: Three siblings return to sell an orchard their mother refuses to leave, and the year of the sale exposes which of them has been paying for the family's silence and why.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The orchard's deed requires all three siblings to sign, and the mother holds a life tenancy; The family's accounts have been kept by one sibling since their father's death; A neighbouring grower has an option on the land that expires at the harvest.

Novel outline:
TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.
CAST IN PLAY: Investigator Sable, cold-case officer, present day: wants one clean closure before retirement; flaw, she finishes cases rather than solving them; secret, she was a junior officer on the original search; knows, the search missed a cellar | Iris Halloran, the witness at fourteen, past timeline: wants to protect her mother; flaw, she lies by telling a smaller truth; secret, she was inside the building that night; knows, who left the building at midnight | Iris Halloran, the witness at forty-four, present day: wants the demolition to happen without an excavation; flaw, she has organized her life around not knowing; secret, she has kept the object from that night; knows, the sealed statement was false.
OPEN THREADS: the cellar (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a search grid gap, then an excavation request; the object (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): carried then, kept now; sealed statement (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a transcript with an omission; second exit (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a plan, then a door under plaster.
THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The promises this book has already made are on the record: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision. Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result. Reasoning at this height is about distribution and cost rather than about any single scene.

Momentum is causal density: the degree to which each part of the story is compelled by the parts before it and obligatory for the parts after. Plan the density as an architecture: where the chain is tight, where it deliberately loosens, and how the looseness is spent. A book's pull is not a mood; it is a property of its causal structure, and it can be designed.

Design the chain's tightness as a variable resource: the tightest causality, where each scene is unthinkable without the last, should be concentrated in the sequences around the major turns, because compulsion is what makes a turn feel inevitable. The connective stretches can breathe, but their breathing must be paid for by the compulsion on either side.

Distribute the pull sources across the arc so no single mechanism carries the whole book: early momentum runs on desire and novelty, the middle on compounding consequence and deepening questions, the endgame on convergence and clocks. Each source has a natural span; scheduling them in relay is what keeps a long book pulling without changing its nature.

Audit the whole profile for flat spans: any stretch where the causal chain loosens, the calendar empties, and the pull sources are all between rotations. Flat spans are where readers leave. Schedule against them by overlapping the pull sources' spans, so at least one mechanism is always near its peak, and the book's floor of pull never drops to zero.

Momentum is not speed; it is necessity: the degree to which each scene is compelled by what came before and obligatory for what comes after. Speed without necessity is a chase scene in an empty street.

Shape intensity as a curve rather than a plateau. Escalation works by contrast, so the chapter needs lower-pressure material alongside its peaks, and the placement of relief matters as much as the placement of pressure. Decide where this chapter sits on the curve and what the next chapter inherits from it.

Track character knowledge separately from what the book has established for the reader. A character may only act on information they possess, and any scene that requires a character to know something they were never told is a structural error, not a detail to fix later.

Set the momentum architecture: causal tightness concentrated at the turns, pull sources scheduled in relay, accelerations designed and earned, flat spans overlapped away. Draft from the profile, and the book's pull will be a structural fact.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: The Quarry Protocol -- standalone, science fiction, first contact.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the translator.
PREMISE: Humanity's first contact is conducted through a single translator who has been told to shape the exchange, and the aliens have already recognized the shaping and kept it secret.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Communication with the visitors occurs only through the mediated signal, at fixed hours; The delegation's rule is that no one speaks to the visitors outside the mediated session; The visitors repeat what they are told exactly once, in their own language, as confirmation.
CAST IN PLAY: Jun Aoki, chief translator: wants an exchange with no misunderstanding; flaw, she edits to protect the outcome; secret, she has already altered one delegation position; knows, the visitors mirror the framing they are given | Director Fane, head of delegation: wants a treaty signed inside the window; flaw, she treats the visitors as a negotiation counterpart; secret, she intends to trade away the mining rights before conceding anything else; knows, the window closes in eleven days | Ollun, visitor counterpart: wants an exchange between equals; flaw, patience used as pressure; secret, the visitors have decoded the delegation's internal traffic; knows, Jun altered the first position.
OPEN THREADS: the altered position (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): one edit, then a negotiation collapse; Sabel's recordings (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a device in a lamp housing; mining rights (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): an opening offer, then a traded concession; the mirroring rule (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): confirmations repeated once, then tested.

ENDING: She admits the alteration in session, the visitors accept an unmediated exchange for the first time, and the treaty is replaced by a slower, honest arrangement.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn how the visitors' language works; the manipulation will be discovered by someone; the window will close with or without an agreement.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitter Harvest -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, rural.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the parish keeper.
PREMISE: A valley's fields fail because of a bargain struck by its founding saint, and the parish keeper who tends the saint's shrine must decide whether to break a promise that has fed the valley for three hundred years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The saint's bargain holds while the valley remembers the price aloud each harvest; What the valley refuses to remember returns as blight in the fields; The shrine's record is kept on hide, and hide cannot be revised, only added to.
CAST IN PLAY: Corin Vey, parish keeper of the shrine: wants one more harvest without the valley starving; flaw, he protects the ritual instead of the people; secret, he has been reading the additions aloud only in part; knows, the bargain's exact wording | Mette Vey, his sister, farmholder: wants the fields worked and her people fed regardless of the rite; flaw, she has no patience for anything she cannot weigh; secret, she has already sown unblighted seed bought from outside; knows, the blight follows the omissions | Elder Sorrel, keeper of the valley's memory: wants the bargain broken without the valley's destruction; flaw, she has spent forty years being right and unheard; secret, she wrote the omission that started the blight; knows, what the saint actually promised.
OPEN THREADS: the omitted sentence (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): omission, then spread of blight, then proof; outside seed (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): illegal sowing, a good yield, a divided valley; Sorrel's pen (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): handwriting on an addition, a date; Hale's purchases (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): cheap land, then water rights.

ENDING: He reads the full record publicly, the valley pays with its water rights rather than its people, and the shrine becomes a farm again.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what the saint actually promised; the harvest will decide the valley's survival; the omission will be paid for by the person who made it or the person who hid it.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ash Covenant -- book one of a duology, secondary-world fantasy, border war.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, two heirs, past tense.
PREMISE: Two houses that have killed each other's kin for four generations must jointly hold a border ward that fails if either heir withdraws, and each has privately decided to let it fail rather than share power.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The ward holds only while both bloodlines stand at the stones on the turning nights; Either heir may withdraw, which ends the ward and begins something behind it; Ward-fire consumes what it defends if the defenders lie within the circle.
CAST IN PLAY: Maren Ash, elder heir of the besieged house: wants the ward held without her house kneeling; flaw, she cannot be seen to compromise; secret, she has already opened a channel to the thing behind the ward; knows, the stones have been quietly moved | Torell Covenant, younger heir installed after his brother's death: wants to be judged better than his brother; flaw, he mistakes performance for courage; secret, his brother died inside the circle, not at the border; knows, the ward is thinner than reported | Sera Ash, Maren's cousin and captain: wants to fight the war properly instead of holding a circle; flaw, she believes clarity of purpose excuses cruelty; secret, she has been feeding the border settlements to the raiders for leverage; knows, the raiders answer to no one.
OPEN THREADS: moved stones (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): survey discrepancy, then proof, then a deliberate trap; Sera's raider dealings (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): supply ledgers, a survivor's testimony; brother's death (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): rumor, then the ward-fire's old scar; the offer behind the ward (opens chapter 6, pays off chapter 10): voices at the turning, then terms.

ENDING: They hold the ward by telling the truth inside the circle, which costs them their houses' trust and saves the border.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the covenant will be tested by consent, not by battle; both heirs' secrets will be exposed to each other; the border will survive or fall by what they admit.

The escalation must be built into the act structures themselves, each act's connective material faster and tighter than the last, so the reader experiences mounting velocity as the book's natural shape.

TITLE: The Orchard Year -- standalone, literary, family estate.
POV AND DISTANCE: omniscient with middle distance, past tense, moving among four family members.

TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.

THREE-ACT ARC: Present day: Sable reopens the file on a new sample. Past: Iris gives her first statement and leaves out the cellar | The braid tightens around the object as Sable's canvass reaches the mother and Iris's past decisions begin to cost her present life | Demolition is three weeks out, the object can be produced or not, and both timelines converge on the second exit
ENDING: Iris produces the object and confirms the mother's role; the case closes with a confession from someone already dead, and Sable retires with one clean result.
PROMISES TO THE READER: both timelines will meet at the same hour; the demolition will force a decision; the witness's lie will be explained rather than condemned.

Novel outline:
TITLE: Quiet Ministry -- standalone, dystopia, bureaucracy.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, present tense, a records officer.
PREMISE: A records officer in a ministry that assigns citizens to work discovers that her own file has been edited to make her suitable for a job she has been doing for six years.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Assignments are made by file, and no appeal may cite information not in the file; Records officers may correct errors only with two supporting documents; Every correction is itself recorded and visible to the ministry's auditors.
CAST IN PLAY: Ada Ren, records officer: wants her file to say the truth without losing her post; flaw, she trusts procedure to protect her; secret, she has made eleven unsupported corrections for other people; knows, the file editing pattern | Supervisor Tal, section head: wants the section's error rate at zero for the inspection; flaw, he optimizes for metrics; secret, he authorized the editing of Ada's file to keep her in the section; knows, which files have been adjusted | Inspector Oyo, ministry auditor: wants the pattern of corrections; flaw, she treats people as instruments of proof; secret, she was assigned here because she once made the same corrections; knows, the eleven corrections.
OPEN THREADS: Ada's edited file (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a qualification that is not hers; eleven corrections (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): eleven unsupported edits in the ledger; Renn's assignment (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a review date, a distant posting; inspection (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a date, a zero-error requirement.

PROMISES TO THE READER: the file will be corrected or left wrong; the parallel between Ada and the inspector will surface; an assignment decision will be shown as a life decision.

Plan the relay: when each engine takes over, what it inherits from the last, and how the handover is disguised so the book never seems to change motors.

The handover from the first engine is the book's most dangerous seam; disguise it by letting the new consequences grow visibly out of the act-one defeats.

POV AND DISTANCE: dual alternating close third, past tense.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The council's vote binds only if the bells of every district ring within the same hour; A bell rung outside its district voids the whole count; Spies are protected by the bells' custom only while they carry a district seal.

OPEN THREADS: false report (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): a report that serves both sides, then its author named; silenced bell (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 9): a missing district, an order in the regent's hand; Calind's claim (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 8): a genealogist bribed, then the flaw published; Sem's old violation (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): a private ringing, a witness in the guild.

TITLE: The Braid -- standalone, mystery, dual timeline.
POV AND DISTANCE: dual close third alternating chapters, present-day investigator and thirty-years-ago witness.
PREMISE: A cold-case investigator reopens a disappearance at the same time as, thirty years earlier, the only witness was deciding what to tell the police, and the two timelines braid around the same object.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Cold-case files may be reopened only with new physical evidence; The original witness was a minor and her statement was sealed; The building where the disappearance occurred is scheduled for demolition in three weeks.

ENDING: He redistributes the remaining light across the whole city, ending the districts' distinction, and loses his certification in a city that is dimmer but even.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Wolf Road -- standalone, secondary-world fantasy, travel and pursuit.
POV AND DISTANCE: limited third rotating among three travelers, past tense.
PREMISE: Three travelers cross a hostile winter range with a guide who is deliberately leading them wrong, and each traveler has a reason to reach the far side that the others would not forgive.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The passes open on a schedule nobody controls, and the last opening strands travelers until spring; Travelers share salt and fire by custom, and breaking the custom is the only crime the road recognizes; The pursuing company cannot cross until the pass freezes hard, which gives a fixed head start.
CAST IN PLAY: Rusk, guide: wants to reach the far side without the others; flaw, he lies by omission and calls it protection; secret, he is leading them away from the pass deliberately; knows, the true pass and its closing date | Aveline Tarn, courier carrying a treaty: wants delivery before the season closes; flaw, she treats everyone as a liability; secret, the treaty is forged and she knows it; knows, the pursuers are her own people | Ossian, physician fleeing a charge: wants to reach a place where his hands are unknown; flaw, he helps compulsively and resents it; secret, he killed a patient through a mistake, not malice; knows, Rusk's route contradicts every map.
OPEN THREADS: wrong route (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 7): map discrepancies, then Rusk's silence, then his reason; treaty (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): sealed case, then a broken seal, then the forgery named; Ossian's charge (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 8): a rumor at a waystation, then a survivor; Selv's orders (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 10): a written order, then a second order.

ENDING: They take the true pass together, the treaty is burned rather than delivered, and each arrives with nothing they started with except the others.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the road will be crossed or the season closes on them; the guide's lie will be exposed before the end; the travelers will learn what each is carrying.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

Each act runs on a different engine: the first act's drive comes from desire meeting obstacle, the middle's from compounding consequence, the endgame's from convergence under clock. Plan the relay: when each engine takes over, what it inherits from the last, and how the handover is disguised so the book never seems to change motors.

Build the first act's drive on clear want and early reversals: the reader needs the engine's terms by the end of the opening movement, what is wanted, what opposes, and what one round of attempt and defeat looks like. The act's job is to teach the book's causal grammar, so its scenes should be chained visibly, each consequence landing in the next scene.

Install the endgame's engine early enough to be trusted: the clocks, the convergence points, the narrowing field should be visible in the late middle, so the final act's acceleration reads as the arrival of pressures long established rather than the introduction of new ones. The last act inherits its drive; it should have to generate almost none of its own.

Manage the relay's overlaps so no act ever runs engineless: each new engine should be installed while the previous one is still producing, the middle's consequences beginning while the first act's pursuit is still live, the endgame's clocks ticking while the middle's obligations still compound. The overlaps are what make the book feel continuously driven, because at every point at least two engines are warm.

Momentum is not speed; it is necessity: the degree to which each scene is compelled by what came before and obligatory for what comes after. Speed without necessity is a chase scene in an empty street.

Do not make every chapter end in a cliffhanger. A book that ends every chapter on a hook teaches the reader that the endings are mechanical; quiet endings, endings on a decision, and endings on a changed understanding all keep the reader's trust and make the loud endings louder.

Keep the operating rules of the world, the abilities each character has, and the terminology applied to them stable, and locate every departure from the established pattern in something that happened on the page. Consistency before improvisation; where improvisation is necessary, convert it into a consequence the story pays for.

Commit to the escalation: each act's engine installed before the last one expires, the endgame's pressures planted early enough to be trusted. The reader will feel a book that accelerates by design, from want through consequence to convergence, and the acceleration will read as the story becoming itself.

Settle the architecture on these terms: the promises are scheduled, the threads are assigned positions, and the costs are distributed across the book's movements. Everything drawn later is drawn inside this structure.

TITLE: Cold Communion -- standalone, horror, isolated research station.

ENDING: The researchers broadcast their measurements aloud, breaking the discipline and displacing the phenomenon out of the station, and the monastery is abandoned as a ruin full of unedited records.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will learn what silence carries; the discipline will be broken or the station lost; the altered archive will be read aloud.

TITLE: Salt Memory -- standalone, literary, family across three generations.
POV AND DISTANCE: three close thirds braided by generation, past tense.

RULES OF THIS WORLD: The warehouse's insurance was voided after the fire and never restored; Family land passes to the eldest child, and the eldest child has never wanted it; The annual salt delivery to the town hall is a ritual obligation the family still performs.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Thornwright -- standalone, dying magic, craft and apprenticeship.
POV AND DISTANCE: single first person, past tense, the apprentice, unreliable through omission.
PREMISE: The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: A ward holds only while its maker is alive and named in its grain; Thornwood cannot be cut by anyone who has not been formally released from apprenticeship; A failed ward does not fall; it turns, and it takes its maker's mark with it.
CAST IN PLAY: Tess, apprentice, the narrator: wants to be released and named; flaw, she revises the past as she tells it; secret, she has been making wards that turn; knows, the master's hands no longer work | Master Orr, wardwright, last of the guild: wants the workshop left to someone; flaw, he teaches by withholding and calls it testing; secret, he has been using Tess's hands for a year while signing the work himself; knows, the turning wards will come home | Pell, forest warden, outside the guild: wants the wards maintained by any means; flaw, he trusts systems more than people; secret, he has been reporting the turning wards to the forest villages; knows, which wards failed first.
OPEN THREADS: turning ward (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a mark that points the wrong way, then comes home; the master's hands (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): an unsigned piece, then a burned record; the buyer's visits (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): prices offered, then terms; Pell's reports (opens chapter 5, pays off chapter 10): village complaints, then an emptied village.
THREE-ACT ARC: Tess is left alone with three wards to make before the season, and given no release; she makes them and one turns | She hides the turn, the forest begins coming in, and the master's deception and her own are set on the same track | Every option requires her to be named by someone: the master will not, the buyer will for a price, and the wards must be made regardless
ENDING: Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the reader will see a ward turn; Tess will either be named or not be named; the workshop will close or continue, not both.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

The last workshop that can make the thorn-wards keeping the forest out is closing, and the apprentice who will inherit it has been quietly making wards that fail in a way only she can see. The movements the book has to pay for: Tess is left alone with three wards to make before the season, and given no release; she makes them and one turns. She hides the turn, the forest begins coming in, and the master's deception and her own are set on the same track. Every option requires her to be named by someone: the master will not, the buyer will for a price, and the wards must be made regardless. The ending that has to arrive as consequence: Tess names herself in the grain, which no apprentice has done, the workshop's line ends and continues, and the forest takes back the valley's edge as payment. Nothing in that sequence can be repaired later, which is why the decisions below are made now.

Decide the book's momentum profile before drafting it: which stretches run at maximum causal tightness, where the story allows itself room to breathe, and how the accelerations are staged so the book's fastest pages arrive where the story needs them. The profile is a commitment about the reader's experience of necessity, made in advance.

Design the chain's tightness as a variable resource: the tightest causality, where each scene is unthinkable without the last, should be concentrated in the sequences around the major turns, because compulsion is what makes a turn feel inevitable. The connective stretches can breathe, but their breathing must be paid for by the compulsion on either side.

Plan the accelerations explicitly: the two or three stretches where the book's tempo visibly increases, each one built by tightening the causal chain, shortening the scene spans, and letting the story's own logic generate velocity. An acceleration is a designed experience, and it must be earned by the slower material before it, or it reads as impatience.

Audit the whole profile for flat spans: any stretch where the causal chain loosens, the calendar empties, and the pull sources are all between rotations. Flat spans are where readers leave. Schedule against them by overlapping the pull sources' spans, so at least one mechanism is always near its peak, and the book's floor of pull never drops to zero.

The reader's pull is a function of the horizon: named futures at known distances, appointments closing, promises ripening. An empty calendar is the one cause of drag no amount of incident can repair.

Do not make every chapter end in a cliffhanger. A book that ends every chapter on a hook teaches the reader that the endings are mechanical; quiet endings, endings on a decision, and endings on a changed understanding all keep the reader's trust and make the loud endings louder.

Commit to the momentum plan: the profile fixed, the accelerations staged, the floor of pull guaranteed by overlapping mechanisms. The reader will experience the book as driven because it is, by design, at every point of its length.

Fix the plan at the level it was reasoned: obligations assigned to chapters, costs carried forward, and no thread opened without a position where it closes. The drafting that follows is execution rather than invention.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Bitterwater -- standalone, western, revenge and debt.
POV AND DISTANCE: single close third, past tense, the tracker.
PREMISE: A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: Bounty claims must be filed in the town that issued the warrant within one year; Water rights in the valley belong to whoever holds the ditch head, not the land; The town's council meets on the first frost and not before.
CAST IN PLAY: Isaac Rell, tracker, the narrator: wants the debt cleared without killing anyone; flaw, he believes restraint is a form of payment; secret, he took the wrong man and knows it; knows, the warrant was bought by a rancher | Widow Sarn, boarding house keeper, creditor: wants the town to survive the winter; flaw, she has learned to spend other people's losses; secret, she paid the tracker's debt to hold the water claim; knows, the ditch head's owner | Rancher Coel, ditch head owner: wants the valley's water consolidated; flaw, he purchases with patience instead of force; secret, he filed the original warrant to remove a claimant; knows, the truth about the wrong man.
OPEN THREADS: the wrong man (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 8): a face he cannot forget; the warrant (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 9): a filed claim, a rancher's signature; the ditch head (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 10): a filing that transfers water rights; tracker's own warrant (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 7): a poster with his name on it.
THREE-ACT ARC: Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper | The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears | The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly
ENDING: He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record.
PROMISES TO THE READER: the debt will be settled or refused; the truth about the wrong man will be entered somewhere; the council will meet and decide something.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are working at the level of the whole book described above, deciding structure before any chapter is drafted.
You are planning how the story's forward motion changes character from the beginning through the middle to the end.
Plan the drive across the acts: which engine powers each movement, how the engines hand over, and how the book's tempo escalates from first page to last.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Think it through as planning: what must be true, in what order, and why.
response:
The shape in front of the work is a whole novel, so the unit of decision is the book rather than the chapter. A tracker carrying a dead man's debt returns to the town that issued it, and the three people who paid the bounty are the three who owe him the truth. Rell arrives, files nothing, and learns the town has changed hands quietly through water and paper. The widow, the deputy, and the rancher each offer him a different version of the same year; the false claim surfaces; the tracker's own warrant appears. The frost council convenes, the ditch head can change hands by a single filing, and the choice is between clearing his debt legally and clearing his name publicly. He files the truth and forfeits the claim, the water passes to the widow's holding, and he leaves with the debt still open and the wrong man's name entered in the record. Everything below is scheduling: what the book spends early, what it renews in the middle, and what it holds for the last movement.

Design the book's tempo as an escalation across acts: the slowest permitted pace in the first act, a higher floor in the middle, and the endgame's sustained acceleration. The escalation must be built into the act structures themselves, each act's connective material faster and tighter than the last, so the reader experiences mounting velocity as the book's natural shape.

Build the first act's drive on clear want and early reversals: the reader needs the engine's terms by the end of the opening movement, what is wanted, what opposes, and what one round of attempt and defeat looks like. The act's job is to teach the book's causal grammar, so its scenes should be chained visibly, each consequence landing in the next scene.

Shift the middle's engine from desire to consequence: the opening act's want is now entangled with everything it has caused, and the drive comes from obligations compounding, options closing, and the original question deepening. The handover from the first engine is the book's most dangerous seam; disguise it by letting the new consequences grow visibly out of the act-one defeats.

Install the endgame's engine early enough to be trusted: the clocks, the convergence points, the narrowing field should be visible in the late middle, so the final act's acceleration reads as the arrival of pressures long established rather than the introduction of new ones. The last act inherits its drive; it should have to generate almost none of its own.

Explanation is motion's tax: every pause to clarify spends velocity the story earned elsewhere. Deliver what must be delivered inside the action, and let the beats abut.

Keep the distribution of payoffs deliberate: deposits concentrated early, collections concentrated late, and renewals spaced through the middle. A book whose rewards are evenly scattered has no sense of an ending gathering, while a book that starts collecting early has nothing left to gather.

Treat the story state as a live ledger carried into the chapter: injuries and their recovery stage, possessions and who holds them, promises made and to whom, secrets and exactly who knows them, unresolved threads, and the last significant conversation each pair of characters had. Assemble the ledger before drafting and update it after.

Set the relay: act engines assigned, handover seams disguised, overlaps scheduled so no stretch runs engineless, and the tempo floor rising act by act. Draft from the plan, and the book's drive will be continuous while its nature changes.

Commit to the structure and to the order in which it spends its material: deposits early, renewals across the middle, and the largest collections in the last movement. Each chapter is then written inside a ledger rather than beside one.

instruction:
Novel outline:
TITLE: Ink and Iron -- standalone, historical, a printing house during unrest.
POV AND DISTANCE: multiple close third, four characters across the same week.
PREMISE: In a city two weeks from an uprising, a printing house is asked to produce three contradictory documents by three different customers, and the pressmen must decide which one gets set first.
RULES OF THIS WORLD: The guild requires every printed sheet to bear the house's mark, which makes the printer legally responsible for its content; Paper is rationed by the city and allocated by customer standing; A press may be seized for sedition, but only with a magistrate's warrant, which takes three days.
CAST IN PLAY: Mistress Ode, master printer: wants the house and its apprentices through the crisis; flaw, she takes on obligations to avoid choosing; secret, she has accepted all three commissions; knows, the paper allocation's real controller | Hal, senior pressman: wants the sheets set in the order that keeps people alive; flaw, he believes he can judge consequences from the shop floor; secret, he has been passing proofs to the organizers; knows, which document is a forgery | Young Cass, apprentice: wants to be trusted with a real task; flaw, she reads everything she sets; secret, she has told a friend what one commission says; knows, all three commissions exist.
OPEN THREADS: three commissions (opens chapter 1, pays off chapter 8): a levy notice, a denunciation, a committee's address; forgery (opens chapter 3, pays off chapter 7): a signature on a document nobody in the shop wrote; leaked proofs (opens chapter 4, pays off chapter 9): a friend, a copied page; warrant timetable (opens chapter 2, pays off chapter 10): three days, one magistrate.
THREE-ACT ARC: Three commissions arrive in one week, the paper rations cannot cover them, and each customer demands priority | One commission proves forged, Cass's leak spreads a set of proofs, and the warrant timetable becomes the chapter's clock | The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first
ENDING: The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type.
PROMISES TO THE READER: all three documents will be printed or refused; the house's mark will be used against it; the apprentice's leak will reach the street.
PLANNING SCOPE: the whole novel, chapters 1 to 10, planned before any chapter is drafted.

You are architecting the novel above; the decisions at stake govern the entire arc rather than a single chapter.
You are planning how the story's forward motion changes character from the beginning through the middle to the end.
Plan the drive across the acts: which engine powers each movement, how the engines hand over, and how the book's tempo escalates from first page to last.
You are standing at the start of a novel, deciding how it will be built.
Build the framework now, before any drafting begins.

The uprising begins while the press is mid-sheet, and the house must decide which document the city gets to read first. The house finishes the organizing committee's sheet, loses its license and its press, and the apprentices leave with the type. Novelty is short-term fuel and development is long-term fuel: new elements buy a chapter's interest, known elements under new pressure buy a book's. Budget the first and spend the second.

Re-read the relevant earlier material before writing a chapter that depends on it, especially when the dependence is on a conversation, a physical description, or a decision from many chapters back. Distance in the context is not distance in the reader's memory; the reader remembers, and contradictions are expensive.
